#1497. PREMIER LEAGUE LIVE: Xabi Alonso on Estevao's future with Chelsea, Roberto De Zerbi confirms James Maddison IS available for Tottenham - and Andoni Iraola on why Liverpool fans can dream

By KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER and JACK GAUGHAN and MATT BARLOW, FOOTBALL WRITER and LEWIS STEELE, FOOTBALL REPORTER

Published: 11:16 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 12:04 EDT, 30 October 2026

It's another action-packed Premier League weekend ahead and the managers have been having their say. Follow the best of it here with Daily Mail Sport...

Xabi Alonso insists there are zero talks being held inside Chelsea about allowing Estevao to leave in January on loan for game time, despite the Brazilian wonderkid struggling for chances to impress.

The 19-year-old stayed sat on the bench during Chelsea’s Carabao Cup shootout-loss to Liverpool on Wednesday. In the Premier League, he has been a late substitute six times, and unused twice. It has seen questions asked of Alonso’s plan for a highly-promising talent.

There is no shortage of rivals who would be willing to take Estevao temporarily. As revealed by Daily Mail Sport this week, multiple clubs at home and abroad are watching his situation.

Before Manchester United visit Stamford Bridge for Saturday’s lunchtime kick-off, Alonso was asked if they would consider finding him a temporary home in this winter window.

‘No, no, no,’ Alonso said. ‘No discussions about that. The season is long and there will be moments for everyone. It's a process for the team, for Este, for myself, but I'm sure that in the season, he will have his games, his minutes. We are still early in the season, but he will be there.

Xabi Alonso insists Chelsea are not discussing sending Estevao out on loan in January

‘It's not about attitude. It's been about the context of games, it's been about the start of the season, and he's a great guy. We are still in October and he will be important.’

Chelsea fans feel as if they have heard this before, and then watched as he failed to come on as a substitute in their Carabao Cup trip to Liverpool. The Blues signed Estevao from Palmeiras for £29million rising to £55m, and he is tied down to a deal lasting into the 2030s.

He had some magic moments in his first season, including scoring a stoppage-time winner against Liverpool in the Premier League and upstaging Lamine Yamal of Barcelona in the Champions League. His lack of opportunities this term has come as a surprise to supporters, who sang his name at Anfield, and led to speculation in Brazil that the youngster is frustrated.

‘It is no secret that all players want to be on the pitch,’ Alonso added. ‘When any of them haven't had enough minutes because of my decision, I have to take the responsibility for that, that they are not as happy as they could be. But everyone has to be ready because in any game, they could be important, they could be part of the team, and Este, his training and his attitude has been good.

‘We are back in Premier League mode, and that is, for me, the main competition for us this year, and it's a big one. It's one that we didn't have that much time to prepare, but it's really important after the last home game that we had (a 2-0 loss to Tottenham).’

Meanwhile, Maxence Lacroix has a hamstring injury which will sideline him for several weeks. Moises Caicedo and Pep Chavarria are fit to face United, but Jorrel Hato is injured. Goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez may return sooner than expected – perhaps even before the international break – as Alonso said: ‘In case he's ready to play, he will need a face mask probably.’

Enzo Maresca has shrugged off Fabian Hurzeler’s thirst for revenge and the suggestion that Manchester City were lucky to beat Brighton in midweek as the managers face off for the second time in four days.

City progressed to the Carabao Cup quarter finals via penalties on Wednesday night, with the Brighton boss insistent that they had created more than enough to knock out the holders.

Maresca’s side are looking to open up an eight-point gap with the Seagulls, who are flying high in third. Hurzeler has confessed to being a ‘bad loser’ but has moved on from Wednesday night.

‘Revenge is more about him [Hurzeler] and not about us,’ the Italian said. ‘This is what he said. Every manager can say something different.

Enzo Maresca does not feel that his side were merely lucky to beat Brighton in midweek

‘It depends on what you see with your eyes. But I respect what he said. Probably the reason why it's so difficult to play against them is because they are always front foot, aggressive and their attack is also very good.’

Instead of returning to the south coast between fixtures, Brighton have remained in Manchester through the week and trained locally on Friday.

Maresca added: ‘If you see the Premier League games they have played, they scored three, four, five goals against any team. That's why I was so happy after Wednesday.

‘It's because yes, they scored two goals, they had some more chances. We also created chances. But we knew that it was a difficult test for us. We dealt quite well.’

Meanwhile, Maresca has claimed that no City star has a guaranteed place in his team despite revealing that shootout hero deputy Geronimo Rulli is not rivalling Gianluigi Donnarumma for the No 1 spot.

‘I think one thing is to say that in this moment Gigio is plus 10 others,’ he said. ‘And another thing is to say undroppable. Yes, there are two different things. There is no player who is undroppable. But in this moment it is Gigio plus 10. In this moment I see it like this.’

Tottenham playmaker James Maddison is available for Saturday’s visit of Crystal Palace despite an injury scare during the victory at Chelsea.

Maddison sparked more fitness fears when he limped off in the 51st minute of Spurs’ 2-0 victory at Chelsea.

After Maddison had endured a slow start to the campaign with caution preached over his fitness following a May return from anterior cruciate ligament damage, his substitution last Saturday looked to be another setback.

But, ahead of the Palace game, Spurs boss Roberto De Zerbi said: 'James is available. This week he didn’t work like the other players, but for tomorrow he is available and he is a special player for us. A special player because of the character and he has unique characteristics.

James Maddison is available for Tottenham despite an injury scare suffered against Chelsea

'For James Maddison or the players who are coming from a long injury, they have to work more than the other players, but he has already four or five weeks he is working very hard and consistently.'

'So, I think it’s not a problem if he loses two days (training), but then we have to analyse if we take risk or not.

'If we take risk like Pedro Porro (against Aston Villa) or (Dejan) Kulusevski.

'We are lucky to have a big squad and it’s important to not take risk with new injuries.'

Andoni Iraola is happy for Liverpool fans to start dreaming of a Premier League title challenge ahead of Sunday’s clash with champions Arsenal, but insisted it is too early for him to start looking at the table.

Victory at Anfield would see Liverpool move to within three points of the Gunners as they look to continue a five-match winning run in all competitions, but Iraola said his focus remains on improvements in performances early in his reign.

'It is still October,' Iraola said. 'We have to take one game at a time and I always say the reference is more or less when we’ve played against each other once so halfway through the season. That’s when you can start to look at the standings.

'Right now, we are in a position where we need to improve and keep getting better.'

Liverpool supporters are able to dream of winning the Premier League - but Andoni Iraola isn't getting ahead of himself

But when asked if he welcomed the growing optimism amongst Liverpool supporters, Iraola added: 'For fans, it is good if they have expectations or they think we can win.'

Arsenal moved level with Manchester City at the top of the table last weekend with a 2-0 win over Everton, but were then on the wrong end of a huge cup upset in midweek, dumped out of the Carabao Cup when they were beaten on penalties by League Two Fleetwood.

'We know Arsenal and how good they are,' Iraola said. 'They have very good players, working a lot in synchronicity and we have to be ready for that challenge.

'It’s going to be a demanding game but we also trust our players, trust ourselves and in the good atmosphere we will for sure have on Sunday. I hope we will be at level to win this game.'

#1496. Hearts' Riccarton Three - 20 years on: The dressing-room rebellion that pulled back the curtain on the madness of Vladimir Romanov's Tynecastle reign and altered the club's trajectory for generations to come

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 13:23 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 13:51 EDT, 30 October 2026

Only those individuals who’d been living in a cave for a year or so would have believed that all was well in Hearts’ world when they recorded a storied triumph over Hibs at Hampden 20 years ago.

A thumping four-nil win in the Scottish Cup semi-final on April 2, 2006, came courtesy of Paul Hartley’s hat-trick with Edgaras Jankauskas also getting in on the act.

As if there wasn’t enough for the maroon hordes to gloat about that afternoon, Ivan Sproule and Gary Smith were sent off for Tony Mowbray’s team.

With lower-league Gretna awaiting Hearts in the final, it should have felt like the good times were rolling. And, to an extent, they were.

The following month, the Gorgie men would beat Aberdeen to wrap up second place in the top flight and earn a place in the Champions League qualifiers.

With Gretna beaten on penalties ten days later, an open-top bus wove its way through the streets of the capital with the old trophy being shown off.

Paul Hartley, Steven Pressley and Craig Gordon hit out at the club's ownership in October 2006

Only six months earlier, Hearts had thumped rivals Hibs in the Scottish Cup semi-final

But the jubilant scenes were a distortion of the real picture. Vladimir Romanov, the Russian-Lithuanian business leader, had bought into the club in February 2005, becoming the majority shareholder eight months later.

He promised lavish investment to establish Hearts not only as the dominant club in Scotland, but as a European force to be reckoned with. Many supporters wearing Cossack hats lapped it up and were disinclined to look beyond the bluff and the bluster — or examine the price tag.

Those with a stronger grasp of the situation saw Romanov for what he was: An erratic egomaniac who’d be ruinous for the club in the longer term. The only question was how quickly it would take for it all to come crashing down.

It hardly required inside knowledge to appreciate that his eccentricities were going to test the patience of Hearts supporters from the get-go.

Despite the side sitting on top of the league after winning their first eight games of the 2005-06 season, Romanov sacked manager George Burley with chief executive Phil Anderton also fired.

Graham Rix, a convicted sex offender, was hired as Burley’s replacement before Valdas Ivanauskas was brought in on an interim basis in March 2006.

The former FBK Kaunas coach was given the full-time gig after winning the cup only to be put on sick leave with stress at the start of the following season.

Ivanauskas’ temporary replacement, Eduard Malofeev, the sporting director, barely spoke a word of English.

The preposterous turnover of managers was just the tip of the iceberg, though.

Rumours abounded that Romanov was in charge of team selection and would often fax in his line-up before kick-off — a matter Rix subsequently confirmed as being true. Players who were fit were routinely shunted to the sidelines for no reason.

At the owner’s behest, a mysterious woman from Eastern Europe joined the physio department. Brandishing a divination stick, she claimed to be able to identify injuries before they happened.

Accustomed to training in mornings throughout their careers, players were told to report for work in evenings — with no explanation. One recalled a session in the dark winding down with a wheelbarrow race.

For many, the final straw arrived when Romanov started to deliver his own motivational team talks.

It may have had the veneer of a professional football club, but it was a circus.

‘The place was an absolute shambles,’ said defender and future Hearts manager Robbie Neilson.

Behind the scenes, the senior players spoke privately about their deepening concerns and contemplated going public with them.

After weeks of procrastinating, they agreed that doing nothing was no longer an option. And so, on October 27, 2006 — just six months after that routing of Hibs — ‘The Riccarton Three’ were born.

Vladimir Romanov promised  Hearts fans that the club would dominate Scottish football

Hearts had lost at home to Kilmarnock the previous Saturday and were scheduled to play Dunfermline at Tynecastle the following day.

The press pack which descended on the training ground inside Heriot-Watt University was larger than normal on that cold morning for a reason. They’d been tipped off that something remarkable would unfold. ‘Bring your popcorn,’ wrote a message from one of the squad.

With Malofeev elsewhere in the building and the rest of the squad sitting in a dressing room, at 12.02pm the doors to the seminar room opened and the show began.

In walked Hartley and Craig Gordon, stony-faced. Between them, beanie hat on his head and holding a piece of paper, was captain Steven Pressley.

By the time the trio took their place at a table filled with microphones, it was clear that the next few minutes were going to blow the doors off the club. This was a dressing room revolution.

‘It was the crossing of the Rubicon,’ said Neilson. ‘As soon as you did that there was no way back.’

Despite knowing that he was unleashing a verbal grenade, Pressley delivered the words with complete calmness.

‘Chaps, just to make you aware that I’m going to make a statement and we’ll answer no questions,’ he said.

‘This is a statement on behalf of a number of the players.

‘I have tried along with the coaching staff and certain colleagues to implement the correct values and disciplines, but it has become an impossible task.

‘There is only so much a coaching staff, a captain, and certain colleagues can do without the full backing, direction, and coherence of the manager and those running the football club.

‘While, publicly, I have expressed the need for unity behind the scenes, I have made my concerns abundantly clear.

‘The last two years have been very testing for the players. Together, we have faced a number of challenges and worked hard at retaining some degree of unity.

George Burley was sacked by Romanov despite winning his first eight top-flight fixtures

‘However, due to the circumstances, morale, understandably, is not good and there is significant unrest within the dressing room.’

Pressley didn’t mention Romanov by name but he didn’t have to. Hartley and Gordon remained silent throughout the address.

And with that, they rose and left, the hush in the room in sharp contrast with the chatter of a normal post-match conference.

Although even the most experienced journalists present were stunned at what they’d witnessed, they knew this much: Nothing would ever be the same again.

Predictably, the fallout was nuclear. Seething with what he saw on Sky Sports bulletins elsewhere in the building, Romanov addressed the entire squad and told them they’d be sold if they didn’t beat Dunfermline. The game ended 1-1.

The three actually started the match. Malofeev gave a strange post-match interview where he angrily insisted there were no problems at the club and the players could say what they liked because it was a ‘democracy’.

A short time later, the actions of Romanov would prove this was not the case.

Pressley was dropped for the game against Falkirk on November 13, was an unused substitute against Rangers on November 19, was then stripped of the captaincy and left the club on December 9 ahead of a January switch to Celtic.

Bizarrely, on the day he was told he’d no future at Hearts, he was offered the assistant manager’s job.

‘I was probably seen as the figurehead of the club at the time,’ he later said. ‘Everybody leaned on me to try and get things done, or get answers within the club.

‘The treatment of some individuals was horrendous. The honesty, the transparency, all the things that I think are really important in the foundations of a club — they were being disregarded.’

Hartley was a substitute against Falkirk and also moved to Parkhead in the January for £1.1million.

Gordon, the most valuable asset, was dropped for away games with Dundee United and Rangers, but remained at the club until he joined Sunderland for £9m in the summer.

As for Malofeev? Hearts didn’t win a game under him. He stayed in charge until Ivanauskas resumed his duties in late November.

With Hearts knocked out of the Scottish Cup by Dunfermline in the New Year, a game in which Gordon was a substitute, Ivanauskas then made way for Anatoliy Korobochka, the latest director of football to be promoted to head coach.

Despite an upturn in results, Aberdeen claimed third place ahead of the Tynecastle side. So much for winning the title.

While the Riccarton Three were never going to topple Romanov purely by speaking out against him, their actions ensured he was never viewed in the same light again by supporters.

Eduard Malofeev failed to win a single match during his short spell in the Tynecastle dugout

When Stephen Frail was made manager in January 2008, he was able to demand that he would have full responsibility for team selection.

By the following year, Romanov had ceded the day-to-day running to Campbell Ogilvie. His visits to Tynecastle became increasingly less frequent.

No doubt, this had much to do with what he knew was coming down the track.

Although Hearts did defeat Hibs 5-1 in the 2012 Scottish Cup Final, the recklessness of the Romanov years was catching up with the club.

The following year, the collapse of his Lithuania-based Ukio Bankas triggered Hearts calling in the administrators who uncovered debts of £15m. A 15-point deduction and relegation followed.

Were it not for the mobilisation of the Foundation of Hearts and the largesse of Ann Budge, one of Scotland’s great sporting institutions would have gone under.

From the rubble, the club was rebuilt. With Tony Bloom involved these days, there’s an authenticity to the current talk of Hearts winning major honours, perhaps even the title one day.

As their supporters prepare to march on Hampden again tomorrow to face Hibs, the part of all of those who stood on the right side of history won’t be forgotten.

#1494. Cup semi-final triumph over rivals Hearts would be the ideal moment to pick up first win as Hibs boss, admits Marink Reedijk

By ANTHONY BROWN, PRESS ASSOCIATION SPORT

Published: 14:00 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 14:01 EDT, 30 October 2026

Marink Reedijk is relishing a “special match” as he aims to belatedly ignite his Hibernian reign with victory over high-flying city rivals Hearts in Sunday’s Premier Sports Cup semi-final.

After three defeats and a draw in his first four matches in charge of the Hibs, the Dutchman goes into his first Edinburgh derby eyeing a first win since succeeding David Gray in September.

Hearts, third in the Premiership, have won all four previous meetings between the two Capital clubs at Hampden, including the 2012 Scottish Cup final, and Reedijk has been made well aware of the importance of the derby during his five weeks in Edinburgh.

“It’s a special match in several ways,” said Reedijk, who revealed that experienced striker Martin Boyle will return after illness.

“This is the type of match you look forward to because it’s not only the derby, it’s also a semi-final, and it’s one step away from a final, so that is a double way of excitement.

“You don’t need to ask anyone here about the derby because they will tell you, and this is also the beautiful thing about it. And we have someone in our staff (former Hibs player Guillaume Beuzelin) who experienced a few, and therefore, of course, he told us about it and he prepared us for what we can expect.”

Marink Reedijk is hoping to pick up his first win as Hibernian boss in the Premier Sports Cup

Hibs celebrate opening the scoring at St Mirren in midweek but had to settle for a 1-1 draw

After the joy of leading Beveren to an unbeaten title triumph in the Belgian second tier last season, Reedijk has found himself struggling for results during a testing start to his Hibs tenure.

“It is interesting because everybody recognises last year with Beveren, but in the beginning at Beveren, we had the same sort of spells,” he said.

“The only thing which is different is that I had a start where we had a pre-season, and you could already put some things in place (in friendlies), and here I started immediately with competitive matches.

“But I have been in these situations as well with Beveren, and we focused on the things we did, and trusted the way we did it, and focused on not only the results.

“I know the results are important, but if the result is not there, is the performance there? And if the performance is there, then it’s a matter of time.

“The performances are getting better and better and better, and therefore, like in Beveren, I think if you keep on progressing, the results will come.”

#1493. Bloodthirsty Brighton feast on rattled Arsenal

Overpowered and overrun, Arsenal were subjected to the sort of gruelling treatment they usually inflict on their opponents. Mikel Arteta’s side did not look anything like Premier League champions here, as Brighton and Hove Albion produced a stunning performance full of swarming energy and breathless bravery.

In the biggest test of their season so far, Arsenal fell woefully short of the standards they have set themselves over the past few campaigns. This sort of thing simply does not happen to Arteta’s side. Well, it did not happen. Not before this monstering on the south coast, where the Brighton fans were whipped into a frenzy by the brilliance of Fabian Hürzeler’s players.

Brighton were everything that Arsenal are expected to be: aggressive, inventive and dominant across the field. They even scored with a set-piece, as one of Arsenal’s great strengths became a sudden weakness. Everywhere Arteta looked, the foundational truths of his team were being shaken by a Brighton storm. It was their first defeat by a three-goal margin since May 2023, also against Brighton.

Remarkably, this is now the third consecutive season in which Brighton have beaten the reigning Premier League champions. They are rarely happier than when they are on the hunt against more illustrious opponents, working as a team to snap at heels and then attacking in numbers. They are known as the Seagulls, but they played more like a pack of bloodthirsty wolves. The ferocity of their off-the-ball work, especially in the first half, was extraordinary.

Not for a long time have Arsenal been as rattled as they were here. David Raya misplaced passes, Gabriel Magalhães lost duels and Bruno Guimarães chased the ball in vain. It was Brighton’s Pascal Gross, rather than Arsenal’s Martin Odegaard, who shaped the game in midfield. It was Brighton’s Charalampos Kostoulas, rather than Arsenal’s Kai Havertz, who offered incisive class in attack.

Gross and Kostoulas both struck from range in a one-sided first half, before Chema Andrés added the third after the break. At half-time, Arteta had sprinted down the tunnel towards the dressing room. Whatever messages he gave to his players, they either did not sink in or did not work. By the end, Arsenal were lucky the scoreline was not even more humiliating.

Arteta’s players had come through some tricky assignments in winning their first seven matches of this season, but this was their toughest test yet and they failed it badly. They did not handle the emotions of the occasion particularly well, either: in stoppage time, a frustrated Declan Rice kicked out at Malick Yalcouyé. He was perhaps fortunate to avoid a red card.

It was the first time that Rice and Guimarães had started alongside each other for Arsenal and it quickly became clear that their £180m partnership will need some work. Arsenal would have hoped their experience in the Premier League would allow for an instant connection but, evidently, that is not the case. Guimarães was hooked after 60 minutes, but might easily have been removed at the break.

Both managers had a similar assessment of the match and how it was won: Brighton did the basics far better than Arsenal. “How we wanted to approach this game was getting into it through small wins,” Hürzeler said. “Everyone speaks about a goal or chance as a win, but a small win can be the first throw-in, the first corner, win the first header, win the first tackle. These small things. If you win these small steps, and celebrate them as a win, then you can gain bigger and bigger wins.”

It was typical of Brighton that one of their new signings produced an excellent performance in midfield. Andrés, a 21-year-old Spaniard signed from Stuttgart at the end of the transfer window, looks to be the latest gem identified by their data-led recruitment model. No one inside the Amex Stadium was thinking about Carlos Baleba, sold to Manchester United, when Andrés made his tackles and won his headers.

Another new signing, centre-back Luka Vuskovic, was similarly impressive at the back. Signed for £46m from Tottenham Hotspur, Vuskovic looks more than capable of going to the top of the game.

This was perhaps the first occasion this season in which Arsenal missed William Saliba, the injured centre-back who has been so fundamental to their success in recent years. The Frenchman can always be relied on to provide calmness and composure at the back, even under intense pressure. Without him, Arsenal were uncharacteristically jittery.

“The amount of technical errors we did in our own half...” Arteta bemoaned. “We didn’t respect any principle of play that you have to get out of those man-to-man situations. That put us always on the back foot.”

Gross, who at 35 is playing as well as ever, opened the scoring with a low shot from range after 31 minutes. Kostoulas then struck the second, from a similar distance, after some end-to-end action resulted in Arsenal’s midfield and defence melting away. The third was the most simple, as Andrés headed in at the back post from an inswinging corner.

Arsenal did have some chances, with Havertz missing the best of them, but there was never a sense that Brighton were vulnerable. The pressure on the home side was never sustained. For Arteta, who now has an extended international break in which to ruminate on this defeat, it all made for an unfamiliar and unexpected pain.

Mikel Arteta said his Arsenal players failed to “respect the game” as their perfect start to the season was ended in stunning style by a brilliant Brighton performance.

Arsenal’s capitulation on the south coast led to their first defeat of the campaign and Arteta admitted that Brighton had a different “edge” and “bite” throughout the match. The Arsenal manager also said the 3-0 loss represented a “big lesson” for his players.

“There are certain basics you need to accomplish in football, especially in the Premier League, that we were very far from,” Arteta said. “From the first throw-in you could sense it, it was so clear.

“It was a really disappointing result and performance. Brighton were another gear up from us. We were extremely poor technically and were not respecting the game.

“It is not going to take away what the team has done in the last six or seven weeks since coming back from the World Cup. What we have done and the way we have competed, and the amount of games we have won, has been remarkable. But this is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level.”

Arteta added that his team did not “respect the principles of play” that were required against Brighton’s intense pressing, and also said his players were guilty of numerous technical errors.

“Credit to Brighton for what they have done because they have overcome us and they had another edge,” Arteta said. “There are a lot of moments when the ball is 50/50 and it changes hands and most of the time it was for them.”

Brighton are the Premier League’s top scorers this season with 16 goals in five matches so far, and this emphatic victory took them up to third place in the table.

“It was a special win,” Fabian Hürzeler, the Brighton head coach, said. “Not only because we played the best team in England but because of the performance. I am really proud of my team. It’s always important to enjoy these moments. We were horrible to play against. My players really trust each other on the pitch.”

Two things, one give credit to them. In the manner that they played and committed to every single action. We were below the standards that are required for us but in the Premier League as well.

When you miss chances like we did it becomes impossible. I want to congratulate Brighton for what they’ve done. It’s a big lesson for us to learn. If I have to describe how the team has played and competed in the last six or seven weeks, has been expectational but today has been a big lesson.

A very disappointing result and performance. Full credit to Brighton the manner they went about the game, they were a different gear from us. We didn’t do the basics right for long periods, especially in the first half. We didn’t win enough duels, and any second balls and that stretches you.

We were poor technically when we had the ball in our own half, we didn’t apply the principles that you need against a team that wants to press you man to man.

Arteta: "There are certain basics that you need to accomplish in the Premier League that we were very far from. The amount of technical errors we did... we didn't respect any principle of play. We were always on the back foot. They had another edge."

Beating the current champions and maybe the best team in England is something special. The result is nice but the performance is what makes it special, the boys showed real courage, real intensity and they were horrible to play against because we did the basics right.

Intensity, intensity, winning the personal duels...we have to have the belief to compete with the best teams in the league. My players really trust each other on the pitch. If one player is out then another can replace him.

Overall we wanted to be really good in every phase. We needed to be at the highest level. We go game by game. After the international break we have a lot of games. After wins like this we have to stay humble and understand why we had this win. We have to keep on going.

I thought we showed great intensity, waited for mistakes and punished Arsenal. It was a strong performance, a very complete performance.

We won the ball high up and attacked really fast. After the last two wins we are full of confidence and wanted to finish really strong before the international break.

I feel really good. I can’t complain. I just try to help the team when I can. I really enjoy life in Brighton, I’m loving it.

I know after the international break we play every three days and a lot of the lads are not used to that. It will be tough. I hope we can compete. We have a big squad this season.

Everton up to fifth but they made hard work of that against Ipswich’s 10 men, but Thierno Barry’s goal proves the difference. Barry unfortunate that his second did not stand because of a contentious offside check.

A short, intricate pass to Willock inside the box and then a surging, twisting run from the halfway line and the perfectly timed pass to Lewis Hall who stroked a first time shot into the bottom corner.

Hull have been outfought so far which is precisely the response Newcastle’s manager had demanded.

The home team are pressing high and all over Arsenal in the early stages. Raya has just made a save to deny Kostoulas.

The perfect start for Newcastle with all their injuries: Joe Willock has put the home side in a strong position against Hull with a clean strike inside three minutes.

We are under way at the Amex, St James’ Park and the Hill Dickinson.

It has been a term tossed around liberally at Newcastle United since Matthias Jaissle arrived as manager, but what does “vertical football” actually mean?

It is the new buzzword in football analysis, the latest fashionable phrase to describe a “new” style of football, and it has been referenced multiple times by both Jaissle and Ross Wilson, the sporting director, since the German coach’s appointment last month.

For some of us of a certain age, vertical football just seems like clever new terminology to describe an old idea.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of today’s Premier League 3pm kick-offs, with Brighton vs Arsenal the pick of the three matches.

Brighton are the league’s top goalscorers so far this season and have amassed the most expected goals, but the champions have the league’s best defence and are seeking five wins from five to start their title defence. There is some welcome needle between Fabian Hurzeler and Mikel Arteta, dating back to Declan Rice’s contentious second yellow for delaying the restart two years ago, as well as the Brighton manager’s comments about Arsenal’s style of play in March.

That 1-0 Arsenal victory at the Amex coincided with Man City dropping points at home to Nottingham Forest on a pivotal night in the title race. Bukayo Saka scored a deflected shot in the ninth minute, and Arsenal held on from there in an ugly but resolute display.

With Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz fit and firing, as well as the introduction of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes to Arteta’s midfield stable, Arsenal’s football has been more technical and enterprising so far this season. Brighton are one of the few teams who will back themselves to play through Arsenal’s press, which should make for an absorbing game.

Elsewhere, Newcastle are looking to bounce back from their shellacking at Leeds at home to surprise package Hull City. Mattias Jaissle’s team took four points from Liverpool and Spurs but there is concern about how many shots they are conceding. Hull remain unbeaten and continue to confound the odds and underlying data, but that surely cannot last forever.

Everton are also one of the division’s unbeaten teams, but will be targeting three points from a home game against Ipswich after three consecutive draws. Ipswich are sitting comfortably on six points after their win at Crystal Palace, though they did have the extra man for the majority at Selhurst Park.

#1492. Under-fire Dons boss Stephen Robinson isn't seeking any assurances from club chiefs over his job

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 13:48 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 14:02 EDT, 30 October 2026

Aberdeen boss Stephen Robinson insists he has not sought any assurances over his position from chairman Dave Cormack despite a woeful run of form.

A 1-0 home defeat to Falkirk on Wednesday night left the Dons slumped in ninth position in the Premiership table with just one win in their last five matches.

A section of the Pittodrie crowd turned on Robinson and his players and booed them off the pitch after another insipid display.

Heading into today’s Premier Sports Cup semi-final clash with Rangers at Hampden, there have been some suggestions that Robinson’s position could be under serious threat.

Whilst accepting the criticism from fans, the under-fire boss insisted it has been business as usual in terms of his conversations with Cormack and new chief executive Adrian Bevington.

‘No, I’m not seeking any assurances,’ said Robinson. ‘I have just had my normal conversations.

Under-fire Dons boss Robinson is not seeking assurances from club hierarchy over his job

‘I speak to the chairman once a week and I speak to Adrian once a week. That’s no different than any other week.

‘So, no, there’s been nothing different. We know the results over the last couple of weeks haven’t been good enough.

‘No one is getting away from that fact and ultimately we deserve the criticism we got. I deserve the criticism, I don’t hide behind that. And I don’t try to throw players under the bus.

‘The players know it needs to be better and they are all in that together. There are no factions, there are no people going off on their own, everyone wants to turn that around.

‘I know given time, this can be very successful. But I also live in the real world. You need to get results that give yourself longevity.

‘Certainly, everybody wants time, but you don’t get given time in football. We’re all well aware of that and results are what dictates that. And what a place to start at Hampden.’

Ahead of this evening’s clash at Hampden, Robinson believes it will be the perfect opportunity for Aberdeen to turn their season around if they can beat Rangers.

Robinson was typically animated during a match that saw his team lose 1-0 to Falkirk

He also claimed that all of the pressure will be on Rangers, given the expectation on them to beat an Aberdeen side who have toiled for much of the season.

‘You haven’t got time to feel sorry for yourself, if there is a moment to put it right a semi final at Hampden is that time,’ he added.

‘As a footballer you always get another chance, sometimes as a manager you don’t and what a chance it is to go to Hampden, a full house with a big support with us. It is certainly the right place to do it and we believe we can.

‘Every semi-final that I’ve been in with Motherwell and St Mirren, we were not expected to win. So I know how to motivate teams and the staff know how to get teams to believe.

‘It’s certainly an opportunity. All the pressure will be on Rangers, and the expectation will be on Rangers.’

Earlier this week, Rangers boss Derek McInnes, who spent eight years with the Dons, backed Robinson to succeed at Pittodrie if he is given time to turn it around.

‘Until you are in this position, you don’t realise how difficult things are and the parameters you have to work under, Derek obviously does,’ added Robinson.

‘I have nothing but total respect for him. He is one of the top managers in the country. Everybody wants time but you don’t get given time in football, we are all well aware of that and results are what dictates that.

‘We face a really good Rangers side. Derek’s built a really good squad, a really big, athletic, strong squad. We are coming up against a team that are in form, a team that are winning football matches.

‘We know that we have to be better than what we are. I’ve been to semi-finals before and I’ve always been the underdog. No doubt that would be exactly the same, rightly. It’s up to us to turn that around.’

Robinson's under-performing Dons team are languishing ninth in Premiership table

On team news, Robinson added: ‘We’ve got a problem at the back, of course, that’s been well documented, with Lewis Mayo, Mats Knoester and Dan Happe. Dan is suspended, but he’s actually ill as well, so he’s got the virus.

‘Kristers Tobers has had a little bit of a setback. There’s a little bit of swelling on his knee, so he won’t be available for selection tomorrow. Chris Cadden won’t be available tomorrow either.

‘We haven’t had to seek our troubles, but again, as I always say, somebody’s misfortune is somebody else’s opportunity.

‘It’s a chance for people who maybe haven’t had opportunities, or people who haven’t been fit, to stand up and be counted. As I said, there’s no better stage than Hampden to do that.

‘It’s a mild hamstring injury (Cadden’s injury). We’re hoping he could be fit for the Hibs game, but at this early stage, it’s still very hard to say. We just know he won’t be available with the quick turnaround for Saturday.’

#1491. Guys like Makhanya and Sterling should feel welcome to speak the truth more often if Rangers are to finally throw off their serial losers tag

Published: 14:15 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 15:19 EDT, 30 October 2026

Olwethu Makhanya is shaping up to be everything Rangers needed in their search for defensive reinforcements in the summer.

A solid presence at the back, a young and hungry talent very much on the up and a leader with real personality.

If it didn’t look so likely that someone will come in before long and offer the Ibrox board the chance to make a healthy profit on the £3million they paid to Philadelphia Union for the 22-year-old, you’d put him down as a nailed-on future captain.

He’s helping set the standards required if Rangers are to overhaul arch-rivals Celtic in the title race and was absolutely spot-on after rescuing an ill-deserved point with a late equaliser at Tynecastle on Wednesday when bemoaning a lack of character at the start of the second half and the fact Hearts worked harder and showed more desire.

It’s the kind of honesty many Ibrox sides of recent years have needed. A public kick up the backside for underperforming team-mates, the footballing equivalent of getting the whip out and a necessary form of assurance for frustrated supporters that there is at least someone inside the dressing room who feels the way they feel, who wants what they want.

It’s why it is to be hoped that manager Derek McInnes’ remarks the morning after were not some attempt to gently slap down the South African.

Defender Olwethu Makhanya questioned the character of this Rangers squad midweek

McInnes, of course, is entitled to his own opinion about the reserves of character within his squad. Maybe he did disagree with Makhanya’s version of events, or his questioning of the side’s resilience.

Alternative viewpoints delivered respectfully are fine. More than fine. They are a sign of a healthy workplace.

It just felt like it was all skirting a little too close to a chastisement of the big centre-back’s comments.

And whether that was the intention or not, being seen to chastise a player whose sentiments are clearly coming from the right place, from a burning desire to make a club with one league crown in 15 years be successful again, is not necessarily the right course of action to take.

It happened, if you remember, with Dujon Sterling back in Philippe Clement’s first season as boss when an April collapse that involved a home draw with Celtic, a 3-2 loss at Ross County and a stalemate at Dundee pretty much killed off hopes of lifting the title.

‘We owe ourselves a performance… because we have been s**t the past three games,’ said Sterling in the aftermath at Dens Park. ‘We are fighting for a title and the way we are playing, it is as if we are not playing for anything. It’s like the season is dead and it is a dead-rubber game.’

It felt like a cry from the heart, a desperate plea to those around him to breathe life into a dying campaign. It was a truth that had to be told.

Clement, meanwhile, was already well on the way to losing the plot at that point, claiming his side were ‘moral winners’ after snatching that draw with Celtic thanks to a late goal and insisting that he was happy his side ‘bossed it’ at Dens.

Criticising Sterling afterwards just made him look even more like he didn’t get it, had lost all sight of what being at Rangers — or any club that has to win at all costs — was about.

‘It’s the words of a player who is disappointed because we lost points and maybe lacks a bit of experience in that way,’ stated the Belgian waffler. ‘That’s things for young players to learn and become better in. It’s more talking out of frustration.’

Manager Derek McInnes disagreed with Makhanya's comments following the Hearts game

That’s the standard response from football persons, of course. The whole business, for some time, has revolved around young players having it battered into them that it’s better to say nothing, to drone on dead-eyed through interviews, bat everything away, put their personality on the bonfire, ‘don’t get too up or too down’.

It’s nonsense, though. McInnes honed his trade in a Nine-In-A-Row Rangers dressing room full of huge characters who built unbreakable bonds while still being able to dig each other out, demand more, be confrontational.

Sure, it happened more behind doors than in the public gaze, but things are different now from the way they were 30 years ago. Social media has changed the landscape so drastically. Fan narratives do drive boardroom decisions and that has arguably been clearer at Ibrox in recent times than anywhere.

There’s a concern still living just under the surface among a large number of Rangers fans that there is an ingrained loser mentality at their club and plenty of evidence to back that up.

Admittedly, the playing staff has changed drastically since then, but it is impossible to forget Billy Dodds reflecting on his time as a first-team coach for interim boss Barry Ferguson and talking about how 70 per cent of signings had been wrong and that the dressing room had a number of weak characters who couldn’t handle adversity.

Even before Danny Rohl left for Red Bull Salzburg last season, he talked about players being ‘too lazy to recover’ in key moments. He also spoke about how some of the squad were ‘very quiet’ when he first took over.

Supporters of Rangers, treated to some amount of failure and in-house claptrap over the last decade or more, need to see evidence that those on the field care the way they do.

The kind of frank analysis delivered by Makhanya — in a calm and considered way, it should be said — need not be the negative so many inside football are programmed to think.

If anything, seeing guys wear their hearts on their sleeve can serve to strengthen the relationship between fans and their favourites in difficult times.

The modern-day audience have had enough of failing players promising to learn lessons and move on. At outfits judged on league titles and facing pressure to win every week, learning lessons is the last thing on the agenda. You really ought to know what needs done by that stage.

Rangers have drawn two of their last three and currently trail leaders Celtic by four points

Punters want to see the real people behind the branding, measure their minerals. And we’re on about more than just those cringeworthy features on club TV where players quiz each other on whether they prefer Jaffa Cakes or KitKats while playing a game of ping-pong. It’s showing a bit of what’s really inside, being properly authentic, that resonates.

In fairness to McInnes, his messaging as Rangers boss has generally been good so far. He didn’t shy away from the paucity of those performances in losing in Europe to Jagiellonia Bialystok and Jablonec.

He hasn’t indulged in deflection. He confronted the speculation that was already beginning to swirl about his future after that Jablonec catastrophe, handled it well and steered the side to safer ground with two excellent back-to-back wins against Celtic.

He has been honest and upfront and entirely understanding of the expectations that rest upon his shoulders.

His team is still guilty of switching off in games. Centre-back Manny Fernandez, although the manager must back him publicly, is the epitome of that.

His players still have to show they can be consistent enough to prevail against a Celtic side that is most definitely there for the taking. They need to keep the pedal to the metal and to deliver 90-minute performances or, at least, maintain control throughout.

It is a squad light on trophies on the CV and with a number of younger players. It is going to need regular reminders as this race plays out.

If Makhanya or Sterling or anyone else want to take it upon themselves to put those reminders out there, it shouldn’t be regarded as a bad thing. And it definitely shouldn’t be discouraged.

#1490. Spitting row mars feisty Millwall-West Ham clash

A spitting row marred the 100th Millwall-West Ham United derby and first for 14 years.

Taty Castellanos was facing trial by video after being accused of spitting on Filip Marschall during Saturday’s febrile 2-2 draw at the Den.

Millwall goalkeeper Marschall made the allegation to referee Paul Tierney, who was expected to include it in an official report that would then be assessed by the Football Association.

Spitting on an opponent is punishable with a six-match ban.

Telegraph Sport has been told West Ham striker Castellanos denies he spat on Marschall and believes he will be vindicated by video footage of the incident.

Lying little prick. Taty didn't spit ❌ pic.twitter.com/5vYxOtKqof

Millwall manager Alex Neil said after the game that fourth official Lewis Smith had confirmed a spitting accusation had been made.

Asked if he had spoken to Marschall about the claim, Neil replied: “I haven’t asked him about it. But it’s like anything else; I’m sure there’ll be footage of it, or not of it, if it didn’t happen.

“I’d be extremely surprised if Fil’s made an accusation and nothing’s happened. But that’s not really for me to deal with; I’m sure the authorities will deal with that.”

West Ham manager Nuno Espírito Santo said: “I’m aware of the allegation. I didn’t see the image; I didn’t speak with Taty. I cannot go much further on that.”

He added: “I’m going to try to look at the images.”

There were also ugly scenes at full time when players had to be separated at the end of a derby that had been at the centre of an unprecedented police operation.

There were six arrests as of 4pm on Saturday for offences including tailgating, assault on a police officer and entering or attempting to enter a stadium while intoxicated.

Eleven men were also arrested at around 7.15pm on Friday on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage.

The group, believed to be Millwall fans, were detained in the vicinity of a known West Ham supporters’ pub in Stratford.

Saturday’s fixture was subject to a five-mile dispersal zone, the largest ever for a football match in London, with officers granted special powers to stop and search people and vehicles without reasonable suspicion and to remove anyone causing disorder.

Riot police were out in force outside the ground, with dog units and mounted officers among 400 personnel deployed – roughly quadruple the usual number for a game there.

Those and other measures – including the use of live facial recognition, a strict segregation policy and a 12.30pm kick-off to minimise supporters’ pre-match drinking time – prevented a repeat of the kind of violence which has marred this fixture down the years.

West Ham fans also received a police escort to a game that saw both sets of supporters hurl foul-mouthed insults at each other throughout.

Plans to keep rival spectators apart after the match were reportedly tested by scuffles that broke out as people left the ground.

If the police were ready for a fight before the game, West Ham’s players were not as Millwall tore into them from the first whistle and dominated a first half in which they scored twice through Caleb Taylor and Camiel Neghli and hit the crossbar through a stunning 35-yard strike by Mark Sykes.

MILLWALL STRIKE FIRST 🔥Caleb Taylor fires the Lions in front! pic.twitter.com/pPffYZD73D

However, the Championship leaders finally turned up in the second half and pulled a goal back through Mohamadou Kanté before Konstantinos Mavropanos equalised with just 10 minutes to go.

ALL SQUARE at the Den 🙌West Ham equalise in the 80th minute.Everything to play for with just 10 minutes remaining 👀 pic.twitter.com/qQmDlyuQmT

That was only after Marschall gestured that he had been spat at by Castellanos following a melee in the penalty area.

Tierney did, though, brandish a red card when Kanté pulled back Kyrell Lisbie as the substitute robbed him of the ball on the halfway line and ran clean through on goal.

The foul denied Lisbie the chance to hand Millwall their first win over their bitter rivals for 22 years, much to the frustration of fans who had roared them on from first whistle to last.

RED CARD 🟥West Ham are down to ten men, after Kante was sent off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity. pic.twitter.com/jRlVwLNiOs

Describing the atmosphere as “absolutely the best by far” since he joined the club almost two years ago, Neil said: “I told the players prior to the game that this game’s a real rarity and, as a player and as a manager, it’s a privilege to be part of it.”

"The fans are up for it, the players are up for it" 💪🏼Lyndon Dykes looks ahead to today's match, and reflects on his strong start to life as a Millwall player.Watch it LIVE on ITV1 🎥 pic.twitter.com/V9nPzbh3Ob

Kevin Nolan, West Ham’s captain, was sent off early but his team-mates defied the odds to win 2-1 thanks to goals from Carlton Cole and Winston Reid either side of a stunning Liam Trotter strike.

In Millwall’s match-day squad that day were… Harry Kane and Ryan Mason.

The last time West Ham and Millwall met, Harry Kane was a Millwall player 😅This is how that game in 2012 played out 👇 pic.twitter.com/OhtVx3caCP

This rivalry was forged in different circumstances from most derby confrontations. There is none of the religious divide of Celtic and Rangers, or the politics of Barcelona against Real Madrid, or the spat over title-winning superiority of Manchester United and Liverpool. This is a tale of proximity, an internecine feud.

“There’s no politics, no nationality, nothing like that,” says Nick Hart, who hosts the weekly podcast Achtung! Millwall. “We’re very similar people, from the same backgrounds, same communities. But it’s in the Millwall supporter’s DNA for West Ham to be the ultimate rivals. Nobody else comes into the equation. You’re brought up on this stuff. It’s your history.”

Though possibly more recent history than might be suggested by the two clubs’ early foundations. The hostility that West Ham will face at the Den is no more about dockland rivalry, north-south London disputes or strike-breaking than the animosity when Manchester United visit Anfield is caused by the building of the Manchester Ship Canal.

“It really is about the hooligan era,” says a podcaster who uses the pseudonym Former West Ham Employee on the West Ham Way podcast. “The two clubs had notorious fanbases. And they grated. It came about through vying to be the No 1, battling to see who had the hardest mob. Whenever we’ve played – or even been in close proximity – things have happened.”

Jake Cooper on making the 500th appearance of his career against West Ham today! 👏Watch all the action with NOW! https://t.co/56JOZ0NPsr pic.twitter.com/lTzXOwXhxd

There have only been 18 meetings between these fierce rivals since the Second World War, but absence has certainly not made the heart grow fonder. Here are some of the feud’s most notable flashpoints.

At the 1972 testimonial in honour of Harry Cripps – the renowned Millwall hard man – police horses were sent on to the pitch after West Ham supporters entered the home section at The Den. Fighting spilt over into the streets surrounding the ground.

An even bleaker turn came in 1976, when Millwall fan Ian Pratt died in a skirmish with West Ham fans at New Cross station that led to his fall under a train.

Leaflets were later handed out in the Den’s Cold Blow Lane end with a grainy picture of Pratt and a declaration in capital letters: “A West Ham fan must die next week to avenge him.”

Millwall plundered four goals on Mothering Sunday in 2004 as Tim Cahill’s double helped them to a 4-1 victory over West Ham at the Den in an incident-filled derby.

The hosts missed a penalty and had another saved by Stephen Bywater, who was later sent off. Violence followed in the stands and the match was named “The Mothers’ Day Massacre”.

Mother's Day Massacre ⏮️A 4-1 victory over The Hammers back in 2004. pic.twitter.com/TLi7xkcVJG

A hundred West Ham and Millwall supporters clashed during a screening of England’s 2006 World Cup match against Paraguay in Canada Square, which led to 16 injuries and one hospitalisation.

The clubs’ League Cup meeting in 2009 at Upton Park was listed as Category Five by police, the most serious risk of violence, and resulted in a Millwall supporter being stabbed in Priory Road, near the ground.

The Metropolitan Police said that “planned” scuffles, which involved more than 100 fans, appeared to have been caused by fans without tickets to the game.

Just spotted one Millwall fan outside the ground in blue boxing gloves. He is also wearing what appear to be slippers, so not sure what that means…

Nuno Espirito Santo has only been through the door at West Ham for a matter of months, but he insisted he is fully aware of the significance of today’s fixture.

When asked about his perception of the rivalry, Nuno said: “Since the fixture list came out, this date has been [important], for both of the clubs. It’s special, special game. We look forward to go and compete against a good team.

“It’s a different game from all of the other games, it’s a special game, the atmosphere will be different… Steve [Potts, first-team coach and former West Ham player] has been involved in many of these games, he’s constantly speaking about how special it is for West Ham fans, so we have a lot of information and we are fully aware of the importance of the game.

On potential unrest between fans and the significant police presence, Nuno added: “What we want most is that everything goes well, both fans supporting their teams and no conflict. We have people inside the club who are taking care of that. We have to focus on our tasks.”

The gaffer on tomorrow's fixture ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/6NG6t4t4Fn

#westham on the way to #millwall via #london bridge #whufc #coyi pic.twitter.com/HrWgJ6UtJY

Riot police are very much out in force outside The Den today for the 100th competitive derby between Millwall and West Ham United and first for 14 years. Dog units and mounted officers can been seen patrolling the perimeter of the ground, with 400 personnel deployed to stop violence erupting between rival fans – roughly quadruple the usual number for a fixture here. There has been no sign of any trouble with less than an hour to go before kick-off.

The game has been scheduled for 12.30pm to minimise supporters’ pre-match drinking time, although plenty of fans have been nursing pints before entering the ground. Other measures in place include the use of live facial recognition cameras, while a dispersal order has been imposed covering a large area around the stadium. Police were also planning to escort West Ham fans from South Bermondsey station, which will also be closed to home supporters for up to an hour after full-time. The latter measure has been deemed safer than holding the 1,800 away fans back following the game.

The Millwall-West Ham derby is one of the most notorious in English football and was most recently marred by serious violence when the sides met at Upton Park for a League Cup tie back in 2009. One man was stabbed and the match itself was interrupted on three occasions by fans invading the pitch.

Alex Neil switches out goalkeeper Max Crocombe for Filip Marschall and names the returning Mathis Servais, Kyrell Lisbie and Alfie Doughty on the bench.

Alex Neil names his Lions XI 👊 pic.twitter.com/MP0N9wMatG

Just the one change from the league leaders’ last league match as Kyle Walker-Peters comes in for the injured Joel Veltman.

Today's teamsheet 📋 pic.twitter.com/EmrxYRhsPd

"We have to quiet them down" 🤫West Ham captain Jarrod Bowen is expecting a hostile atmosphere at The Den today 🗣️Watch all the action with NOW! https://t.co/56JOZ0NPsr pic.twitter.com/9tp2225Rq8

The Metropolitan Police will have 400 officers on the streets of east London for this match – about four times the norm for a Championship fixture – and it has enforced a Section 35 dispersal order in the area highlighted on the map below.

A Section 35 order authorises a Police Constable and a Police Community Support Officer in uniform to “exclude a person from an area for a period of up to 48 hours with an Inspector’s authority”.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of the highly anticipated Championship match between Millwall and West Ham United as the two clubs meet officially for the 100th time. This fixture has not been staged since 2012, and the intervening 14 years have done little to temper the ill-feeling between their passionate supporters, who will be anxious to claim bragging rights over their Dockers Derby rivals. The Metropolitan Police have placed a Section 35 dispersal order in the area surrounding The Den and will deploy 400 officers on the streets of east London.

Acrimony between the two clubs has existed since the late 19th century when Millwall Athletic, originally Rovers, battled it out against Thames Ironworks, later renamed West Ham at the Athletic and Memorial Grounds. Sixty of the two clubs’ 99 meetings came between 1899 and 1915, and while they played just seven times between 1946 and 1987, the irregularity of the game only added to its mystique, which has often spilt over into the ugly.

Both head coaches spoke at length about the significance of today’s match, with Alex Neil, in the Millwall dugout, describing it as an encounter that means “absolutely everything” but imploring his players to keep “cool heads”. His counterpart Nuno Espírito Santo revealed that he had been well advised about the game’s importance by Steve Potts, his first-team coach and former West Ham player.

Since the club’s last meeting in 2012, West Ham have ascended into the Premier League, moved into the London Stadium and won the Uefa Conference League, only falling back into England’s second tier last summer where Millwall have remained for all but two seasons. The Lions brushed maddeningly close to promotion in their last campaign as they pushed for an automatic spot until the very last weekend of the regular season before falling to Hull City in the play-off semi-finals.

Much of the pre-match talk will centre on the clubs’ long-standing rivalry, but beneath the bile and belligerence is an intriguing football match between two sides. Millwall are missing 11 first-team players and face the daunting task of stopping a West Ham side who have found their feet in the Championship, scoring 16 goals in their last four league matches.

#1489. 'We're not in Disneyland!': Mikel Arteta fires warning at Arsenal wonderboy Max Dowman, 16, after red card - and says it's not his first offence... as he admits Fleetwood loss left him 'p***ed off'

Published: 10:24 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 15:26 EDT, 30 October 2026

Mikel Arteta has told 16-year-old Max Dowman 'we are not in Disneyland' as he insists his age does not give him a free pass following his red card against Fleetwood.

Dowman was sent off in the 86th minute of Arsenal's shock Carabao Cup defeat by Fleetwood on Tuesday after kicking out in retaliation to a challenge by Harrison Neal.

It was the second time he has been sent off this this month, having also seen red while representing England's Under-19s.

After the club's appeal was rejected by the FA, Dowman will now miss Arsenal's Premier League matches against Liverpool, Hull City and Newcastle.

As the teenager left the field, manager Mikel Arteta gave him a scathing look and uttered a few words to the attacker, understood to be: 'Get to the changing room, Max.'

And on Friday he suggested Dowman should have kept his cool under provocation.

Arsenal star Max Dowman (second from right) looks shocked after the referee shows him a red card at Fleetwood Town

Manager Mikel Arteta has words with the distraught youngster as he leaves the field

Arteta said: ‘I haven't seen the reaction to my reaction. But you have to understand the context, the relationship that I have with him and what we discussed just before we went out.

‘You want to always have the best reaction, the beautiful one. But do you want to see the reaction of his team-mates when they have to play with the 10 men, you want to see that? What do you expect?

‘I don't know. Or the England (Under 16) ones, they are his age, 16, the same. What is their reaction?

‘Whether it’s right or wrong, that's the reaction. And the reaction when I don't win, you know what is? I’m p***** off big time.

‘We have to be ready for that, this is the environment and this is the reality. Otherwise we are in Disneyland. We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League at this level.

‘We look after him so much that you cannot imagine, and at the same time we are going to be demanding that anybody continues to earn the right to play. Otherwise what are the rest of the boys going to tell me? It needs to be fair, that's all.’

He further explained that his touchline reaction was borne out of frustration having told Dowman to not react to such a scenario before the game.

‘I thought we discussed that before the game,’ the Spaniard said. ‘It was related to what could happen. Not only the red, but the 10 seconds before, the way he (Dowman) comes to receive the ball, what kind of ball that is, and after that if he gets tackled, what happens next. Exactly that.’

Arteta revealed he had spoken with Dowman about the incident. 'I had a talk with him yesterday,' he said. 'No issue at all. I've done it, so I try to prevent that.

'That's why I'm so protective of these things, and especially with young players, because we have made those mistakes. And you know how much you can get punished and how much it can change what happens next.'

On the FA’s decision to reject the Gunners’ red card appeal, he said: ‘Very disappointed, to be fair. Especially with the reckless tackles that he received, and then his reaction is minimal in relation to the action.

‘(We’re) disappointed that it's not been overturned after looking at the action back.

‘We have put every argument on the table to make a case for it. Not only the action, but when you look back at it in slow motion, the previous action and Max's action, it's clear that obviously we have a very different opinion.

‘And on top of that, I think you have to read the context of the player, the age.’

The severity of the challenge is also an issue for Arteta. ‘It could have been really bad, yeah,’ he said. ‘And we are lucky today that he hasn't had a broken foot. That's clear.’

#1487. O'Neill hits out at critics as Celtic boss issues surprising response to McGregor's midweek comments

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 15:03 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 15:30 EDT, 30 October 2026

Celtic manager Martin O’Neill has claimed some of the club’s critics are only seeking to cause division within the camp.

On the back of a 2-2 draw with Dundee United earlier this week, Celtic skipper Callum McGregor claimed they are playing like a basketball team who lack control in matches.

McGregor also appeared to question the fact that Celtic started the match effectively with three strikers across the frontline in Kasper Hogh, Camilo Duran and Callum Osmand.

‘It’s not really having a nailed-on profile for each of the positions,’ said McGregor. ‘The players behave like a winger, or they behave like a striker.

‘You can get away with it for a few games but if it’s a striker playing as a winger, you are going to get that behaviour a lot of the time.

‘You’ve got enough quality so you can score goals and get away with it. But we have to try to get the team functioning the way it should.

O'Neill is satisfied with Celtic's start to the season despite criticism over performances

‘Then that will alleviate all the other problems that we are encountering, where it becomes a bit like basketball, you lose control and spend the next 15 minutes trying to get possession back.’

At half-time in the game against United at Parkhead, O’Neill took Hogh off and reverted to a more traditional system with Jota and Haissem Hassan coming on as wingers to replace the misfiring Dane and Osmand.

Celtic eventually fought back to claim a point, but McGregor’s comments became the subject of much scrutiny.

It is not the first time a senior player has spoken out this season, with Cameron Carter-Vickers claiming that Celtic’s style of play was ‘random’ after the Old Firm defeats to Rangers.

O’Neill insists he actually agrees with McGregor’s comments — but has vowed to find a solution at the top end of the pitch.

The veteran boss also appeared to snipe back at some of the critics who have claimed that there is unrest among the squad.

‘I’ve said this to you before, I totally agree that Osmand is actually really a centre-forward,’ said O’Neill when asked about McGregor’s verdict.

‘I’ve said it at the press conference, that he is essentially a centre-forward who probably would play off somebody strong alongside him.

‘I'm not so sure that he could lead the line on his own. And that Duran is really a centre-forward.

‘So the players are getting to know each other. It’s really as simple as that. So I’m in total agreement with Callum. We’ll sort it out.

The manager admits that the likes of Camilo Duran are currently being played out of position

‘We seem to be doing okay domestically, trying to sort it out.

‘There’s a few players that haven’t had a chance. [Jordan] Lotomba hasn’t had a chance yet to play. There’ll be moments, absolutely.

‘Young [Joel] Van Den Berg has trained today. So over the course of the next number of weeks, between now and Christmas, I think everybody will be on the field of play.

‘And then it’s a matter of establishing right positions as much as possible.

‘Players have played out of position before. I don’t know whether it was a big issue when young Osmand came on in the Benfica game and set us alight.

‘I come in here [to the press conference] every single week and I’m most of the time pretty buoyed by things.

‘Don’t try and throw a lot of divides in. At the end of the day, we’re doing fine.

‘A lot of lads here didn’t even do pre-season with us. A number of players came in quite late on, so it will take time for us.

‘So we need to hang in there, and at this minute I think we’re hanging in.’

With Rangers playing Aberdeen in the semi-finals of the Premier Sports Cup, Celtic travel to Falkirk tomorrow knowing that a victory would send them seven points clear of their Old Firm rivals.

O'Neill added: ‘I think we’ve done fine, we’re leading the league with a four-point gap at this minute, which is nothing at all at this stage of the season.

‘We fought back and retrieved those kind of leads on a couple of occasions last season.

‘We’ll try and get a result or two in European football which would be nice, but domestically we’ve been fine.

‘Falkirk had a bit of a stodgy start, but they are flying now, so we know it’ll be a difficult game for us.’

#1486. Bruno Fernandes has 'TARNISHED' his Man United legacy after his public criticism of Michael Carrick - and peace talks might be 'papering over the cracks', warns Alan Shearer

Published: 15:30 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 15:47 EDT, 30 October 2026

Alan Shearer has claimed that Bruno Fernandes has 'tarnished' his Manchester United legacy following his fallout with Michael Carrick over the last couple of weeks.

The Red Devils captain raised eyebrows when he questioned his manager's tactics after their side's 4-1 defeat by Como in the Champions League, and was subsequently left out of the team for their later loss against Bournemouth.

He spoke out just a matter of days after Lisandro Martinez had questioned United's activity behind the scenes, and left his United future in doubt.

That's according to all-time Premier League leading scorer Shearer, who claimed Fernandes' previous success is now marred.

'Fernandes is going to have to go out and perform, which he hasn't done for large parts this season,' Shearer told Betfair. 'I know he's been Man United’s go-to player for a long time now, he's been their best player, but it's no way for the captain to behave.

'He owes the manager a performance, he owes the club a performance, and he owes the fans a performance.'

Bruno Fernandes (right) has 'tarnished' his Manchester United legacy after criticising Michael Carrick (left), according to Alan Shearer

He added: 'I think he has tarnished his legacy at the club. I think the reaction that you saw at the end of the game against Bournemouth last week was pretty telling whose side the fans are on and it's Michael Carrick's, not Bruno Fernandes’, despite what he's done for the club.

'Whether that was part of him speaking to the manager and thinking, woah, I have got this wrong here. I don't know.'

Fernandes and Carrick held clear-the-air talks after the 3-0 Bournemouth loss, and many expect the midfielder to return to the side this weekend against Chelsea.

But it's unclear what will follow. Shearer, meanwhile, isn't convinced all is well.

'Fernandes and Carrick’s peace talks could’ve and probably should’ve happened before the game last week,' he added. 'Then there might not have been as much noise.

'Are they just papering over the cracks? I've been in a situation myself where I've not really got on with the manager in terms of Ruud Gullit and I guess you'd have to be on the inside to know what's really going on, but it would seem strange for him saying what he said, being left out and then being reinstated and then walking out as captain this week.

'It's not a good look, is it? It's pretty chaotic.'

Shearer suggested that crisis talks between Carrick and Fernandes may be 'papering over the cracks' amid the side's struggles

Old Trafford bosses decided not to sack Carrick with United in 16th place in the Premier League table, one point clear of the relegation zone.

The 45-year-old still faces a battle to improve results and performances and convince his employers that he remains the right person for the job.

Sources confirmed that Carrick has been given a second chance, and said that everyone is focused on showing a response on the pitch at Stamford Bridge following United’s worst start to a league season in 40 years.

The United boss was left in limbo after chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox held crisis talks on Monday with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and co-chairmen Joel and Avram Glazer.

The first indications that Carrick had earned a reprieve came shortly before 8am on Tuesday when he arrived at Carrington dressed in a club tracksuit and oversaw training as the players returned after a day off.

He had also turned up at the training ground on Monday but was there to watch United’s Under-21s play in a behind-closed-doors game against Hull City alongside his No2 Steve Holland and Under-18s coach Darren Fletcher. He stayed for three hours before leaving with his son Jacey, a member of United’s Under-18s.
