#1484. All that money spent and Spurs do not have a proper striker or goalkeeper

For all the money spent, Tottenham Hotspur have started this season without a reliable out-and-out striker and short of a top goalkeeper. And it is already costing them dear.

We keep hearing that Dominic Solanke will be the man to give Spurs a goalscoring threat, but how long has it been since we have seen him fully fit and firing? Maybe not since his Bournemouth days.

Antonin Kinsky may have finished last season well, but there was further evidence in this defeat that he is well short of the best goalkeepers in the division.

It is a puzzle how Tottenham signed 10 new players, but did not upgrade two of the most important positions on the pitch.

Only when Aston Villa were out of sight and the game was effectively over did Spurs break their Premier League goal drought. And even then it was a midfielder, Conor Gallagher, and a defender, Jan Paul van Hecke, who were on target.

Solanke had gone off just before Villa scored their second goal, which highlighted the big difference between the two sides on Saturday and where Spurs are badly lacking.

Zion Suzuki, the Villa goalkeeper, launched a long ball upfield, Nicolas Jackson managed to lay it off for Johan Mazambi, who returned the favour. Jackson touched the ball past Micky van de Ven’s challenge before beating Kinsky with a well-struck shot.

Spurs are stunned as Nicolas Jackson doubles Aston Villa's lead 😳📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/il7NKbgFCQ

It was an excellent goal, but Kinsky got a good hand to it and a top goalkeeper would have pushed it around the post. On the evidence of the first half, when he made four saves, Suzuki would have also stopped the ball creeping into the net.

Suzuki cost Villa in the region of £30m and he looks a more than able replacement for Emiliano Martínez. Spurs, on the other hand, have not had a top-class goalkeeper since Hugo Lloris and it is a puzzle that so much faith has been placed in Kinsky.

Spurs spent most of the summer firmly denying any links to Jackson before Villa signed him from Chelsea for an initial £47.5m that could rise to £65m. Given the London club paid an initial £75m for Sávio and committed to a £60m obligation to make Omar Marmoush’s season-long loan permanent, Jackson might have been a relative bargain for them.

Asked if Tottenham had made a big mistake by failing to sign a proper number nine, head coach Robert De Zerbi said: “The transfer market was long. The situation changed many times. There was also the financial rules, at the end of the transfer market. And we had to respect the rules.

“We didn’t sell the players who we thought, in the beginning, there was the possibility, the chance to sell. There are a lot of reasons. I think the club and the coach, we are not sleeping, we know the characteristics of the players, we know everything. And if we didn’t make any different decisions, it was because we couldn’t.”

That sounded a bit like excuses, but De Zerbi did not put up much of a defence for Solanke as he said: “We need more from him, for sure, but he’s one of my players. I like Dom as a player and I stay with him until the end. He needs to stay better, to feel better. The physical condition is not good enough, but it’s normal for him. Maybe he is not confident enough in himself at this moment, because he’s much better than this. I think we can’t say everything is bad, but it’s not enough.”

It was Sávio who forced Suzuki into making a brilliant double save from him in the first half, when Tottenham were well on top. The Japan international also stopped an Archie Gray shot from squirming through his legs and into the net, and dived to turn another Sávio effort around his right-hand post.

Jackson was not the only Villa new boy who upstaged Tottenham’s expensive new attackers. Manzambi not only assisted for Jackson, but also marked his first start for the Midlands club with a goal that put the visitors ahead in first-half stoppage time.

Johan Manzambi is off the mark for Aston Villa, and what a time to do it! ⚽️📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/rLRbbUM4Jm

Andrew Robertson will have been disappointed with his attempt to clear the ball, John McGinn played it into the path of Boubacar Kamara and his scuffed shot fell into the path of Manzambi, who found the back of the net.

Substitute Mohammed Kudus was correctly denied an equaliser following a VAR check before Jackson’s goal and a brilliant strike from Emiliano Buendía that effectively clinched a first league win of the season for Villa.

Emi Buendia, that is a BEAUTIFUL strike 😮‍💨📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nNplbL7mpd

Unai Emery, the head coach, spent years watching Martínez and Ollie Watkins win games for Villa with decisive actions, and is hoping this was evidence that Suzuki and Jackson can do the same for him.

“They are here for it [making the same impact],” Emery said. “His commitment, Zion is really very good. His commitment, Nico Jackson as well is fantastic. But every player needs to understand how we can feel better collectively, how they can help us with their qualities, and how we can collectively exploit our best performance.

“Today we made one clear step forward. Zion is keeping his performance like he did before. Jackson today clearly improved his performance. This is the way forward and the example for the other players.

“Manzambi played a good match, but he’s not yet understanding everything we need on the field with our positioning. He’s a fantastic player and must feel free playing to try to exploit himself and his qualities. But, of course, always under our structure.”

Speaking after the match, former Spurs man Joe Cole was critical of the club’s summer business which has left them without an out-and-out goalscorer and a weak defence

"You can't rule them out of a relegation battle"Steven Gerrard and Joe Cole have major concerns for Spurs 😬🎙️ @lynseyhipgrave1 | 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/JivM5pNfM9

Plenty of fans leaving before full-time...

and heartbreak for the ones that stayed...

"It's a long international break, you don't want to be in the bottom three"John McGinn on the 'relief' for Aston Villa to pick up their first league win of the season 😅🎙️ @lynseyhipgrave1 | 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/Gl38uj1pig

We’ve got a three-week international break after this weekend, so there’s a little while before both teams will be back in action, but this is what awaits them when they return:

"The fans deserved the win." 👏Emi Buendia shows his appreciation to Aston Villa supporters after a much-needed victory 💜🎙️ @jules_breach | 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/Qjn6RihNGD

John McGinn is also speaking to TNT now, so we’ll get you his quotes soon.

Villa only had seven touches in the Spurs box in that second half, but that was enough to secure two goals and all three points.

Spurs thought they had pulled themselves level while Villa were only 0-1 up after 60 minutes, but VAR judged Robertson to be offside.

Spurs thought they had their first Premier League goal of the season...Until VAR ruled it out for offside 😬 pic.twitter.com/FJsrLhm0FG

Emi Buendia, that is a BEAUTIFUL strike 😮‍💨📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nNplbL7mpd

Aston Villa have jumped with their first win of the season, while Tottenham have sunk back into the relegation zone.

“We were looking for this win from the beginning. We had a really difficult start of the season in terms of results and not finding our best football but I think today we showed a really good character.”

And that is it! A second late consolation goal is not enough to stem the boos from the stands.

Late action from Tottenham but they leave it too late to get a result. Another loss at home sends De Zerbi back to the drawing board.

This will be the last of the game probably as Maddison is fouled outside the area for Spurs’ third free kick in quick succession. Robertson takes it and sends a perfect delivery to the back post.

It is the first one that Mings has been caught under and van Hecke gets there to send it past Suzuki.

Another foul for Spurs, on the corner of the box. Maddison to take again and Mings does great work to judge the path of the ball and head it out from the centre of the box.

Callagher gets the ball in midfield and feeds Savio on the left who pulls it back. The ball he sends into the box is cleared from a crowd of bodies by Barkley.

Though Savio takes the corner quickly, it comes out to the edge of the area. Bentancur rises to meet the ball lifted in to the box and flicks it on behind himself towards goal, and it just goes wide of the post.

Maddison stands over it, and goes for goal, curling it very well, though Suzuki is in the right place to punch it away. It falls to Kudus, whose follow-up is a much less exciting effort, sailing over the bar.

We will have seven minutes added on here.

Kudus has been fouled as he try to get forward. Spurs are still looking for a second goal and Savio is fouled on the left side of the box. Cash gets a card for it and it is a very interesting position, not far from the touchline.

It has been given as a Gallagher goal for now.

But it is just too little too late for Spurs. No celebration from De Zerbi and hardly a cheer from the fans remaining in the stadium.

Tammy Abraham has come on by the way, replacing Jackson for the final few minutes.

A consolation for Spurs! They have their first league goal to almost no reaction from their fans.

Kudus cuts the ball back and it is not clear whether Cash or Gallagher get there first to poke it home.

The Spurs fans are leaving in droves. All you can hear in the stadium now are the rejoicing Villa fans.

McGinn comes off for Ross Barkley and Kamara off for Mbaye

Spurs replace Bentancur and Tonali with Lucas Bergvall and Connor Gallagher

This is absolutely what Villa needed. They have been great out of possession, just patient and disciplined and taking their chances when they come.

This is going to be a long three weeks for De Zerbi. Spurs have not managed a shot on target in the half, despite all their dominance on the ball.

That must be the final nail in the coffin for Spurs.

Gomes makes a great run, sending the ball out to McGinn on the right win. Rather than send the ball in to the box, he sends it out to the edge of the area and there is Buendia. He runs on to it late, finding the top left corner with an immaculate strike.

Villa have been calm without the ball in this half. Spurs have dominated possession but Villa have been very organised in defence.

Gray is fouled 35 yards out and Maddison takes the free kick. It only meets the first man in the box, who is Ruggeri, who clears.

Spurs are having no luck and have just not been able to get themselves in front.

Marmoush gets the ball from Maddison on the edge of the area and takes a shot on the turn. It’s blocked by Lindelof for a corner.

Savio takes again but Suzuki punches it away in the centre of the box.

Kudus tries a ball from on the right of the area, looking to find Robertson at the back post but Suzuki again comes confidently to claim it.

Change for Villa as Manzambi comes off to make way for George Hemmings.

17 minutes for Spurs to find a goal...or two.

Tonali comes close! From 35 yards out, the Italian takes a touch to shift it onto his left foot and sends a curling effort towards goal. Suzuki dives but can’t get there and the ball just whistles past the top far corner of the goal.

At least Spurs’s heads haven’t gone down but they still have nothing to show for it.

Savio sends a cross in from the right but there’s only Buendia in the box to meet it. He sends it out and Jackson finds himself with it again on the left side. Villa’s play breaks down but they are not backing down.

Well it’s gone from bad to worse for Spurs.

Jackson gets his first goal for his new club and van Hecke has got to do better there.

He gets on the end of an incredible long ball from Suzuki, and van Hecke does not get close enough to challenge him. He takes a touch to get it past van de Ven and sends it past Kinsky from the edge of the box into the bottom corner. The keeper gets a hand on it but it comes in off the post, almost in slow motion.

James Maddison will be coming on shortly.

Tonali sends a ball across to Savio on the right corner of the box, and his low ball in goes out the back for a corner.

Solanke can’t control it as it comes in and that will be his last action before he makes way for Maddison.

Marmoush goes down on the edge of the box, pushed by Joao Gomes, earning a free kick.

Robertson and Marmoush standing over it, just on the left of the area. Robertson is the one to take, lifting it towards the back post but Suzuki comes out to claim easily.

So close for Spurs! A fantastic run from Robertson but the defender strays just offside just outside the box. He takes the ball down to the back line, drawing Suzuki off his line, and it is crossed back past the keeper and bundled over the line by Kudus.

Huge cheers before VAR takes a look. The wait goes on.

Ruggeri intercepts a loose ball in midfield and makes a run down the left side. He lifts a ball towards the centre of the box, but Betancur beats the waiting Manzambi to it, bringing it down and nudging it towards his keeper.

Savio again on the right edge of the box lifts a ball across the box towards the back post, but Suzuki judges it well and comes off his line to claim it.

We’re back underway as Kinsky had to receive a bit of treatment there.

Tonali plays it in for Savio but it’s intercepted by a Villa shirt. It’s played out for Jackson on the left wing to have a run and he gets past van Hecke very easily to reach the edge of the area and take a shot – which goes high and wide.

Unai Emery warned Nicolas Jackson about getting unnecessary bookings yesterday after having to substitute him on a yellow card at half-time last week. 30 seconds into the second half, Jackson got a needless yellow car for stopping a free-kick being quickly taken. Emery pointed straight to his head when it happened.

Savio tries to find Bentancur as he makes a run down the centre of the field. The midfielder gets a head on it but it heads the wrong way.

But the game is opening as Spurs push, and Villa go on the counter with Manzambi running down the left side. He feeds a ball through to Jackson who carries it into the box but Kinsky judges it well and comes out to block the shot.

Spurs are pressing very high now and Villa have dropped very deep, especially their midfield.

Savio tries to put a ball in to the box but it’s trapped by Manzambi who plays the ball out. Ruggeri gets the ball back in to midfield to Buendia, who tees up Manzambi for a run into the box. The Swiss international is closed down well though.

Time to see how Spurs will react after that goal.

There’s still plenty of fight left as Kudus sends the ball out to Savio, trying to get to the touchline to cross a ball back in but Ruggeri stays on him.

Spurs: Mateus Fernandes for Mohammed Kudus

And as I’m typing this , it’s an early yellow for Jackson for a silly foul. Here we go!

Johan Manzambi is off the mark for Aston Villa, and what a time to do it! ⚽️📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/rLRbbUM4Jm

It looks like Mohammed Kudus will be on at half-time for football. He’s been going through his own half-time warm-up. Matt Cash has been doing the same for Villa, so maybe we will see him too.

In all fairness to Spurs, they have pushed for a goal all half and only been denied by some fantastic keeping from Zion Suzuki.

Here are some of the biggest saves of the half:

Zion Suzuki with a double save to deny Spurs an opener 🧤📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/b7WITUtjf2

Back-to-back huge saves from Zion Suzuki! 🤯📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/uXKkicEeer

Predictably, there were boos from the home fans at half-time. That was the ninth half of Premier League football Spurs have failed to score in. They should have done and would have done if it weren’t for the heroics of Zion Suzuki in the Villa goal. Manzambi’s goal was only Villa’s second in the League this season and this is the first time they have led in a League game.

Spurs looking shaky now as they come close to conceding a second, seconds before the whistle finally blows.

Boos around the stadium as the players head down the tunnel. De Zerbi has work to do.

Spurs have not come from behind to win since November 2024.

This is a tall challenge now, as van Hecke is the first to go into the book for a foul on Jackson.

To rub salt in the wound, Spurs have a decent shout for a free kick on the edge of the box before that as Gomes pushes Mateus Fernandes as he makes a run into the box.

Well this is the last thing Spurs would have wanted. Minutes before half-time Manzambi puts the vistors in front.

Robertson slides to try and stop a ball going out for a corner but he only finds McGinn. He sends it into the box and finds Kamara, who takes a shot. It bounces towards goal and Manzambi pokes it past Kinsky for the lead.

Van de Ven is off the pitch on his feet, sporting an impressive bruise now. Spurs are down to 10 as they try to get the swelling down.

There will be five minutes added, though play is yet to resume as van de Ven receives treatment for a cut below his eye.

The last thing Spurs need now is to be forced into another defensive change after losing Porro.

Wan-Bissaka picks up the ball sent out to him on the wing by Manzambi, who is fouled by Marmoush.

The free kick is outside the area, but McGinn takes looking goalwards.

Mings makes the run looking to get his head on it, but van de Ven goes up with him and gets there first to clear it, though the Dutch international takes a blow to the head and goes down for treatment.

Joao Gomes races forward, sending the ball to Ruggeri on his left. He tries to put it in the box, but it goes out the back off Archie Gray for Villa’s first corner.

McGinn delivers but it comes off Solanke, who clears. No luck yet as we head towards half-time, despite plenty of action in front of goal.

Roberston again with a sliding cross that Lindelof sends out the back.

Another corner for Spurs, but it is headed away again by Mings, who gets up high. That’s Spurs’s seventh corner.

Great long ball from Robertson to try and find Marmoush but Suzuki comes far outside his area to control it with his chest on the bounce and play it away with his feet.

Villa get a free kick inside as Bentancur catches Manzambi, but the Swiss international goes down and receives some treatment on the pitch. He has to go off for a minute, but he is on his feet.

But Spurs come again and it’s Tonali this time. He takes a shot from outside the area, and would have beaten Suzuki low on the right, but the shot is just wide.

Spurs get a corner, delivered by Savio, and it’s headed on to Solanke at the back post. He heads it towards goal but it’s blocked by Wan-Bissaka. Cries for handball, but it’s cleared.

Marmoush makes a very well-timed run to get on a long ball from van Hecke, and does well to stay onside. But his first touch is not good enough and Suzuki can come to collect.

Jackson picks up a ball from Kamara, played over him into the Spurs half. He puts it into the centre of the field towards Buendia, who tees up Manzambi but his shot from distance sails over the bar.

Villa now having a spell. Manzambi gets onto a loose ball in midfield and lays it off to Buendia who feeds Jackson in the centre of the field. He does well to keep the ball down and turn round van Hecke to take a shot on the edge of the area, but he skews his shot wide.

He should be hitting the target at least from there but you can see how desperate both sides are to get their noses in front here.

Jackson gets around Gray and runs into the box on the left side. He pokes a ball through to Buendia, who takes a shot on goal at the near post, but Kinsky gets down to his left to stop the shot.

Mings almost causes a catastrophe for Villa as he and Lindelof close a loose ball down. Suzuki comes out to claim, but the defender pokes it towards him, almost past him under pressure and the keeper has to send it out the sideline.

Four huge saves by Suzuki as Spurs have had five early shots in total to Villa’s single shot on target. They are finding a lot of joy against the left side of Villa’s defence.

Fernandes has an attempt from distance, but drags his shot wide.

Well Spurs are really pushing for a goal!

It’s a perfect first involvement for Gray, as he times a perfect run to get behind Ruggeri to pick up a ball from Savio. He lets it run inside the box but it flashes across the face of goal, just tipped away by Suzuki.

Another attempt denied immediately after as Savio connects perfectly with the volley on the edge of the area, and Suzuki dives down to his left to parry away.

Incredible start for the Villa keeper and Spurs can smell a goal coming.

Spurs had started on the front foot, but let’s see how they handle this change.

Porro went straight down the tunnel when he went off. It was a problem with his left leg. That’s a blow for Spurs, as Porro offers an attacking threat.

Early concern for Spurs as Porro has gone down and is looking very frustrated. Archie Gray has gone out to warm up, but this is a huge blow for De Zerbi if Porro has to come off.

He had been missing due to a muscle injury but it’s not clear if that’s the issue here. He has been very good so far today, helping build play and bringing huge amounts of experience.

And a shot on target next for Villa as Manzambi has an effort from just inside the 18-yard box off his left foot, but Kinsky makes a relatively easy save as the ball boucnes towards him.

Villa get their first chance, as Jackson races down the left side but van de Ven is content to stay close and as no Villa players follow him into the box, van Hecke is the one who clears his cross into the box.

Suzuki has been good with his feet since joining Villa, but he’s kicked about three balls straight out of play so far today.

No wonder De Zerbi had his t-shirt pulled over his head. Tottenham looked certain to score their first Premier League goal of the season through Savio. Suzuki didn’t know too much about the first shot, which hit him, but reacted well to tip the second over.

Tonali crosses a great ball in from the left and Savio has two great chances from close range but Suzuki blocks the first with his chest and tips the second over the bar.

The corner, delivered by Savio, is headed out by Mings and Villa keep control.

Suzuki plays a long ball out down the field, and as Jackson and van de Ven tussle to reach it, the defender is shoved to the floor and gets the free kick.

Spurs are putting a lot of pressure on Villa as they try and play the ball out, and McGinn loses the ball again in midfield. Spurs surge forward again but Mings gets his head onto the ball crossed into the box and Villa survive again.

Savio takes but it is headed out. It falls to Porro outside the box who lifts another ball in, but the Villa line holds firm and clears for a throw in from the left side.

Marmoush tries to run into the box but a well-time challenge by Kamara gets the ball off him.

Villa lose the ball in midfield and it’s played up to Solanke. Lindelof comes across well but concedes a corner.

Watch for some long balls from Tyrone Mings down the channels for Nicolas Jackson today. The pair had a little chat before kick-off with Jackson seemingly telling Mings where he wants the ball launched to.

Tottenham XI: Kinsky, Porro, Van Hecke, Van De Ven, Robertson, Tonali, Bentancur, Savio, Fernandes, Marmoush, Solanke.

Subs: Dubravka, Tosin, Senesi, Gallagher, Maddison, Udogie, Gray, Bergvall, Kudus.

Tottenham XI: Kinsky, Porro, Van Hecke, Van De Ven, Robertson, Tonali, Bentancur, Savio, Fernandes, Marmoush, Solanke.

Subs: Dubravka, Tosin, Senesi, Gallagher, Maddison, Udogie, Gray, Bergvall, Kudus.

Both teams are coming out of the tunnel now, greeted with plenty of noise from the home and away fans.

The stakes are very high for a match so early on the season and kick-off here we come!

This is the second fixture of the week, as Brentford stormed past Chelsea last night 3-0.

Nottingham Forest vs Coventry (Sat 5.30pm)

Led out by the skipper 🫡 pic.twitter.com/5MLh8ZpvU4

It's almost time ⏰#COYS pic.twitter.com/EewgmTnngl

Just heard on TNT that Newcastle have won more games at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in 2026 than Tottenham have...

An early goal here for Villa could be catastrophic for the home team.

Neither club have had any players called up for England, but plenty of players will be leaving to join up with their national teams abroad.

From Spurs, Pedro Porro has retained his place in Spain’s squad. Both Micky van de Ven and Jan Paul van Hecke have been called up for the Netherlands and goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky will join the Czech Republic squad, still awaiting his first senior cap.

Among the Villa players to receive call-ups, Johan Manzambi will be leaving to join the Switzerland squad, while captain John McGinn has been called up for Scotland once again. Zion Suzuki will leave to join Japan in the three-week break as well.

No Mathys Tel in the Spurs squad. De Zerbi has given him plenty of chances, but Tel has always been one of the first players the head coach has criticised this season.

"I don't see any player that would strike fear into me."Steven Gerrard and Glenn Hoddle give their thoughts on Spurs' transfer business and current squad 💰🎙️ @lynseyhipgrave1 | 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/eM22XDDAjs

“We have to improve in everything, because like I said, after the game we conceded the first goal in a bad way, because we knew what was the plan in the defensive phase. One long ball on Gakpo is not enough to concede a goal. Also the second goal could have closed Gakpo better and stronger, and the third goal is an individual skill of Szoboszlai.

“We can improve in the qualities of the play. I think we created more chances than the other games, also because Liverpool played with more courage.

“There was more space to attack, to make one-to-one, but I have experience enough to say that sometimes when you are the coach of the team, without you knowing the reason, you are able to score, you can score. And other times, another situation where I think you are playing well, not fantastic, but well enough to score, enough to win, and you don’t win.

“You have to stay calm, to be confident in what you are doing, what the players are doing. They have my full confidence. We move on and we keep going to be better day by day, but not by words, but by fact.”

“Similar, like us, but their potential is a huge potential. They signed, spending, a lot of very good players, but they need as well, time to get compact everything and to achieve understanding their idea.

“Of course, (Roberto) De Zerbi, he’s a fantastic manager. He played fantastic football here and performed fantastic here in Brighton. He did a fantastic job before as well, in Shakhtar, and in Italy, and after Brighton, a fantastic job in Marseille.

“And now, when I can watch them, they are in this process, but of course, they are getting better, they compete fantastic, even losing against Liverpool.

“Of course, being very, very demanding defensively for us, trying to impose and dominate our moment with the ball as well during the game. This is the challenge. Of course, Tottenham, I expect them to be in the top four.”

Two changes for Villa from the side that lost to Nottingham Forest, with Johan Manzambi and Joao Gomes entering the mix. It’s a first full debut for Manzambi since joining the club from Freiburg over the summer. Gomes returns having served his suspension following a red card against Brighton on the opening weekend.

Representing Aston Villa ✊ pic.twitter.com/5xnjiPnRny

Only one change from the team that faced Everton, as Pedro Porro returns to the starting XI, replacing Archie Gray. Carabao Cup goal-scorer Connor Gallagher is on the bench.

Our Spurs side to face Villa 📋🔢 @krakenfx pic.twitter.com/Xgpl4Hx9VV

Good afternoon and welcome to our coverage of today’s bottom-of-the-table epic: Tottenham Hotspur vs Aston Villa. This tie is incidentally the match-up between the last two winners of the Europa League, though so far neither of them have looked like European champions.

It is definitely fair to say that this season has not started the way either of these teams would have wanted, as the host side currently sit in what is apparently their favourite position – 17th – and the visitors are all the way in 19th, only above Coventry.

Despite getting off to a fairly convincing start in the Champions League with a 3-2 win over Club Brugge, Villa only scored their first league goal last week in their match against Nottingham Forest, though it was a futile one as they still lost 2-1 at Villa Park.

Tottenham meanwhile are still waiting for their first league goal, despite putting one past Liverpool in their 3-1 defeat in the Carabao Cup third round. With no European football and already out of one cup competition, Roberto De Zerbi has only the FA Cup in January and the rest of the league season to drag Spurs out of the perpetual rut they appear to find themselves in. They sit only one point above Villa as they have been able to see out two 0-0 draws – against Everton and Nottingham Forest – instead of one.

There has been plenty of talk about the money spent by both teams, without the results yet to show for it. The total sits around half a billion between them, adding to the mounting pressure on both De Zerbi and Unai Emery. Summer signings for both teams have struggled to land, something which will not be helped by the upcoming international break.

But before then, the teams have 90 minutes to try and get their seasons up and running, and we will be bringing you the team news, lineups and all the action from the match! Stay tuned!

#1483. With McGregor now questioning Celtic's approach, isn't it clear something is badly wrong there?

Published: 14:35 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 16:19 EDT, 30 October 2026

Celtic captain Callum McGregor talking about strikers playing as wingers and his team not having the right shape threw up all manner of issues.

One of them is that time is surely up for Kasper Hogh at centre-forward, £11million club-record signing or not.

When manager Martin O’Neill spoke to the media yesterday, he talked about Callum Osmand really being better through the middle than out on the left. A more pertinent point, though, is that it really doesn’t make sense any longer to keep playing Camilo Duran on the right.

There is, after all, a £9m man in reserve in Haissem Hassan who was signed to play out on that flank.

It just looks ever more like Celtic didn’t really think hard enough about what kind of way they wanted to play when they bought all these blokes.

What’s become clear is that it’s better if it doesn’t involve Hogh, now 13 games without a goal, unless there’s some masterplan to start sticking two up front. Even then, you’d be considering your options.

Callum McGregor was frustrated by his side's display in Wednesday's draw with Dundee Utd

There’s an argument O’Neill doesn’t play to the Dane’s strengths and that does hold water. However, Hogh has got to be able to adapt. If he can’t, what does it say about the decision, and whoever was ultimately responsible for it, to sign him in the first place?

What does a clever, senior figure such as McGregor joining Cameron Carter-Vickers in calling out the structure and organisation of the team say too?

Celtic might still be top of the table, but they’re all over the shop from top to bottom.

If Rangers can’t win the league this term, particularly given the fact they cannot possibly keep spending the way they have been without access to significant funds from UEFA competition, you do wonder when they ever will.

Hibs game looks like being D-day for Robinson at Dons

Aberdeen boss Stephen Robinson really started to bear the look of the condemned man in the wake of his side’s home defeat at the hands of Falkirk during the week.

The bullishness from earlier in the campaign had gone. He gave a thoroughly unconvincing answer on BBC when asked what progress, if any, had been made since the summer. He sounded like a bloke who knows he’s not far from the firing squad.

‘Ultimately, you have to get results,’ he said. ‘Otherwise, you know the inevitable.’

Unless it turns into a procession, a loss to Rangers in Saturday’s Premier Sports Cup semi-final is unlikely to seal his fate. The home game against Hibs next weekend, though, is a different kettle of fish entirely.

Time appears to be running out for Aberdeen manager Stephen Robinson to get things right

If the Dons are to be meeting any of their key performance indicators, they need to be better than Hibs. They need to be finishing above them in the top half of the table. And that’s the bare minimum.

What’s more, the Easter Road side are hardly in tip-top shape. Marink Reedijk’s time as head coach has got off to an underwhelming start. Sporting director Malky Mackay is under pressure over poor recruitment. They are there for the taking.

If Robinson can’t get the better of them at home ahead of an international break, a real time for the club to take stock, he’s in bother.

Those in the Red Army willing to make almost any sacrifice to see him nudged out the door should consider one thing, though.

If the management team get dumped, chances are first-team coach Stephen Craigan will be back all over our tellies and radios in his old role as media mouthpiece. And who really wants that?

#1482. Harry Kane beat Kylian Mbappe to the Ballon d'Or by one of the smallest margins EVER: Full results are revealed after England captain's triumph

Published: 17:30 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 17:33 EDT, 30 October 2026

Harry Kane beat Kylian Mbappe by a slender 28 point margin to be crowned as winner of the Ballon d'Or.

Kane claimed football's ultimate individual honour on Monday night, becoming the first Englishman to win since Michael Owen in 2001.

His success came off the back of a stunning year with Bayern Munich and England, with the forward netting a staggering 73 goals during the 2025-26 season.

Kane's goals spearheaded Bayern Munich's domestic Treble, while he also captained England to third place at the World Cup.

A full breakdown of the results has now been revealed, with Kane topping the vote by receiving 1,055 points from an international jury of 100 journalists.

Mbappe, who had also been seeking to win the award for the first time in his career, finished agonisingly short with the Real Madrid and France star receiving 1,027.

Harry Kane won the Ballon d'Or by just a 28-point margin, the full vote breakdown has revealed

Kylian Mbappe narrowly missed out on winning the award for the first time in his career

The gap is shorter than the closely fought battle between Rodri and Vinicius Jr in 2024, with the Spaniard having triumphed on that occasion by just 41 points.

Lionel Messi's 2019 triumph over Virgil van Dijk is the narrowest margin of recent votes, with just seven points separating the pair.

Previously Matthias Sammer beat legendary Brazilian forward Ronaldo to the honour in 1996 by one point, with the same margin also seeing Sir Bobby Charlton beating Eusebio in 1966, when just 22 people voted.

In total, 40 of the voters had ranked Kane as their top choice, earning him 15 points each time, with Mbappe receiving 23 first place votes by comparison.

Kane was left out of the top ten by two journalists, while three overlooked Mbappe.

Lamine Yamal, who was widely viewed as a front-runner for the award alongside Kane and Mbappe, ultimately ended 174 points behind the winner.

Rodri and Messi completed the top five having earned 726 and 612 points respectively.

Since 2022, the current system is based on voting by a large panel of international journalists from the top 100 FIFA-ranked countries, and top 50 for the Ballon d'Or Feminin. Only a single journalist from each country in these rankings is given a vote.

Lamine Yamal ultimately ended in third place in the vote, finishing 174 points behind Kane

Kane and his wife Kate Goodland shared a kiss after he won the striker award (left) and Ballon d'Or (right) on Monday night

Each journalist must establish a ranking of top ten players from a list of 30 named players also designated by France Football.

A first place vote is worth 15 points, with the number reducing until tenth position, where players secure one point.

Voters are asked to take into account individual performances and their decisive and impressive character.

They are then requested to consider their collective role and the trophies won, before weighing up a player's class and fair play.

Kane had celebrated on Monday night with friends and family, including his wife Kate, after receiving the award at the London Palladium.

Kane made sure to pay tribute to Kate, who he married in 2019, after seeing off competition from Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe to win.

He said: 'To my wife, Kate, my best friend. We've been through ups and downs for sure. You're my biggest supporter. I actually felt like you wanted this more than me myself.

'The anxious wait for us to find out, I know it's been horrible for you, here it is - we've done it! You always want the best for me, you sacrifice yourself to help me achieve my dreams, and I know they're your dreams as well, so it wouldn't be possible without you.

'This is a trophy that we celebrate, not me. This is me and you, it's all the family, all our close-knit team, so I just want to say thank you, I love you.

'Can't wait to enjoy this and celebrate tonight for sure. Love you.'

The couple share two daughters, Ivy and Vivienne, and two sons, Louis and Henry.

And Kane also made sure to reference them in his acceptance speech at the glitzy ceremony at the London Palladium.

'My kids sat home watching, it's definitely past your bedtime, especially as we're [the ceremony] a little later than we hoped,' he said. 'So to Ivy, Vivienne, Louis and Henry. You're the reason I do this.

'I don't think you'll fully maybe appreciate bringing this trophy home. I'll bring a few others home, but this one is a special one, so I can't wait to see you and celebrate with you.

'I want to set a good example being a father but also being a professional and what it means to work hard, what it means to believe in yourself. I love you very much.'

The couple are both from Walthamstow and Kate has been the rock by her husband's side for years.

Kate is a sports science graduate and professional fitness coach, with 382k followers on Instagram.

The couple posed for photos on the red carpet at the London Palladium Theatre

Kane proposed in the Bahamas in 2017 and they married two years later, now living happily in Bavaria where they have settled well since the striker elevated his game to another level, dominating the Bundesliga.

During his emotional address on stage, he also thanked his parents. He said: 'Wow, wow, wow. I am almost speechless. Being here in London has made it extra special. Made it a good omen for me tonight.

'Thank you to everyone who voted for me, I can imagine it was tough this year. Mum and dad, what a moment. All those years, the sacrifice, the support you gave me. Taking me to training, coming to watch me play. No matter where it was, even to this day you're there.

'All those traits you have given me have allowed me to be successful and be here tonight.'

And Kane got royal approval as he hit the summit of world football's personal awards from Prince William.

'Huge congratulations to Harry Kane on winning the Ballon d'Or!' William wrote in a post on Instagram. 'What a fantastic achievement and so deserved.

#1481. Man United interested in Barcelona star Fermin Lopez as they look to bolster attack after Benjamin Sesko injury blow

Published: 18:08 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 18:21 EDT, 30 October 2026

Manchester United have shown an interest in Barcelona’s attacking midfielder Fermin Lopez as they look to add to their goalscoring options in the next transfer window.

The Spain international, 23, is rated in the £70million bracket and is also coveted by Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea after netting five times for the Catalans this season.

Lopez was ruled out of last summer's World Cup triumph with a foot injury. However, he has long had admirers at Old Trafford, even if there is an acknowledgement that United’s finances may be an issue.

The club have been linked with Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin this week, a player they looked at but didn’t move for during his last year at Everton.

United fear their Slovenian striker Benjamin Sesko could be out until at least January with a shin injury and desperately need cover for the 23-year-old, as manager Michael Carrick is left without a recognised centre-forward.

Daily Mail Sport understands a move for Calvert-Lewin is viewed as difficult given the fierce rivalry between the two clubs.

Fermin Lopez is rated at £70million and is also coveted by Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea

Calvert-Lewin has revitalised his career at Leeds after joining on a free transfer in the summer of 2025, following an injury-plagued end to his time at Everton.

The England striker is also believed to be discussing a new deal at Elland Road, such has been his impact. The 29-year-old has scored 20 goals in 49 appearances for Leeds, including five in ten games at the start of this season.

United will also look at defenders in January if any spare funds are found.

#1480. SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The BAF (also known as mammalian SWI/SNF) chromatin remodelling complexes are essential regulators of nucleosome positioning and transcription factor binding1,2. Loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in genes encoding components of the BAF complexes are among the most frequent across cancer types3. However, a unifying mechanism that explains their widespread disruption remains unclear. Here we disrupted BAF function through pharmacological inhibition and ARID1A deletion across various mammalian cell types and tissues and observed a conserved chromatin response: increased accessibility at CTCF-binding sites. ARID1A LOF alone was sufficient to drive these changes, which demonstrates that canonical BAF (cBAF) disruption is the key driver of CTCF gain. Genomic profiling showed increased CTCF and SMC3 occupancy, which reveals an antagonistic relationship between cBAF and CTCF–cohesin complexes. Furthermore, cBAF loss restructured 3D genome organization, which led to a strengthening of topologically associating domain boundaries and subdivision of large domains into smaller insulated structures. Long-range enhancer–promoter loops were replaced by shorter, promoter-proximal loops anchored at CTCF-enriched sites. To determine how CTCF function is enabled following cBAF loss, we profiled CTCF-interacting cofactors and found that CTCF binds directly to fully assembled PBAF. After cBAF depletion, PBAF was recruited to sites of increased CTCF occupancy, which demonstrates that there is an antagonistic switch between SWI/SNF subcomplexes. In vivo, conditional Arid1a deletion in primary mouse cells resulted in the expansion of a highly proliferative population marked by elevated accessibility at CTCF sites. This phenotype was fully reversed by either Ctcf or Pbrm1 deletion, which establishes that cBAF and the activity of CTCF and PBAF have contrasting roles.

The BAF complex remodels chromatin by repositioning or evicting nucleosomes, which enables transcription, transcription factor (TF) binding and DNA replication1,2,3,4. Genes encoding BAF subunits are among the most frequently mutated in cancer, with LOF alterations present in around 20% of patients across nearly every tumour type3,5,6. Despite the widespread involvement of BAF complexes across cancers, a unifying mechanism of how BAF LOF contributes to transformation across diverse tissue types has not been clearly established.

In mammals, BAF complexes are highly diverse and feature numerous non-catalytic auxiliary subunits. So far, three main BAF complexes have been characterized in mammalian cells: the cBAF complex, the polybromo-BAF complex (PBAF) and the non-canonical BAF complex (ncBAF). Each of these has distinct and overlapping biochemical properties, chromatin targets and roles in disease7,8,9,10,11. The mechanisms by which mutations in BAF complexes promote oncogenesis include impaired chromatin accessibility at key enhancers and promoters and altered dynamics of interactions between transcriptional co-activators and TFs3,4,12,13. However, it remains unclear whether BAF LOF affects chromatin structure beyond nucleosome positioning and whether different BAF subunits have distinct or shared functions across tissues.

Beyond nucleosome positioning, epigenetic and transcriptional programming is controlled through higher-order architectural remodelling of the genome. However, it is unclear whether BAF complexes regulate 3D genome organization, despite growing evidence that other chromatin remodellers have a role in higher-order chromatin folding14,15,16. Although architectural proteins such as CTCF and cohesin have been extensively studied17,18,19,20, how BAF influences higher-order chromatin structures and regulates chromatin topology has not been fully explored. BAF complexes have a crucial role in nucleosome remodelling, and emerging links have been identified between other chromatin remodellers and higher-order genome organization21,22,23. On the basis of these findings, here we propose that disruptions in BAF function converge on a unifying mechanism of 3D genome reorganization. This mechanism could explain how distinct BAF LOF mutations drive oncogenesis across multiple tissue types.

Because BAF mutations predominantly cause LOF5,6 and ARID1A is the most frequently mutated BAF subunit with recurrent truncating alterations24, we modelled BAF dysfunction through ARID1A deletion (cBAF LOF) and the compound FHD-286, a SMARCA4 and SMARCA2 inhibitor24,25,26,27,28,29. We treated 15 human cell lines—including cancer cells from diverse tissues, human embryonic stem (hES) cells and non-cancerous immortalized lines—with FHD-286 for 24 h (Fig. 1a,b). All treated cell lines were BAF wild-type (WT) except SHSY5Y, which carries a SMARCA4 missense variant of unknown function (p.R973W)30. We also generated six isogenic lines using RIVA (lymphoma), Raji (lymphoma) and SUM159 (breast cancer) cell lines with heterozygous ARID1A (ARID1AHet) or homozygous ARID1A (ARID1AHom) deletions or knockdown via short hairpin RNA, as well as WT ARID1A.

TF motif enrichment was calculated using a previously published algorithm24,41. TFs classified as ‘multi-lineage shared BAF-dependent (closing)’ were closing in at least two cell lines and those classified as ‘common BAF-antagonistic (opening)’ were opening in at least two cell lines. ‘Enriched for tissue specificity TFs’ were selected from published tissue-specific enrichment data39,86,87,88,89,90. Bars show robust multivariable linear model coefficients ±95% Wald confidence intervals (CI) and P values are from two-sided coefficient tests with Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjustment. Icons in d created in BioRender; Debek, S. https://biorender.com/4tx6w5k (2026).

Using ATAC–seq to assess chromatin accessibility, we identified regions where chromatin either opened or closed following BAF complex loss or inhibition. Analyses of sites with reduced chromatin accessibility (in closing peaks) did not identify TFs common across cell types. Instead, TFs in closing regions were specific to the cell type (for example, SOX5 in skin, HNF4A in liver and SPI1 in lymphoid and myeloid cell lines; Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). Many of these TFs interact with BAF complexes (for example, JUN, BATF, NFKB2, ETS1, SPI1, POU5F1 (also known as OCT4), SOX2 and SOX10)21,24. This result supports the notion that BAF complexes modulate cell-context-specific TF activity3,31,32,33,34,35,36,37,38. By contrast, opening peaks were enriched for CTCF motifs in 20 out of the 21 cell lines (Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Figs. 2, 3 and 5). Opening CTCF peaks showed significantly lower cross-cell-type variability than closing TF peaks, which indicated that there is cell-context-independent CTCF regulation by BAF (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Notably, the CTCF effect was not driven by a small number of loci. Instead, it was an intermediate but broad and coordinated shift across many sites. For example, in RIVA cells, a comparison between ARID1A knockdown and WT cells showed that CTCF motif peaks accounted for 47% of opening peaks and 5% of closing peaks in ARID1A-deficient cells (Cohen’s h = 1.30, Cramer’s V = 0.51; Extended Data Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 1).

These effects were conserved in mice. FHD-286-treated mouse cell lines and primary Arid1aHet B cells from Arid1a conditional knockout mice24 also showed the gain in CTCF-site accessibility (Fig. 1d,e). Overall, the strongest gains occurred in lymphoid and myeloid lines, which also show the highest baseline CTCF mRNA and protein expression across healthy tissues and cancers30,39,40 (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1d). An orthogonal TF motif enrichment method, HOMER, confirmed CTCF enrichment across cell lines, with lymphoid and myeloid tissues ranking the highest (Supplementary Fig. 6a). We focused our subsequent experiments on lymphoid (RIVA) and breast cancer (SUM159) models (Fig. 1g,h).

To directly measure occupancy, we performed CTCF chromatin immunoprecipitation with sequencing (ChIP–seq) in ARID1AHet and WT cells. Chromatin regions that opened after ARID1A deletion showed increased CTCF binding in both lymphoma and breast cancer cells, with stronger gains in the lymphoid line (Fig. 2a,b). Because CTCF cooperates with cohesin at topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries18,41,42,43,44, we next profiled the core cohesin subunit SMC3. SMC3 occupancy increased globally, most prominently at sites with both enhanced accessibility and higher CTCF binding (Fig. 2a,b and Supplementary Fig. 6b). Moreover, the majority of newly accessible CTCF sites overlapped with SMC3 peaks (Fig. 2c). mRNA levels of CTCF and subunits of cohesin and BAF complexes were unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 6c), as were CTCF protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 6d). This finding indicates that the CTCF gain reflects increased chromatin binding rather than protein abundance.

Density plots show CTCF and SMC3 ChIP signals at opening and closing regions (n = 2 clones for RIVA, n = 3 clones for SUM159). b, Example genome browser view of CTCF and SMC3 ChIP–seq. c, Overlap of ATAC-seq analysis of CTCF-gained sites with cohesin binding in ARID1AHet and WT RIVA and SUM159 cells. d, Top, schematic of ATAC–seq after CRISPR-mediated CTCF deletion in ARID1A WT background (CTCF CRISPR); CTCF deletion in the ARID1AHet background (ARID1AHet CTCF CRISPR), or in ARID1AHet and WT cells, each subjected to a negative control targeting the luciferase gene (ARID1AHet and ARID1A WT). Data are from n = 2 independent experiments using distinct clones of each genotype, which generated n = 3 biological replicates in total, with 3–4 technical replicates per biological replicate. Two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) P values for genotype × time interaction are indicated in the graph. Error bars represent mean ± s.d. Right, immunoblot showing overexpression efficiency. Gel source data are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1.

To test whether CTCF itself drives the gain in accessibility, we acutely depleted CTCF by CRISPR in WT and ARID1AHet lymphoma B cells and performed ATAC–seq 48 h after transfection with CTCF-targeting Cas9 ribonucleoprotein. During this window of time, CTCF loss does not lead to effects on viability or proliferation45,46 (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 3). Principal component analysis (PCA) separated samples by genotype (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 4a). Consistent with previous observations24, ARID1A mutations caused loss of accessibility at NF-KB2, NF-KB1, REL and RUNX1 motifs (Fig. 2f). Moreover, CTCF depletion in the ARID1AHet background restored accessibility at CTCF sites to WT levels without affecting other TFs (Fig. 2g,h). These results establish these peaks as bona fide CTCF sites and rule out CTCF as a driver of the other TF-related changes. Accessibility gains correlated genome-wide with the expression of nearby genes, which therefore links them to transcriptional output (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Delta-delta analysis revealed that 93.5% of peaks (1,971 out of 2,108) that opened at CTCF sites in ARID1AHet cells reverted towards WT when CTCF was depleted (Fig. 2i, Extended Data Fig. 1f and Supplementary Fig. 6e,f). To test whether ARID1A heterozygosity acts as a LOF alteration, we compared chromatin accessibility profiles of ARID1AHet cells to those in which ARID1A was completely knocked out. Differential accessibility profiles in ARID1AHet cells strongly overlapped with those of ARID1AHom SUM159 cells and of ARID1A-knockdown RIVA cells, in which full knockout is not viable (Extended Data Fig. 1g).

To determine whether the increased accessibility at CTCF motifs reflects altered nucleosome positioning at the motif itself, we inferred nucleosome positions using nucleoATAC47. The analysis identified a subset of CTCF sites with a nucleosome positioned directly over the CTCF motif in WT cells. This motif-centred nucleosome was displaced in ARID1AHet cells and restored in ARID1AHet cells with CTCF also depleted. This result couples nucleosome displacement after cBAF loss to CTCF occupancy (Extended Data Fig. 1h).

As stronger CTCF sites drive loop extrusion48, we ranked CTCF ChIP–seq peaks by baseline WT intensity and observed that stronger peaks gained greater accessibility in ARID1A-deficient cells than weaker ones (Extended Data Fig. 1i and Supplementary Fig. 6g). These data suggest that ARID1A controls higher-order chromatin organization through CTCF and cohesin distribution.

To test whether the CTCF response occurs in non-transformed cells, we treated hES cells (MEL-1) with FHD-286 for 24 h. CTCF and SMC3 binding increased, although more weakly than in cancer lines (Supplementary Fig. 6h). This result probably reflects the dependence of pluripotent cells on SWI/SNF for stemness and differentiation that is triggered by prolonged pan-BAF inhibition. To uncouple the immediate chromatin response from differentiation, we engineered an ARID1A dTAG degron in hES cells and performed ATAC–seq, CTCF ChIP–seq and ARID1A ChIP–seq after rapid ARID1A depletion (Extended Data Fig. 2a). CTCF-site accessibility increased at both 6 h and 24 h, with strong enrichment already at 6 h (Extended Data Fig. 2b). ARID1A ChIP–seq confirmed loss of ARID1A occupancy (Extended Data Fig. 2c), and CTCF ChIP–seq showed a consistent, broadly distributed gain across more than 10,000 pre-existing CTCF peaks rather than de novo sites (Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). Furthermore, at the same regions that showed gain of CTCF, we observed a strong loss of ARID1A, which suggested that these loci were previously bound by ARID1A, which prevented CTCF binding (Extended Data Fig. 2c). To validate our findings in an independent setting, we performed a short FHD-286 treatment time course in RIVA cells. CTCF accessibility increased as early as 4 h after treatment, with a progressive increase at 12 h and 24 h, which indicated that CTCF responds rapidly to BAF inhibition. These results provide support for direct chromatin antagonism between BAF activity and CTCF occupancy (Extended Data Fig. 2e).

If CTCF functionally mediates the pathogenic consequences of cBAF loss, concurrent CTCF impairment should attenuate them. Consistent with this idea, patients with alterations in both ARID1A and CTCF showed significantly improved overall survival compared with those with an ARID1A alteration alone (Fig. 2j). To test whether this result reflects a deficit in the ARID1A-loss-driven proliferative advantage, we isolated primary mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from embryos carrying conditional floxed alleles of Arid1a, Ctcf or both. Deletion was induced by Cre–GFP transduction followed by sorting of GFP-positive cells, and efficient recombination was confirmed by genotyping (Supplementary Figs. 7 and 12a). Arid1a-deficient MEFs proliferated faster than empty-vector controls, and concurrent Ctcf deletion restored proliferation to near-WT levels (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g). This finding indicates that the fitness advantage due to cBAF loss depends on CTCF.

If CTCF gain drives the proliferative phenotype of ARID1A loss, CTCF overexpression alone should phenocopy it. In RIVA lines overexpressing CTCF in ARID1A WT and heterozygous backgrounds, CTCF overexpression in WT cells accelerated growth to ARID1AHet levels (Fig. 2k). High CTCF expression was also associated with more aggressive disease and worse clinical outcomes in patient data (Extended Data Fig. 2h).

CTCF works with the cohesin complex to form TAD boundaries that confine genomic interactions in specific regions42,49. To directly assess the impact of ARID1A deficiency on chromatin 3D architecture and CTCF-associated loop formation at high resolution, we performed Micro-C50,51 on ARID1AHet and WT lymphoma cells. Consistent with the gain of cohesin and CTCF occupancy, ARID1AHet cells showed increased intra-TAD contacts that were strengthened more than weakened (Fig. 3a), and a global shift towards intra-TAD over inter-TAD interactions (Fig. 3b). Moreover, in line with the gain in CTCF binding, ARID1AHet cells showed TAD splitting at higher frequency than merge, loss or complex rearrangements (Fig. 3c), with new boundaries visible in formerly continuous TADs on contact maps (Fig. 3d). To test whether CTCF gain drives this splitting, we examined insulation scores at sites of differential CTCF and SMC3 binding. Regions gaining CTCF showed increased insulation (a lower insulation score indicates fewer cross-boundary contacts; Fig. 3e), and boundaries overlapping CTCF peaks had higher CTCF binding in ARID1AHet cells than in WT cells (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Fig. 8a). Thus, enhanced CTCF occupancy drives TAD splitting and boundary insulation after cBAF loss.

For CTCF and SMC3 log2 fold change tracks, red and blue indicate positive and negative log2 fold change values, respectively, between ARID1AHet and WT ChIP–seq peaks. Right, proportion of promoter loops in split TADs and TADs selected randomly (two-sided proportion test). h, Aggregate peak analysis plots anchored on Mustache-called loops in WT and ARID1AHet cells (bottom) and the connectivity difference (top) between the conditions. i, Schematic representation of the hypothesis. cBAF loss leads to stabilization of CTCF and cohesin binding and increased intra-TAD interactions at the expense of long-range inter-TAD interactions.

To test whether these structural changes are functional, we measured promoter connectivity in split TADs. Split TADs showed a higher proportion of promoters gaining connectivity than both WT counterparts and random unchanged TADs (Fig. 3g). This finding indicates that splitting reinforces local promoter interactions by limiting longer-range contacts. Indeed, genes in strengthened TADs had increased expression in ARID1AHet cells, whereas genes in weakened TADs were unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 8b,c).

One of the main functions of TADs is to enable connection and coordination between genes contained in their borders. Because genes in TADs tend to manifest coordinated epigenetic marks necessary for coordinated expression levels52,53,54, we asked whether splitting disrupts this coordination. We performed RNA-seq and ChIP–seq for H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me1 and H3.3 marks in ARID1AHet and WT cells, then compared concordance in split, single (preserved boundaries with altered strength) and stable (preserved boundaries and strength) TADs. Split TADs showed greater discordance in chromatin marks and transcription than stable or single TADs (Supplementary Fig. 8d–g), which indicated that splitting establishes distinct chromatin environments. Thus, cBAF normally maintains regulatory coordination by preventing CTCF from subdividing shared domains. Finally, structural loops showed increased connectivity in ARID1AHet cells (Fig. 3h), a result consistent with enhanced cohesin stalling at gained CTCF sites. Together, these results show that cBAF loss reshapes 3D chromatin architecture through increased CTCF and cohesin activity (Fig. 3i).

To test whether BAF insulator antagonism is conserved beyond mammals, we examined Drosophila S2 cells, which use a diversified insulator repertoire, including Ctcf, Beaf and Su(Hw). CRISPR depletion of osa, the Drosophila ARID1A orthologue and a core subunit of the BAP complex, increased chromatin accessibility not only at Ctcf motifs but also at Beaf and Su(Hw) motifs (Extended Data Fig. 2i,j). Thus, SWI/SNF loss broadly opens architectural protein-binding sites across metazoans, which indicates that cBAF normally restrains engagement of multiple insulator classes.

To identify CTCF cofactors that might mediate 3D architectural changes after cBAF loss, we performed immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectrometry (IP–MS) for CTCF in lymphoid cells. CTCF co-precipitated ISWI subunits, consistent with its previously reported role in CTCF function21, and all PBAF-specific subunits (PBRM1, ARID2, PHF10 and BRD7) together with BAF-shared subunits (SMARCC1, SMARCC2, SMARCE1, SMARCB1, SMARCD1, SMARCD2, SMARCA4, SMARCA2 and BCL7A). By contrast, cBAF-specific and ncBAF-specific subunits were depleted relative to IgG (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 9a). Reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments for BRD7 and PBRM1 recovered CTCF and the PBAF-specific subunit ARID2 but not the cBAF-specific subunit ARID1A (Fig. 4b). IP–MS for PBRM1 recovered all expected PBAF subunits and CTCF at levels comparable to PBAF core subunits (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Table 3 and Supplementary Fig. 9b). These data reveal a previously unknown association between CTCF and all subunits of the PBAF complex.

To confirm that CTCF and PBAF interact directly, rather than being co-precipitated on the same DNA fragment, we performed additional CTCF IP and western blot experiments in the presence of endonuclease. The CTCF–PBAF interaction was preserved after DNase and RNase treatment (Extended Data Fig. 3a), and was detected in breast cancer (SUM159) and Burkitt lymphoma (Raji) cells (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). This result confirms the reproducibility of the relationship across cell types.

To assess whether CTCF associates with fully assembled PBAF, we performed glycerol gradient fractionation and profiled cBAF, PBAF, ISWI, CTCF and cohesin subunits in RIVA ARID1AHet cells and SUM159 ARID1AHom cells alongside their WT counterparts. PBAF components distributed to higher molecular mass fractions as expected. In both cell lines, CTCF co-migration with PBAF-containing fractions was increased in ARID1A-deficient cells compared with WT cells, with the strongest shift in SUM159 ARID1AHom cells (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e and Supplementary Fig. 9c,d). ChIP–seq for PBRM1 and BRD7 showed increased binding in ARID1A-deficient cells, with PBRM1 gained broadly and BRD7 less robustly (Fig. 4d,e and Supplementary Figs. 10 and 11). Because PBRM1 is the last subunit to be incorporated during PBAF assembly55, the broader PBRM1 gain is consistent with the preferential recruitment of fully assembled PBAF to gained CTCF sites after cBAF loss.

The preferential CTCF–PBAF interaction suggested that cBAF and PBAF have opposing roles at CTCF sites: cBAF restricts CTCF function, whereas PBAF promotes it. Because FHD-286 targets both complexes, we asked whether the FHD-286-mediated net chromatin effect primarily reflects cBAF inhibition. ATAC–seq profiles from FHD-286 treated and ARID1A-depleted cells showed strongly overlapping differential peaks and concordant directionality, which indicated that FHD-286 phenocopies cBAF loss (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Integration of FHD-286-induced accessibility changes with ARID1A and PBRM1 ChIP–seq in SUM159 cells revealed that peaks that lost accessibility were enriched for cBAF binding, whereas peaks that gained accessibility were enriched for PBAF binding (Extended Data Fig. 3f–h). This finding indicates that the FHD-286 phenotype is driven largely by cBAF inhibition rather than an equivalent blockade of all BAF assemblies.

To determine whether PBAF remains functionally engaged under FHD-286 treatment despite loss of cBAF, we examined ARID1A and PBRM1 occupancy by ChIP–seq after FHD-286 treatment in SUM159 cells. ARID1A occupancy decreased, whereas PBRM1-associated signals increased, which indicated that pharmacological-mediated BAF inhibition does not eliminate the PBAF program and instead enables a gain of PBAF-linked chromatin function (Fig. 4f). CTCF IP in FHD-286-treated RIVA and SUM159 cells showed preserved CTCF–PBAF association, which indicates that this interaction is not disrupted by the inhibitor (Extended Data Fig. 3i).

To dissect subcomplex-specific contributions, we performed ATAC–seq in cells treated for 24 h with the following inhibitors or degraders: BRD-K98645985, which inhibits ARID1A and ARID1B in cBAF9; FHD-609, which degrades BRD9 in ncBAF27; PBRM1-BD2-IN-8, which inhibits PBRM1 in PBAF56; and FHT006710, which degrades both BRD9 and BRD7 in ncBAF and PBAF. Degraders efficiently depleted their targets without altering ARID1A expression (Extended Data Fig. 3j), and dimensionality reduction separated samples by the complex targeted (Fig. 4g). PBAF inhibition decreased accessibility at CTCF sites, a result consistent with a CTCF-enabling role (Fig. 4h,i). By contrast, cBAF inhibition and ncBAF degradation increased CTCF motif enrichment (Fig. 4h,i), with inferred CTCF binding increased at peaks opened by PBRM1 inhibition (Extended Data Fig. 3k). Thus, PBAF enables CTCF binding, whereas cBAF and ncBAF antagonize it, a result consistent with previous findings that BRD9 loss increases CTCF binding in haematopoietic stem cells57.

To test whether the proliferation gain in ARID1AHet cells depends on PBAF, we generated heterozygous and homozygous deletions of the PBAF subunit ARID2 in the ARID1AHet background. ARID1AHetARID2Het and ARID1AHetARID2Hom cells proliferated slower than ARID1AHet cells in an ARID2 dose-dependent manner (Fig. 4j,k), which eliminated the proliferative advantage of ARID1A loss. This finding indicates that PBAF activity drives the accelerated proliferation of ARID1A mutant lymphoma cells, but does not exclude the fact that loss of other genes could produce similar proliferation effects.

To test whether CTCF, cohesin and PBAF gains colocalize at the same genomic sites, we developed an unbiased multimodal clustering model that integrates ATAC–seq, CTCF ChIP–seq and PBRM1 ChIP–seq data across ARID1AHet and WT cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). This model identified 16 chromatin-state clusters (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

Clusters G1–G8 (CTCF-gain clusters) showed increased CTCF binding in ARID1AHet cells. All CTCF-gain clusters except G3 and G4 also gained PBRM1 and SMC3 binding and expression of the nearest gene, with cluster G8 showing the largest changes (Extended Data Fig. 4d). All clusters gained BRD7 binding, an independent PBAF subunit not used for clustering, as well as the ATPase SMARCA4, consistent with active PBAF remodelling. The same regions gained H3.3 but not H3.1 marks (Extended Data Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 11), which indicated elevated nucleosome turnover at sites of CTCF, PBAF and cohesin gain.

After integration of the inhibitor and degrader ATAC–seq data, the top CTCF-gain clusters G1–G5 gained accessibility after cBAF or ncBAF disruption, mirroring the ARID1AHet versus WT pattern, and lost accessibility after PBAF inhibition (Extended Data Fig. 4e). This result further demonstrates that PBAF enables CTCF binding when cBAF is lost. Clusters G1–G5 also gained accessibility across a panel of multiple cell lines treated with BAF inhibitors (Extended Data Fig. 4f), which indicated that these are sites shared across tissues. Overall, 60–90% of sites in these clusters contained the M1 CTCF motif, which is associated with strong CTCF binding and insulator function58,59, compared with less than 50% in other clusters (Extended Data Fig. 4g). CTCF-gain clusters were also enriched for TAD boundaries, with the strongest gains in insulation at clusters G1–G5 (Extended Data Fig. 4h,i). Together, these data establish that cBAF loss drives TAD reorganization at sites that gain CTCF, PBAF and cohesin, with PBAF functionally replacing cBAF to enable CTCF-mediated insulation.

Given that PBAF preferentially localizes to promoter–proximal regions6,8, we speculated that cBAF normally maintains long-range enhancer–promoter loops that collapse into short-range promoter–proximal interactions at CTCF–PBAF sites after ARID1A loss. Analyses of Micro-C contact frequency by genomic distance showed that newly opened CTCF peaks in ARID1AHet cells have increased short-range interactions peaking around 500 kb and reduced long-range contacts above 1 Mb (Extended Data Fig. 5a), whereas unchanged CTCF sites showed no such shift. Opened SMC3 peaks showed the same distance shift (Extended Data Fig. 5b), a finding consistent with cohesin-mediated rewiring.

To determine how chromatin rewiring affects promoter function, we performed single-cell multiome profiling in ARID1AHet and WT cells and scored each gene by the correlation between expression and connectivity inferred from peak co-accessibility (Extended Data Fig. 5c). Genes with increased connectivity in ARID1AHet cells showed elevated transcriptional activity (Extended Data Fig. 5d–f). CTCF peaks that gained occupancy after ARID1A loss showed enhanced connectivity and more promoter–enhancer contacts (Extended Data Fig. 5g), and genes overlapping these peaks were upregulated (Extended Data Fig. 5h). PBRM1-bound regions gained in ARID1AHet cells showed the same pattern of increased connectivity, additional promoter–enhancer loops and elevated gene expression (Extended Data Fig. 5i,j), as did sites gained by the independent PBAF subunit BRD7 (Extended Data Fig. 5k,l). Thus, cBAF loss drives PBAF and CTCF to rewire promoter–enhancer contacts towards short-range promoter–proximal interactions that increase gene expression.

We have thus far shown that cBAF deficiency triggers a CTCF gain-of-function program with two hallmarks: enhanced intra-TAD insulation with domain subdivision and increased promoter–enhancer connectivity. To test which of these hallmarks depend on PBAF, we generated additional Micro-C profiles in ARID1AHet and ARID1AHetARID2Hom RIVA cells. The increased intra-TAD contacts (of single TADs) seen in ARID1AHet cells were attenuated in ARID1AHetARID2Hom cells, with log2(fold change) distributions centring near zero (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Furthermore, the intra-to-inter-TAD ratio, elevated in ARID1AHet cells, returned to WT levels in ARID1AHetARID2Hom cells (Extended Data Fig. 6b), which indicates that there is reduced insulation after PBAF loss in the ARID1A-deficient background.

After stratification of TADs by their ARID1AHet behaviour, ARID2 deletion partially but selectively rescued the strengthening class. That is, strengthened TADs lost contact enrichment in ARID1AHetARID2Hom cells, whereas weakening TADs were unchanged (Extended Data Fig. 6c). Genome-wide Micro-C signals at TAD boundaries, strengthened in ARID1AHet cells, were reduced towards WT levels in ARID1AHetARID2Hom cells (Extended Data Fig. 6d), and representative loci show attenuated boundary strengthening and TAD splitting after ARID2 deletion (Extended Data Fig. 6e).

We next tested whether the promoter–enhancer connectivity gain in ARID1AHet cells depends on PBAF. To that end, we performed additional single-cell multiome analyses that included ARID1AHetARID2Hom RIVA cells (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Connectivity in ARID1AHetARID2Hom cells shifted back towards WT levels (Extended Data Fig. 7a,b), and loops strengthened or gained in ARID1AHet were reduced after ARID2 deletion (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d,i), which indicated that PBAF contributes to the formation or stabilization of these new promoter–enhancer contacts. Expression of genes near gained CTCF or PBAF sites was partially restored towards WT levels in ARID1AHetARID2Hom cells (Extended Data Fig. 7e–h). This result links PBAF-dependent rewiring to the transcriptional consequences of cBAF loss.

As PBAF deficiency only partially rescued the ARID1AHet chromatin phenotype, we tested whether ISWI, a remodeller previously linked to CTCF function and recovered in our CTCF IP–MS data (Fig. 4a), is also involved. We deleted the ISWI catalytic subunit SMARCA5 (also known as SNF2H) in ARID1AHet RIVA cells and performed ATAC–seq. Loss of SMARCA5 strongly reduced accessibility at CTCF motifs in ARID1AHetSMARCA5Hom cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a), which indicated that ISWI is a major contributor to nucleosome remodelling at CTCF motifs after cBAF loss, with PBAF subsequently reinforcing CTCF-dependent insulation and loop architecture.

We next tested whether ISWI is required for the ARID1AHet proliferative phenotype. In independent CRISPR clones, ARID1AHetSMARCA5Hom cells proliferated significantly more slowly than ARID1AHet cells (Extended Data Fig. 8b), which eliminated the proliferative advantage of ARID1A loss. The reduced proliferation rate relative to WT cells is consistent with ISWI loss reducing CTCF accessibility below WT levels (Extended Data Fig. 8a). Thus, like PBAF (Fig. 4j,k), ISWI is required for the proliferative consequences of cBAF loss. However, we cannot exclude the possibility that loss of other essential genes could produce comparable proliferation phenotypes. Our data establish that ISWI activity is necessary, not that it is specifically required.

On the basis of these new data, we favour a model in which PBAF and ISWI contribute to CTCF gain-of-function in the setting of cBAF deficiency, consistent with the antagonistic relationship between cBAF and CTCF for chromatin architecture. At the same time, PBAF and ISWI may act through distinct mechanisms at distinct genomic loci or converge on the same sites. We therefore compared CTCF binding, PBAF binding and ISWI-dependent accessibility. Approximately half of ISWI-dependent CTCF sites were also associated with PBAF. Conversely, about half of shared CTCF and PBAF sites lost accessibility after SMARCA5 deletion (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Thus, PBAF and ISWI frequently converge on the same CTCF-linked regulatory elements, with smaller subsets preferentially dependent on one or the other.

Mutations in components of the BAF complex are particularly common in lymphoid malignancies, with ARID1A the most frequently mutated subunit60,61. More than 35% of diffuse large B cell lymphomas (DLBCLs) carry BAF mutations, and DLBCL arises from germinal centre B cells, which cycle between the highly proliferative dark zone (DZ), where they undergo rapid division and somatic hypermutation, and the light zone (LZ), where they are selected for affinity-matured antigen receptors62,63,64 (Fig. 5a). Each zone is defined by distinct chromatin and transcriptional states. Because the DZ-to-LZ transition involves extensive chromatin and architectural reorganization54,65,66,67, we asked whether ARID1A loss might disrupt this program through CTCF. ATAC–seq of WT germinal centre B cells showed that CTCF motif accessibility was significantly higher in DZ than LZ cells (Fig. 5b), which suggested that there is a CTCF-dependent component to the DZ state. Conditional Arid1a heterozygous deletion in mice can skew the germinal centre reaction towards the DZ24, and reanalyses of ATAC–seq data from these mice revealed that CTCF motifs were the most enriched in newly accessible regions (Fig. 5c). Together, these data link DZ expansion in Arid1a-deficient germinal centres to increased CTCF accessibility.
