#1479. Michael Carrick hits back at Gary Neville after his former Man United team-mate accused players of being unprofessional - and opens up on crunch meeting with struggling stars

Published: 18:30 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 18:30 EDT, 30 October 2026

Michael Carrick has rejected claims that his Manchester United stars have been unprofessional, and vowed to stand by them in the face of fierce criticism from pundits and fans.

Carrick’s former teammate Gary Neville accused some players of not going to bed at the right time or keeping to a healthy diet, while Wayne Rooney said they need ‘a firework up their a**e’ for the performances that have left their head coach fighting to save his job.

United fans turned on the team following Sunday’s 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth at Old Trafford, applauding Carrick down the tunnel before immediately venting their anger at the players.

Asked if he has encountered the unprofessional behaviour insinuated by Neville, Carrick said: ‘No, I haven’t. Gaz says a lot things!’

After United decided to give their head coach more time to turn the season around, he met with the players when they returned to Carrington on Tuesday and spoke about the backlash from fans.

‘Just to be clear, it was more for them to understand that I'm right in there with them. There's no way that I'm separated from that,’ said Carrick ahead of Saturday's crucial game at Chelsea.

Gary Neville (left) said Man United players were 'unprofessional' but Michael Carrick (right) insists he is standing by them in the face of criticism

‘As much as I totally respect and appreciate the response from the supporters, I'm right there with them and we'll go through this together.

‘It was mixed feelings for me. To have the appreciation from the supporters and that connection and that respect is something I feel strongly about.

‘It wasn't a nice situation, but to feel that was important, of course. But it didn't make me feel better in the fact that I'm with the players 100 per cent.

‘We're all in it together and I've told the players that. I'm happy to say that. I didn't feel comfortable being separated from that in any way, shape or form.

‘That's my group, they're my players and this is my football club, so we have to all be in it together.

‘That includes the supporters. As hard as it is at the moment, I totally get that. I get their feelings. When we get through this, we'll be a lot stronger as a whole.

‘We need to play better and we need to show certain things better. But the connection with us is as strong as ever.’

The fans also targeted United’s owners, the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, as well as chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

On his meeting with the players, Carrick added: ‘It's pretty clear. It's not always rosy and nice conversations between anyone, whether that's between me and the players, whether that's between me, Jason or Omar or the owners. It's the hard truth at times and it's what we need to move forward.’

#1478. Alisson’s brilliance takes the breath away to show way forward for Liverpool

Andoni Iraola spun on his heels, turned his back to the action and began to bite his nails. Managers often envisage the worst outcome when the clock ticks down, and here, in the 93rd minute, Bournemouth had a corner.

He needn’t have worried. As the set-piece was swung in, Alisson Becker moved powerfully off his line and plucked the ball from the air, a catch that essentially confirmed Liverpool would leave Dorset with three points. It was a catch, too, that put the gloss on another impeccable personal afternoon.

When Iraola took charge at Anfield, one question he had to answer – given Bournemouth had conceded 167 goals in his three years in charge – was whether he could make Liverpool defensively resilient. This dour 1-0 success, though, proves he is taking them in the right direction: he is the first Liverpool manager since Joe Fagan in 1983 to start with five unbeaten league games.

Alexander Isak might have scored the goal that leaves Bournemouth winless in the Premier League but this success owed everything to Alisson’s enduring brilliance – a comment that also applies to Virgil van Dijk – the enormous promise of Jérémy Jacquet and the grit of Ronaldo Araújo.

You go to top level football matches hoping to see something that will take your breath away and how Alisson did that in the 17th minute with a reflex save from an Evanilson backheel, the shape of his body resembling a fielder in the slips diving to prevent a boundary.

It proved to be the foundation stone from which Liverpool were able to build and inflict Bournemouth’s first home defeat since January. There are plenty of [valid] questions to ask of Liverpool’s attack at present but, defensively, it is starting to come together.

“It was a really good fight,” Alisson said, in that self-effacing way of his. “But we have to improve a lot – on the ball and sometimes off the ball as well but we improved in the second half. We adapted to the opponent and that’s what we are doing.”

Any manager with a well-drilled defence stands a chance of improving and that is what Liverpool are doing. Only four weeks ago the discussion was about how easy it was for teams to play through their middle – remember that chaotic afternoon at Newcastle to start? – but that is changing swiftly.

Since Iraola replaced Jeremie Frimpong with Araújo at right-back, three consecutive Premier League clean sheets have followed. Araújo, the Uruguayan on loan from Barcelona, revels in doing the dirty work while Jacquet, the £60m signing from Rennes, oozes quality.

“He’s [Jacquet] very young and adapted really well to the Premier League,” Iraola said. “The first games, he was physically feeling the change of rhythm and I had to sub him. This was a step forward. He looked solid until the end. He’s in a good place physically and I hope he can continue his development.”

Don’t confuse positivity about one aspect of the team as being a guide to its collective health. There was always a chance this contest would become a cagey affair and, Evanilson’s chance aside, the opening 45 minutes were as flat as you could imagine.

Iraola again played his three £100m+ signings but Bradley Barcola is still adjusting to the physicality of English football and Florian Wirtz is still finding it difficult to impose himself on a game; patience with the German will not be infinite.

He would do worse than to look at Isak, who is now on a run of four goals in four league games and is influencing games in the manner Liverpool envisaged when they broke the British transfer record to sign him last August.

Isak had an unusual afternoon. His only shot in the first half almost took out some low-flying pigeons, a cross early in the second half was sliced so badly that the weekend hackers on the nearby Queens Park golf course would have felt a flood of sympathy but then he got his third opening.

Cody Gakpo, who could have been in Manchester City blue had the cards played out differently earlier this month, wriggled down the right flank and squeezed in a cross that Isak seized upon and turned in from six yards. Liverpool never looked back.

Alexander Isak grabs his fourth Premier League goal of the season! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/5ehwhl1it4

“A striker’s job is like this,” Iraola said, who badgered Isak persistently to press Bournemouth’s defence. “He had a couple of crosses that he did not hit properly or control. He has to help us to be closer to the box, to play in the opposition’s half and have more meaningful possession. And then if the team is playing there, he will receive rewards in terms of goals.”

One, ultimately, was enough to see off Bournemouth, whose start to the campaign is something of a riddle. They shouldn’t be anywhere near the relegation places but that is the reality and Thursday’s historic Europa League win in Real Sociedad couldn’t mask the home crowd’s frustration.

“Our attitude and effort is good,” head coach Marco Rose said. “But, at this level, small things and little details decide games.”

Speaking to Sky Sports after the match, Iraola said: “I’m obviously happy with the result because I know this is a difficult place to come, very difficult place to get three points. And we could see it, especially in the beginning of the game. In the first 20 minutes we weren’t at the level [required] and it cost us. We finished the first half better and in the second half we played better, but that beginning of the game has surprised us, not surprised us [because] we knew where we were coming but it [was] difficult for us.”

Jeremy Jacquet has made the kind of quietly authoritative start to his Liverpool career that showed why there was such excitement in February within the club when they completed his deal. So much focus on so many players but Jacquet has never been anything other 7.5/8 out of 10.

"Let's go! One of many!" Virgil van Dijk giving Jérémy Jacquet his POTM award after Liverpool's 1-0 win at Bournemouth ⭐️ pic.twitter.com/6xWvjmrF8Y

"That's a big moment to me to play with Virgil!" 🫡Jérémy Jacquet after Liverpool's 1-0 win at Bournemouth! pic.twitter.com/UsTimGME39

Cody Gakpo has been Liverpool’s stand-out forward this term and he was at the heart of Isak’s goal this afternoon. Speaking about the job the Dutchman is doing to fill the void left by Mohamed Salah on the right flank, Ashley Young said on Sky Sports: “Players have to step up when you lose big players and you get the opportunities. I think Cody Gakpo is doing that. He’s a bit fortunate [in the build-up to Liverpool’s goal] but you create your own luck. He gets the ball down the line, that’s what you want to do and he puts the ball in the box. That’s what Isak’s waiting for.”

Fair play to anyone who retained Brobbey in their Fantasy Football teams this week...

4 - Brian Brobbey is the fourth player in Premier League history to score a hat-trick against the side starting the day top of the table, after Robbie Fowler v Aston Villa in November 1998, Dirk Kuyt v Man Utd in March 2011, and Romelu Lukaku v Man Utd in May 2013.Unstoppable. pic.twitter.com/vygVYazIQD

Maresca’s side maintain their immaculate record, but boy were they made to work for it this afternoon.

Sunderland are still 5-3 down but have not given up the ghost. Surely the best match of the season so far?

It ends goalless at Elland Road after Mitchell’s goal was disallowed for offside. Kamada went close to breaking the deadlock in the final stages...

Daichi Kamada can't guide his header on target! ❌ pic.twitter.com/AgKM6Q9apq

Bournemouth lose at the Vitality for the first time in 13 matches as Iraola makes a winning return to the South Coast. Liverpool were hardly impressive, but to their credit they managed the final stages of this match with a minimum of fuss.

Andoni Iraola returns to the Vitality Stadium with a win! ✅ pic.twitter.com/FSgvE6EGFB

Bournemouth are awarded a corner but Brooks’ delivery goes straight into the inviting gloves of Alisson.

Koumas pressures Petrovic, but the goalkeeper shows off some tidy footwork to escape the danger.

Bournemouth cannot get out though, and Petrovic is forced into a routine save off Koumas moments later.

Bournemouth win a free-kick in a dangerous position after a handball, but Scott cannot get his strike up and down fast enough and it sails over.

Haaland gets in on the act, but only after a VAR check. That should be that...

Erling Haaland has now scored against all 25 teams he has faced in the Premier League ✅⚽ pic.twitter.com/X9uqcrgbwk

Araujo gets his pocket picked in the corner but Jebbison cannot compose himself and blasts his cross off the other side of the pitch.

Liverpool go the other way and win a corner, but Mac Allister puts too much air on his delivery and it is easily dealt with.

Rayan wins a free-kick as he holds off Kerkez on the halfway line. Bournemouth then switch play to the far side but Truffert’s speculative effort flies well over the bar.

Nyoni shows off his composure on the ball, playing simple passes on the half-turn to keep play flowing. The midfield area is quite congested, which suits Liverpool at this point in the game.

Liverpool are baiting Bournemouth’s press in an attempt to play around their front line. They are doing a good job at holding on to the ball and frustrating their opponents, for now.

Gravenberch and Koumas are on for Gakpo and Isak.

Brooks has brought some energy to Bournemouth’s forays down the left. He attempts to slip a ball into the left channel but Nyoni is wise to it and positions himself perfectly to cut it out.

Liverpool have dropped deep and Bournemouth wait patiently for an opening. They eventually find Tavernier in the left half-space but his cross flies over everyone.

That is his last contribution to the match as Rose rings the changes: Tavernier, Smith and Christie make way for Brooks, Jebbison and Cook.

Truffert spins in a teasing ball from the left but Jacquet does well to flick the ball away from the danger zone.

Wirtz and Barcola make way for Nyoni and Munoz. Quiet afternoon from both of the outgoing players.

A stunning block from Hill prevents Isak pulling trigger as he looked to have the goal in his sights.

Truffert clears the resulting corner to safety.

Isak is concentrating his efforts in more central areas and here he almost gets played in behind but the ball just runs away from him. Better.

Worth mentioning that Jacquet has been fantastic in all phases of the game. Plenty of advanced regains and tidy passes forward.

It’s raining goals in Manchester and no prizes for guessing who has scored for Sunderland. Brobbey has his hat-trick.

Brobbey has his hat-trick and the look on Enzo Maresca’s face as he assesses the defending from his team. They’ve been great pouring forward, less so trying to stymie Sunderand’s attack. But this is one of those games where you just sit back and enjoy the unfolding drama. It’s been so good from both teams.

Semenyo gets his second goal of the afternoon to extend the league leaders’ advantage.

Chance! Jacquet jumps and wins the ball well inside Bournemouth’s half and his intervention sends the ball into Isak’s path. The forward just drags his effort wide and turns out he was in an offside postion anyhow.

What an afternoon this is turning out to be. There have been more slices than on an erratic day on the local municipal golf course and Ronald Araujo is the latest to be afflicted by the condition. None of that will matter to Andoni Iraola, though, as Alexander Isak’s fourth goal in four Premier League games has given Liverpool a huge advantage. They haven’t played with fluency but the breakthrough was significant.

Isak opens the scoring at the Vitality, finally getting into the box and sweeping in from close range. So much credit has to go to Gakpo who tiptoes past two Bournemouth defenders by the touchline before spearing a cross infield, and while he may not be attributed with the assist owing to a touch off Wirtz, his delivery makes it all the way through to Isak who taps in.

Alexander Isak grabs his fourth Premier League goal of the season! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/5ehwhl1it4

Adams has been superb as one of Bournemouth’s two midfield sentries. Kerkez looks to have been played into the left channel but the American swoops in and shields the ball out of play before staring down his Hungarian opponent.

Mitchell thinks he’s given the visitors the lead but his goal is ruled out for offside.

Tyrick Mitchell's opener is disallowed for an offside in the build up! ❌ pic.twitter.com/7y975TxaUj

Liverpool give up possession in Bournemouth’s half and Christie strides forward releasing Rayan before continuing his run to the near post. The Brazilian picks out his team-mate but Christie gets too strong a contact on the ball and the ball sails wide.

Truffert passes the ball straight to Gakpo inside his own box but Adams is on the scene in a flash and snaps into a tackle and takes the ball away from the Liverpool forward.

The second has already settled into a holding pattern, with neither side creating much. Isak makes a run down the right hand side and, with players loaded in the box, he blasts the ball high into the sky and beyond his team-mates. That pretty much sums things up.

Wirtz has given the ball away twice in the first minute of the second half. Carragher is on Sky Sports commentary duties and he says he’s surprised to see him back out on the pitch.

Szoboszlai concedes a foul on the far side but the subsequent delivery is too heavy and sails over everyone.

No half-time changes from either manager.

3 - This is the first time that @ManCity have taken the lead three times in the first half of a Premier League match.Overall, it's just the seventh time in competition history that a side has gone ahead on three separate occasions in a first half.Canvas. pic.twitter.com/JaQ4qDarls

Isak’s first-half heatmap makes for interesting reading. The good news, for Liverpool fans, is that he’s stationed himself predominantly in the final third. The bad news... those positions have been everywhere but the box.

There must be significant temptation to drift out to the wide areas and drop deep when the ball is not coming to you, but surely Liverpool need their No 9 closer to Bournemouth’s goal?

Bournemouth 0 Liverpool 0Leeds United 0 Crystal Palace 0 Manchester City 3 Sunderland 2

Big chance missed from Haaland of all people to make it 4-2 to City in what has been a pulsating, spell-binding first 45 minutes. It’s fast, furious and a helluva lot of fun to watch. Brilliant from Ndiaye to tee up Haaland who shoots wide of a post. A game for attackers shall we say ...

There are significant advantages to having a goalkeeper who is 6ft 5in with long arms and massive hands. Brobbey’s shot cannons off Guehi and would have looped over a number of goalkeeper but Donnarumma sticks out a giant arm to help nudge the ball over the bar and keep City 3-2 in front in the fifth minute of first half stoppages

Not a pretty half from the returning Iraola’s side, who will need to be much better in the second period to challenge for the three points.

Bournemouth have dropped points late on in a number of matches this season and will perhaps rue not being able to capitalise on their early advantage.

City are in front. Again. Semenyo this time, he fires the ball beyond Roefs having collected a loose ball int he box.

Antoine Semenyo gets his first goal of the season! 🎯 pic.twitter.com/1n2W5Cyxz0

A relatively slick Liverpool move sees the ball worked out to Araujo on the right who has minded to bomb on with increasing frequency, and while he’s able to win a corner, Szoboszlai’s delivery is cleared with a minimum of fuss.

Iraola came into this game saying that his side held an advantage having played two days earlier than Bournemouth in midweek. You would never have guessed it from what we have witnessed here today.

And right on cue, a frustrated Isak attempts a specultative effort from range which sails high and wide.

Sunderland are level again as Brobbey scores after lengthy VAR check for offside.

Sunderland fans sing “F--- VAR” and City fans boo the delay while they both awaited the verdict, which has now gone Sunderland’s way

Brian Brobbey levels it AGAIN! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/YvelzwnmY8

Can’t hold a lead today City. Wow, Sunderland are level again in an instant and it’s that man Brobbey again. There’s a VAR check going on to check for offside

So, this is not a rush to make a sweeping criticism, it’s simply an observation. But Liverpool fans will be looking at Bradley Barcola and  waiting to see that first burst, that moment of electricity, that has showed why they bought him. It’s like you look for a touch, a pass, a moment of skill. He’s just had a shot saved but it all seems very tentative for him at the moment. And that is what he needs - a moment.

Jacquet does brilliantly to close down Christie as the Scot was stealing into the box and looking to pull the trigger.

Chances! Barcola forces Petrovic into an awkward-looking save, before follow-up efforts from Wirtz and Gakpo are charged down.

Mac Allister is fouled 25 yards out moments later and Szoboszlai gets another go. Here, he drags his effort just wide.

It’s all happening at the Etihad. Cherki restores City’s lead with his third Premier League goal of the season.

It’s a great finish from Cherki to put City back in front but it doesn’t happen if Ndiaye is quick to read Danso’s risky pass and win possession. Sharp as a button in that moment.

Rayan Cherki puts Manchester City back in front! 💫 pic.twitter.com/PP4MAV9kw3

A really poor piece of defending from Kerkez gives Bournemouth a free-kick out on the right. Tavernier spins in an inswinger but Van Dijk heads clear. Truffert launches another assault on Liverpool’s box off the second phase but Alisson is wise to it and gathers.

It appears that Liverpool are beginning to settle, they take the opportunity to circulate the ball in front of Bournemouth’s first line of pressure, waiting for the right moment to pounce. The final pass is poor, though, and Araujo through-pass goes all the way through to Petrovic. It was aimed at Isak ...I think.

Some signs of life from Liverpool, as they create a substantial overload down their left, Kerkez, Mac Allister, Barcola and Isak meeting on that flank. Barcola attempts a sprint into the channel off the shoulder of the ball-side centre-back but he is deemed offside. Looked close, but a bit better from Liverpool.

Araujo has the chance to launch a long throw into the box but Silva beats Van Dijk to the summit and Petrovic gathers the loose ball.

Scott then sprays a wonderful ball over to Rayan on the right but his cutback to Tavernier comes to nothing after the midfielder loses the ball. Liverpool then spring a counter of their own, but Bournemouth recover and charge down a hopeful Gakpo effort from the edge of the box.

Liverpool will not be pleased with their start to this match. They’ve struggled to string more than three passes together without ceding possession and Isak has cut an isolated figure up top.

First time that Bournemouth have gone through the gears and the move ends with Alisson Becker saving brilliantly from Evanilson. It’s a funny stadium, here, as it can be quiet then all of a sudden a tempest whips up and you can sense the mood changing. Liverpool are struggling for alacrity and Andoni Iraola is keeping an eye on Florian Wirtz, who is moving gingerly after taking a bang to his left foot.

Some start at the Etihad. You had to wonder if a big early missed chance from Nilson Angulo was going to haunt Sunderland with City taking the lead just a few minutes later through a quite sublime free-kick from Enzo Fernandez. But Sunderland have immediately hit back. Maresca will decry the defending but it’s brilliant from Enzo Le Fee, who surges forward and then splits Nunes and Dias with an inch perfect pass that Brobbey takes beautifully in his stride before finishing.

On Fernandez’s free-kick before then, he’d very much shaped as if he’s going to cross the ball from a free-kick on the right side of the penalty area. He’d clearly spotted an opening in the top right though and, while giving the firm impression to Roefs he was going to whip in a cross, he obviously had other ideas. The execution was immaculate but it was telling just how effectively he’d managed to deceive the Sunderland goalkeeper. It was world class

A slight mix-up sees Kerkez and Wirtz bump into each other by the touchline. The Germany international limps away and grimaces but should be fine to continue.

Chance! Alisson makes amends with a stunning save. Tavernier had hit the by-line and lasered a cross to Evanilson who, with the ball slightly behind him, improvised and flicked it toward the near post. Alisson gets down swiftly and turns behind for a corner which comes to nothing.

Jacquet gives away a needless foul on the near side but Scott’s delivery goes straight into Alisson’s hands. The Brazilian’s throw out is poor, though, and Scott darts into Liverpool’s box, just unable to pick out a team-mate.

Barcola is presented with green grass to run into, but just as he builds a head of steam Hill comes across in a flash and snuffs out the foray forward.

Woah, Brobbey responds immediately, stealing in between City defenders before slotting past Donnarumma.

Instant response from Sunderland as Brian Brobbey equalises! 💥 pic.twitter.com/et6AHGPAbl

Enzo Fernandez opens the scoring at the Etihad with a direct free-kick from out wide. Really poor from Roefs who was caught napping. That’s Fernandez’s first City goal.

Enzo Fernandez gets his first Manchester City goal in style! 🤩 pic.twitter.com/fVOnJvACYY

Wirtz earns a free-kick just outside the D. Bournemouth feel aggrieved as there looked to have been an earlier foul on Scott and to make matters worse Szoboszlai is standing over the ball.

His effort leaves Petrovic rooted to the spot but the ball veers just wide of the mark.

Evanilson’s willingness to drop deep is asking questions of Liverpool’s centre-backs. Do they follow him and risk disrupting their backline coverage?

The hosts attempt to work a short corner routine but Truffert’s eventual through-ball is too strong and the ball rolls out for a Liverpool goal-kick.

This wouldn’t go down as a fixture you would circle for being noteworthy but make no mistake this is a huge afternoon for Liverpool. They have had some days at the Vitality Stadium in recent years and last season’s defeat put a huge dent in Arne Slot’s hopes of trying to find a revival. It’s also a big test for Bournemouth, coming down from the euphoria of beating Real Sociedad. Let’s see how it all transpires.

Evanilson makes a smart run into the right channel and while Jacquet gets his foot on the ball he’s instantly smothered by Scott and the ball goes out for a Liverpool goal-kick. A sign of how high both sides will be willing to jump in search of the ball.

Both sides will look to force mistakes out of the other and Szoboszlai is able to pick Adams’ pocket on the halfway line. He offloads to Araujo who runs into a cul de sac down the right flank.

We are under way at the Vitality. Bournemouth are in their customary black-and-red home shirts kicking from right to left and Liverpool are in their white away kit and red shorts.

The players have emerged from the tunnel, Van Dijk and Smith at the front of the lines. A few pyrotechnics add to the atmosphere but one thing missing is the accidental sitting in the wrong dugout from the returning Iraola. He knows where he’s going.

Here is a reminder of today’s squads in full:

Liverpool: Alisson; Araujo, Van Dijk, Jacquet, Kerkez; Mac Allister, Szoboszlai; Barcola, Wirtz, Gakpo; IsakSubstitutes: Mamardashvili, Gomez, Tsimikas, Frimpong, Gravenberch, Nyoni, Munoz, Koumas, Ngumoha

The Egyptian king grabbed his first hat-trick for Trabzonspor yesterday, in a 4-0 win over league-leaders Galatasaray no less. That’s his seventh goal in eight matches.

When Salah is happy, we're all happy 👑👑👑 pic.twitter.com/DtzaOl3hD3

"He's certainly very quick"Jamie Carragher's first impressions of Bradley Barcola ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/oXjzXBuZwm

Since losing to Arsenal 3-2 on January 3, Bournemouth have not lost at the Vitality in 12 matches, picking up four wins and eight draws.

Jan 7: Bournemouth 3 Tottenham Hotspur 2Jan 24: Bournemouth 3 Liverpool 2 Feb 7: Bournemouth 1 Aston Villa 1Feb 28: Bournemouth 1 Sunderland 1Mar 3: Bournemouth 0 Brentford 0Mar 20: Bournemouth 2 Manchester United 2Apr 22: Bournemouth 2 Leeds United 2May 3: Bournemouth 3 Crystal Palace 0 May 19: Bournemouth 1 Manchester City 1Aug 29: Bournemouth 1 Everton 1Sep 8: Bournemouth 4 Lincoln City 0 (League Cup)Sep 12: Bournemouth 2 Brentford 2

Andoni Iraola returns to Bournemouth this weekend knowing what to expect from players he understands so well. Sadly, I do not mean Liverpool’s.

Having built his reputation creating a hard-working, well-drilled team rich in potential, Iraola is responsible for infusing those same characteristics into the most expensively assembled squad in Liverpool history.

His first six games demonstrate it is no quick fix. The Basque coach is the first Liverpool appointment to work with more than £700m of recent signings while being entitled to feel he has been dealt a bad hand.

Everything Iraola has said and done so far screams that he is searching for the right blend in his starting XI while having to eradicate negative traits, with and without the ball. It was telling that the excellent performance of his youngsters against Tottenham Hotspur in midweek offered the clearest hint of Iraola’s vision than anything we have seen with all the high-priced stars on the pitch.

There is a reason the Kop stood to acclaim the energy and application of youngsters Lewis Koumas, James McConnell and Trey Nyoni – and why Iraola keeps name-checking them. Iraola is indebted to them for issuing a reminder of the non-negotiables that come with being a Liverpool footballer; regardless of price tag and reputation, leaving everything on the pitch is compulsory. It is a concern that so many of the renowned players need to hear that message.

Jurgen Klopp named Florian Wirtz in his first squad as Germany manager and has said that fans must refrain from expecting “special moments” from the Liverpool playmaker as a matter of course.

Of Wirtz, he said: “I think he’s the player who covered the most ground at Liverpool this season, so the willingness is absolutely there.

“We have to move away from the idea that we need to see special moments from him. He is there to help us as a team. We have to make sure that Flo feels comfortable with us.”

Wirtz has delivered seven goals and 11 assists in his 54 Liverpool appearances.

Adam Smith, 35, played for Iraola 81 times and he admitted his former manager’s visit to the Vitality will be a sentimental affair. He said: “It’s going to be an emotional day for everyone I think, [for] our ex-manager and some of our players that have played under him, but we’ll be up for the game for sure.”

Your Eagles at Elland Road 🦅 pic.twitter.com/QGBqKJoSD1

📋 Your #LUFC XI... pic.twitter.com/U0fRnjJLjv

Bournemouth signed Truffert from Rennes in the summer of 2025 to replace Kerkez – who had just joined Liverpool – and the left-back has been a revelation at the Vitality. So much so that this week he earned himself a call-up to Zinedine Zidane’s first France squad.

Truffert topped the charts for most overlapping runs by any player in Europe’s top five leagues last season and laid on five assists.

Virgil van Dijk says Liverpool are still a work in progress at the moment and there are a lot of positive signs ahead of their game against Bournemouth💪Watch Super Sunday live: https://t.co/0AejI4B8dF pic.twitter.com/oSMxxIw9lQ

Speaking before his return to the South Coast, Iraola said: “I know where we are going [the Vitality], and I know the stats they have there [unbeaten in 12 matches], not only in their stadium, overall, I think if you see the games they’ve lost in a long while, you realise how difficult it is to beat Bournemouth.

“But, I suppose I also have the advantage that I know them very well, they also have the advantage that they know me very well, so you never know who has more advantage in that sense.

He added: “On a personal side, I’m very much looking forward to meet them [his former players], to hug them. It’s players that I love, staff that I’ve been working with who I appreciate so much, and I was pushing for them [against Real Sociedad] when they were playing their first European game. I wish them all the best, but there is another part, which is the most important one right now that we need to go there and win.”

Just the one alternation to the side Rose fielded last weekend as Christie comes in for Kluivert.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the Premier League match between Liverpool and Bournemouth as Andoni Iraola returns to the Vitality Stadium for the first time since his big move up north. The Basque propelled Bournemouth to new heights, guiding the club into Europe and his successor, Marco Rose, ensured they made a winning start to life on the Continent by defeating Real Sociedad in midweek.

Previewing Iraola’s Vitality Stadium return, Craig Beazley, host and creator of the Up The Cherries In All Departments podcast, said: “We’ve now got the Andoni Iraola return … Andoni is very much a legend really, there should be a statue of Sir Eddie Howe and Sir Andoni Iraola [outside the ground] as well.”

Across three seasons, Iraola guided Bournemouth to 12th, ninth and sixth in the Premier League, winning 47 of his 127 matches in charge (37 per cent).

Liverpool are still acclimatising to his exacting style of play and their results suggest as much. They are 10th in the table having drawn three and won one, impressing in flashes but struggling to maintain consistently productive final-third patterns and pressing structures. Deploying Ronald Araújo at right-back has proved effective, though, with Liverpool conceding just two goals in their last four matches.

The Cherries are searching for their first Premier League win of the season and have retained the 4-2-3-1 shape from the Iraola days, with Rose preferring a similarly vertical attacking strategy. They continue to leverage their strengths in transitions and in wide areas as Adrien Truffert rains in crosses for any one of Bournemouth’s exuberant frontline to pounce on.

Elsewhere, Manchester City welcome Sunderland, who also secured a Europa League win during the week, to the Etihad while in-form Leeds United host Crystal Palace knowing a win would lift them into the top four.

#1477. Emiliano Martinez reveals his finger 'won't ever return' to normal after injury left him playing like a 'zombie' during World Cup: 'I cried every day'

Published: 19:19 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 19:33 EDT, 30 October 2026

Emiliano Martinez has revealed his finger will never return to normal after he played through injury to represent Argentina at the World Cup.

Martinez broke and dislocated a finger in the warm-up before playing for Aston Villa in their Europa League final triumph over Freiburg in May.

The 34-year-old told Argentine journalist Gaston Edul’s YouTube channel that he cried after seeing x-rays having feared he would be ruled out of Argentina's World Cup title defence.

After receiving support from Argentina boss Lionel Scaloni, Martinez explained a decision was taken to avoid undergoing surgery that would have ruled him out of the tournament.

Martinez was instead provided with a special glove from Adidas to protect the injured finger, which he admitted meant he could not grasp the ball properly.

'It will never go back to how it was,' Martinez said. 'I am still playing with pain.'

Emiliano Martinez has revealed his finger will never return to normal after he played through injury to represent Argentina at the World Cup. Source: YouTube/Gastón Edul

Martinez sustained a broken finger before playing for Aston Villa in the Europa League final

The shot stopper wore a special glove from Adidas to protect his injured finger to ensure he could play at the World Cup, but admits he will need surgery in the future

'The day before Algeria I was diving with one arm, diving like a zombie.

'If I put my hand down I was seeing stars. It was brutal. Every single night I was crying because my finger looked like a sausage.

'But these are the risks you take for the national team, I’d do it again.'

Martinez added that a summer transfer to Italy – with Juventus having targeted the star – ultimately collapsed as a direct result of the injury.

'I got an x-ray and it was broken again,' Martinez said. 'That is when a transfer to a club fell through because of the finger.

'They said it was possible for me to play like that, that I needed surgery, but Chelsea didn't, they didn't care. One day I will need surgery.'

Martinez, who joined Chelsea for £7.5million in the summer, is currently recovering from a broken jaw sustained in their victory over Everton earlier this month.

#1476. Why Burnley gambled on Fabio Celestini, an unknown Swiss inspired by Che Guevara who boxes, dances and was an electrical engineer, to spark their season back to life - and why his new players are already worried about him

Published: 22:00 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 22:00 EDT, 30 October 2026

Not many football managers have a tattoo of Che Guevara, dance in their free time and speak five languages.

But they are just three quirks which add to the layers of intrigue around Burnley's new boss Fabio Celestini, an unknown Swiss tasked with saving the Clarets from double relegation and dropping into the third tier for the first time since 2000.

After four wins in the last year, with morale in the gutter, Burnley announced Celestini as Nicky Hayen's successor on Wednesday. Many fans will have dropped their marmalade. Who? Celestini's CV is promising but this is an almighty gamble and they cannot afford for things to go wrong.

The Clarets sit 22nd in the Championship and have won just one home game inside 90 minutes in 2026. Their summer was an unmitigated disaster – they had woeful pre-season results, went 71 days without a manager, sold last campaign's top scorer Zian Flemming on deadline day with no replacement, and their chief executive, James Holroyd, walked out in September after difficulties working alongside chairman Alan Pace.

The club is in £142million of debt, according to their latest accounts, with £13m in cash in the coffers. The phrase 'basket case' comes to mind.

Celestini's appointment falls squarely on the shoulders of new chief football officer Diego Lopez, another stranger to English football, and it is one Burnley's players are unsure about.

Fabio Celestini is facing an uphill battle to avoid relegation with Burnley, who sit 22nd in the Championship

Belgian boss Nicky Hayen lasted just 12 league matches - and won only once

Burnley have not been in the third tier since 2000 but are staring down the barrel of a second successive relegation

Daily Mail Sport understands that some members of the squad have reservations about Celestini's style of play – he has favoured a possession-based 4-2-3-1 throughout his career, a system which Hayen tried and failed to implement during his time in charge.

Many clubs have turned to outsiders and succeeded – just look at table-toppers Middlesbrough under Kim Hellberg – but the lack of Championship experience in Burnley's management structure leaves Celestini to navigate a steep learning curve without much support.

On the bright side, Celestini inherited a similarly shambolic case at Basel in October 2023 and thrived. The Swiss giants were bottom of the table and had had to cancel their goal of the month award, because they hadn't scored any. Celestini saved them from relegation, restored the feel-good factor by re-signing club legend Xherdan Shaqiri, and won them the league and cup double the following season.

The 50-year-old former Switzerland midfielder – who won 35 caps for his country and played against England's Golden Generation at Euro 2004 – also has a promotion on his ledger from his time at Lausanne and a Swiss Cup with Luzern. He also led Lugano into Europe and managed Sion.

'Celestini is a determined, ambitious personality, but he can also be a stubborn coach and that has caused issues at several clubs,' Swiss football expert Craig King (@FootballSwissEN on X) tells Daily Mail Sport.

'He is capable of providing clubs with a short-term bounce before it eventually deteriorates. He has strong ideas, but his stubbornness often tends to rub people the wrong way.

'It seems that inevitably, he loses control of his teams somewhere along the way and can never get them back on track.'

His time at Russian giants CSKA Moscow, last season after he left Basel, followed that trend.  He had found out about their interest on a holiday with his dancer wife, Fanny, in the Seychelles, and took the plunge, rocking up with a Spanish-speaking coaching coterie. He even appointed his wife to help edit video clips for analysis and support in aspects of communication, a club source tells Daily Mail Sport.

He enjoyed a strong start at CSKA – he won the Russian Super Cup in his first match and they led the Russian Premier League after 11 games. Going into the winter break, they were just four points off top in fourth.

'Fabio has done a tremendous job,' the club's general director Roman Babaev said during that hiatus. 'There was beautiful football.'

By the end of Celestini's tenure in May, Babaev was describing a 'lack of self-confidence and a lack of belief in their ability to turn the situation around'. He added: 'We agreed that things could only get worse – the head coach doubted the team was listening to him.'

Celestini won 35 caps for Switzerland and appeared against England at Euro 2004

Burnley are Celestini's eighth club as a manager, having left CSKA Moscow by mutual consent in May

What changed? Reports in Russia claimed that over the winter break, players had been unimpressed with the lack of physical and defensive work, with too much emphasis on attacking and set-pieces. They lost their first three games back after the break, suffered a humbling 4-0 thrashing by Krasnodar in the Russian Cup, and went winless in Celestini's final five matches in charge.

In the space of two months, everything had unravelled. After defender Moises was sent off in the drubbing at Krasnodar, Celestini reprimanded the player in the dressing room – but the Brazilian hit back, questioning his manager's competence in front of the team. Moises was subsequently suspended and the club took Celestini's side.

'I felt like something was missing, I wasn't feeling well, something wasn't right. Other players started saying they weren't feeling well,' Moises later reflected in the documentary We Are CSKA. 'To become a champion, you need to cleanse yourself of all dirt. I blurted it all out because I knew what was simmering inside us all.'

Celestini is still well thought of at CSKA and was always willing to take accountability rather than criticise his players publicly. Former manager Viktor Goncharenko claimed that he ultimately failed because he 'didn't find common ground with the CSKA veterans', such as legendary goalkeeper Igor Akinfeev, and didn't have enough Russian coaches. He left with the club sixth in the table.

Celestini's task now is to turn around a flailing Burnley. His first assignment will be on Saturday at Turf Moor against in-form Portsmouth. Based off how he describes himself, he does not come across as a disciplinarian. Celestini says he does not like implementing fines and is not a fan of throwing things across a dressing room.

'This kind of half-time behavior might only work once a season,' he once said. 'It's like an electric shock.'

At his heart Celestini appears to be an idealist. Earlier in his career he established a foundation to support players from underprivileged backgrounds and he set up a football school in Havana.

His tattoo of Cuban revolutionary Guevara cost 180 Swiss francs (£163). He has lost count of his tattoos by now, also inking his kids and a depiction of good triumphing over evil.

Celestini appears to be an idealist. Earlier in his career he established a foundation to support players from underprivileged backgrounds and he set up a football school in Havana

Daily Mail Sport understands some Burnley players have reservations about Celestini's possession-based 4-2-3-1, a system which Hayen failed to implement

'I started reading about (Guevara), studying him. My tattoo depicts him without his military beret. There are no political references,' he said. 'What attracts me to him is that he fought his whole life for those who had nothing to do with him, and I've also fought a lot in my life, so I decided to get it.'

Another of his heroes is Nelson Mandela: 'He also dedicated his entire life to his ideas. Anyone who fought for their ideals is important to me. I admire people who take the time to help others. I don’t consider myself a good person, but I’m not a hypocrite.'

Away from football, Celestini – who speaks Italian, French, Spanish, German and English – also dances with his wife and enjoys boxing. A former electrical draughtsman, he has a good work ethic and, we hear, made a strong push for the Burnley job.

A source at the Clarets, who were also interested in Rob Edwards and Carlos Corberan, insists that Celestini was their first choice. Now they are counting on him to deliver a minor miracle.

#1475. Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The N7-methylguanosine (m7G) modification is one of the most prevalent tRNA modifications, mainly catalysed by the METTL1–WDR4 protein complex1,2,3,4. The m7G methyltransferase METTL1 has been linked to oncogenic transformation and the maintenance of several aggressive malignancies; however, the clinical implications of therapeutically targeting a tRNA-modifying enzyme have not been established. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a highly selective and potent first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1. Treatment of numerous cancer cell models (including leukaemia, melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma, oesophageal cancer and small cell lung carcinoma) with STM9005 blocks cell growth, causes differentiation changes and dysregulates cell cycle progression. These cellular effects were accompanied by a selective decrease in m7G on a subset of tRNAs and a reduction in their expression levels, which impacted the translation of oncogenic mRNAs. We show that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and significantly prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin. Collectively, our results provide a strong proof of concept that targeting of tRNA methylation is a promising avenue of anti-cancer therapy and illustrate that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 represents a therapeutic strategy against a number of aggressive malignancies.

Over 150 RNA modifications have been described to date, with transfer RNA (tRNA) being one of the most highly modified RNA species5,6. tRNA modifications are critical for the folding, stability and function of tRNA2,7,8. One of the most prevalent tRNA modifications is m7G1,2. It is deposited at position 46 of tRNA (m7G46) by the METTL1–WDR4 heterodimeric protein complex, with METTL1 functioning as the catalytically active component of the complex, and WDR4 having a scaffolding and RNA-binding role2,3,4. The m7G modification on tRNA has been shown to have an important role in stabilizing the tRNA structure, regulating the translation of mRNA and influencing a number of cellular processes, including stress response and oncogenesis9,10,11,12,13. Recent studies have shown that METTL1 may also deposit the m7G modification on mRNAs and microRNA precursors14,15,16, although at a substantially lower rate compared with the m7G levels on the tRNA fraction.

Many studies have implicated the role of the epitranscriptome in the development and regulation of cancer17,18,19. An increasing amount of evidence shows that dysregulation of tRNA modifications and their pathways contributes to the pathogenesis of human disease, including cancer6,18. Notably, upregulation of METTL1 and its catalytic activity has been linked to oncogenic transformation as well as the initiation and maintenance of aggressive haematological and solid malignancies, including acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), melanoma, glioblastoma, liver and lung cancers11,20,21,22. Moreover, the non-catalytic function of METTL1 has recently been linked to the development of sarcomas through its interaction with the multi-tRNA synthetase complex23.

To date, epitranscriptomic drug discovery efforts have largely focused on the targeting of the m6A mRNA modification and its regulators24,25,26,27. Early prototype inhibitors of METTL1 have recently been described and support the feasibility of pharmacologically inhibiting METTL128,29. However, their limited potency and selectivity render them unsuitable as tools to assess the molecular and therapeutic impact of targeting METTL1 catalytic inhibition. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a potent and highly selective first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1 that demonstrates significant anti-tumour activity across diverse cancer types through the reduction in m7G on tRNA substrates of METTL1.

We performed a high-throughput screen of 250,000 diverse drug-like compounds. After initial hit triaging, STM4529 was identified as a singleton non-S-adenosyl methionine (non-SAM)-related hit that inhibited METTL1 with a half-maximum inhibitory concentration (IC50) of around 15 μM (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analysis showed that STM4529 binding to METTL1 was competitive with the SAM analogue S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH), indicating its binding to the catalytic site of METTL1 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). After extensive chemical optimization of potency, selectivity and in vitro and in vivo absorption–distribution–metabolism–excretion properties, we identified STM9005 (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Note 1a).

a, The chemical structure of STM9005. b, Representative biochemical activity assay showing inhibition of the METTL1–WDR4 enzyme complex using a concentration range of STM9005 and the less active analogue STM9001. c, Representative METTL1 cellular target engagement of STM9005 and STM9001 was assessed using the InCELL Pulse assay. STM9005 inhibited recombinant METTL1 enzyme activity with an IC50 < 13 nM, a value restricted by the lower detection limit of the assay (Fig. 1b). To use a more sensitive assay system and to verify binding to METTL1 in an orthogonal system, we performed SPR analysis, which demonstrated direct stoichiometric high-affinity binding of STM9005 to METTL1 with a Kd of 2 nM (Extended Data Fig. 1d). Moreover, using a cellular target engagement assay, we confirmed cell penetration and binding of STM9005 to METTL1 in cells with an IC50 of 13 nM (Fig. 1c). STM9005 was found to be highly specific to METTL1 as it had no effect on the activity of other RNA-methyltransferases (METTL3/14, METTL16, BCDIN3D, TSG1 and NSUN2) when used at comparable concentrations (Extended Data Fig. 1e), and exhibited greater than 10,000-fold selectivity for METTL1–WDR4 when tested against a broad panel of 49 RNA-, DNA- and protein-methyltransferases (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 1). Moreover, no significant off-target toxicity liabilities were identified when STM9005 was tested in a broad panel of 97 kinases (KINOMEscan, Eurofins DiscoverX; Supplementary Table 2) and over 70 assays testing a range of receptors and enzymes commonly associated with drug toxicity (SAFETYscan 47, Eurofins DiscoverX; Supplementary Table 3).

To further investigate the cellular activity of STM9005, we applied RNA mass spectrometry (MS) to assess the specific effect of STM9005 on the m7G modification level of tRNA from the previously known METTL1-dependent AML cell lines MOLM-13 and OCI-AML211,30,31. We observed a significant decrease in m7G levels (Fig. 1e), but not in the levels of the m1A and m5C RNA modifications (Extended Data Fig. 1f). To further quantify the cellular effect of STM9005 on m7G-modified tRNA, we developed an antibody-based m7G detection assay (Meso Scale Discovery (MSD)), which enabled us to measure the effect of STM9005 on tRNA-Val. This demonstrated a concentration-dependent decrease in tRNA-Val-m7G after treatment with STM9005 with an IC50 of 34 nM (Extended Data Fig. 1g), confirming potent inhibition of tRNA modification by STM9005 in cells at nanomolar concentrations. Moreover, we confirmed STM9005 acts specifically on the METTL1–m7G tRNA axis, as we observed no significant effect on m7G modification of 18S ribosomal RNA (Extended Data Fig. 1h).

To characterize the binding of STM9005 to METTL1 further, we performed X-ray crystallography, confirming unequivocally that STM9005 binds to the SAM-binding site of METTL1 (Fig. 1f, Extended Data Fig. 1i, Extended Data Table 1 and Supplementary Note 1b). Notably, part of STM9005 binds in a pocket not previously observed in METTL1 crystal structures, where it forms molecular interactions such as the hydrogen bonds between Tyr184 and the central carbonyl moiety of STM9005, and a pi-carbon interaction between Phe159 and the tetrahydroisoquinoline methyl of STM9005, providing the basis for its high affinity and selectivity. In strong support of this, STM9001, a diastereomer of STM9005 in which the tetrahydroisoquinoline methyl is in an opposite orientation, is around 100-fold less active (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a,g), providing further evidence of the specificity and binding mode of STM9005 (Extended Data Fig. 1i and Supplementary Table 1).

The observed binding of STM9005 to the catalytic pocket of METTL1 did not impact the RNA or protein levels of METTL1 after in vitro treatment (Extended Data Fig. 1j,k), in contrast to the significant and selective effect observed on the m7G tRNA modification levels (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 1f,g). Finally, pharmacokinetic profiling of STM9005 in mice after a single intraperitoneal (i.p.) dose of either 10 or 30 mg per kg showed good bioavailability with maximal plasma exposures of 13 and 56 μM, respectively, and a half-life of around 1 h. Importantly, at the 12 h time point, STM9005 plasma levels remain above the METTL1 cellular IC50, indicating METTL1 inhibition in vivo over a period of at least 12 h (Fig. 1g).

Taken together, these data establish STM9005 as a potent, selective and bioavailable catalytic inhibitor of METTL1 that is suitable for both in vitro and in vivo investigations.

To investigate the anti-cancer potential of STM9005 in cellular models, we initially screened the impact of STM9005 treatment in three different cancer cell panels using colorimetric assays which measure metabolic activity (MTS assay). For these experiments, we used cancer cell models that were either previously reported to be sensitive to the genetic inhibition of METTL111,32,33, or their METTL1-dependency status (sensitivity or resistance) was validated here using CRISPR-based genetic disruption of METTL1/Mettl1 (human and mouse, respectively) in competitive co-culture assays (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). We observed a dose-dependent reduction in the proliferation of human leukaemic cell lines (Fig. 2a), primary mouse AML models (Fig. 2b) and human and mouse solid cancer models (Fig. 2c) from different tissue origins (skin, lung, pancreas, colorectal, oesophageal and soft tissue). Investigating the direct effect of STM9005 on cell growth using a methylene blue assay, we observed highly potent, dose-dependent effects on the fitness and growth of a subset of these cell lines (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Additional reprofiling in proliferation assays using ATP quantitation under optimized culture conditions confirmed the anti-proliferative activity of STM9005 at submicromolar concentrations in these cells (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3b). By contrast, the diastereomer control compound STM9001 was significantly less potent in these systems, consistent with its reduced activity against the catalytic activity of METTL1, providing strong evidence that the anti-proliferative effects of STM9005 are due to METTL1 catalytic inhibition (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3b). There was also a significant dose-dependent negative effect seen in the colony forming potential of MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+-driven primary mouse AML cells after ex vivo treatment with STM9005 (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Notably, the cancer models that appeared to be independent of METTL1 genetic loss (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b) were also not significantly impacted after treatment with STM9005 (Fig. 2d). To confirm that the anti-proliferative effects of STM9005 are mediated specifically through METTL1, we assessed its impact in two insensitive (OE33, mPDAC2) and two sensitive (B16F10, mPDAC1) cancer cell lines with a loss of METTL1 or Mettl1 after CRISPR–Cas9 targeting. STM9005 treatment in both sensitive and insensitive cell lines resulted in no additional negative effect (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e) despite the absence of METTL1 protein (Extended Data Figs. 2a,b and 3a), consistent with the small molecule exerting its mechanism of action specifically through inhibition of METTL1’s catalytic activity.

In the context of haematological malignancies, pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 using STM9005 caused significant and dose-dependent myeloid differentiation in both human and primary mouse models of AML (Fig. 2f,g and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Moreover, we and others have previously shown that genetic inhibition of METTL1 negatively affected various cancer models by impacting their cell cycle status11,20. To examine whether the observed effect on cell cycle is dependent on the catalytic activity of METTL1 we analysed a panel of solid cancer cell lines with different tissues of origin and mutational background and showed that treatment with STM9005 causes a significant disruption of cell cycle, with a dose-dependent increase in cells in G0/G1 phase and a significantly decreased number of cells in S phase (Fig. 2h,i and Extended Data Fig. 3g,h) as the most common changes across the cell lines tested. Moreover, western blot analysis of cell-cycle-related markers confirmed the observed cell cycle dysregulation seen in the various cancer models tested here (Fig. 2j,k). Moreover, annexin V analysis showed no significant levels of apoptosis after treatment with STM9005 (Extended Data Fig. 3i).

These data confirm the importance of METTL1’s methyltransferase activity in maintaining both haematological and solid cancers, and that pharmacological inhibition of its enzymatic activity is sufficient to elicit anti-cancer cellular effects.

To assess the molecular changes caused by treatment with STM9005, we analysed its impact across different layers of the transcriptome. We first performed modification-induced misincorporation tRNA sequencing (mim-tRNA-seq) to investigate the m7G modification status on tRNA fractions from B16F10 melanoma tumours and a primary mouse MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+-driven AML. Analysis of the mim-tRNA-seq data revealed a highly specific and significant reduction in the m7G46 mark in known m7G-modified tRNAs—a result that was highly similar between both cancer models (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 4).

Subsequent investigation of differential tRNA expression from the same two cancer models showed selective downregulation of a subset of m7G-modified tRNAs after pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Table 5), which was validated using northern blotting across a panel of m7G-modified tRNA substrates (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 4a).

We previously showed that the catalytic function of METTL1 drives the translation of key oncogenic proteins, including CDK4 and KDM1A, by modifying and stabilizing a subset of tRNAs11. To explore the dependence of these outcomes on METTL1’s catalytic activity, we performed western blotting using a panel of cancer models from diverse tissues, confirming that CDK4 and KDM1A protein levels were reduced after STM9005 treatment in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 4b), while the same was not seen with corresponding mRNA levels (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d). To verify that STM9005’s mechanism of action is mediated by inhibition of the m7G–tRNA axis, we performed rescue-of-phenotype experiments by overexpressing either the established METTL1–m7G tRNA substrate Arg-TCT or the METTL1 biomarker CDK4, a known substrate of Arg-TCT11. Notably, overexpression of Arg-TCT tRNA in both a solid cancer and a leukaemia model (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 4e–g) led to a partial but significant response to STM9005 and an increase in the viability of the cancer cells. Similarly, overexpression of Cdk4 in both a solid cancer and a leukaemia model (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 4h–j) mirrored the partial rescue of phenotype seen when using Arg-TCT tRNA overexpression, supporting the conclusion that the cellular effects caused by STM9005 treatment are dependent on the m7G–tRNA molecular pathway, which is maintained by the catalytic activity of METTL1.

To further validate that STM9005 acts specifically by inhibiting the catalytic function of METTL1 we overexpressed wild-type (WT) METTL1 and mutant (MUT) METTL1 carrying two amino acid changes in the catalytic domain (L160A/D164A for human METTL1 and L154A/D157A for mouse Mettl1). Forced expression of WT METTL1/Mettl1 significantly increased cellular resistance to STM9005, whereas viability did not improve in cells overexpressing METTL1MUT/Mettl1MUT (Fig. 3g,h and Extended Data Fig. 4k,l), confirming that STM9005 exerts its effects through the inhibition of the catalytic activity of METTL1. Moreover, the reduction in the levels of known m7G-dependent protein substrates, such as CDK4 and KDM1A, is reversed when WT METTL1 is overexpressed, while the same is not seen with overexpression of METTL1MUT (Extended Data Fig. 4m). This further accentuates that STM9005’s activity is specifically driven by the catalytic inhibition of METTL1.

To assess the wider downstream effects of STM9005 treatment on global translation, we used ribosome sequencing (Ribo-seq). After treatment with STM9005, Ribo-seq and mRNA sequencing (mRNA-seq) changes were moderately correlated (r = 0.6368; Extended Data Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 6), suggesting that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 affects gene expression at both the transcription and translational levels. Ribosome-protected RNA fragment (RPF) density analysis showed that, after treatment with STM9005, there was a significant increase in A-site ribosome occupancy at codons associated with m7G-modified tRNAs compared with those associated with non-m7G modified tRNAs (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c and Supplementary Table 7), suggesting ribosome stalling at sites that are dependent on m7G-modified tRNAs for decoding. Importantly, treatment did not reduce the protein levels of METTL1 (Extended Data Fig. 1k), METTL3 and WDR4 (Extended Data Fig. 5d) at any of the concentrations tested, confirming that the effects seen can be attributed to the catalytic inhibition of METTL1, rather than a global translation defect. To further validate our Ribo-seq findings, we compared genes downregulated in our Ribo-seq dataset with a published SILAC-based proteomic dataset from METTL1 knockdown and METTL1(WT)–WDR4 overexpression studies11. Genes downregulated after STM9005 treatment showed significant overlap with those reduced after short-hairpin-RNA-mediated depletion of METTL1 (shMETTL1; P < 1 × 10−5; Extended Data Fig. 5e and Supplementary Table 8) and were likewise enriched among genes upregulated by METTL1(WT)–WDR4 overexpression (P < 1 × 10−5; Extended Data Fig. 5f and Supplementary Table 8), further confirming on-target, catalysis-dependent effects on the METTL1-regulated translatome. This demonstrates that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 using STM9005 selectively alters the m7G-modified tRNA pool and therefore impacts translation, in concordance with our previous findings using genetic downregulation of METTL1 levels11.

To assess the molecular changes caused by treatment with STM9005 on the mRNA transcriptome, we performed mRNA-seq and differential expression analysis using three cancer models (OE21, LoVo and B16F10) treated with either vehicle or STM9005 (Supplementary Tables 9–11). Gene Ontology analysis of differentially expressed genes showed that treatment with STM9005 dysregulates several key oncogenic pathways, including pathways such as those regulated by MYC, PI3K–AKT–mTOR, p53 and, as shown earlier, the cell cycle (Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Tables 12–14).

Previous studies have associated METTL1 with the transcriptional regulation of MYC and its pathways12,34. However, there is a lack of evidence directly linking the catalytic function of METTL1 to the regulation of MYC. To directly address this, we investigated whether the observed changes in expression of MYC, caused by isolated catalytic inhibition of METTL1, were evident at the MYC protein level. Indeed, western blot analysis confirmed that treatment with STM9005 leads to a dose-dependent decrease in MYC protein levels in two independent cancer models (Extended Data Fig. 6b), while the same reduction was not seen at the mRNA level (Extended Data Fig. 6c), showing that METTL1 regulates MYC protein levels through its catalytic function. To explore the potential of STM9005 treatment impacting cancer growth through the downstream regulation of MYC levels, we performed rescue-of-phenotype experiments by overexpressing MYC in a human and a mouse solid cancer model. Our experiments showed that MYC overexpression increased viability after treatment with STM9005 compared with the empty vector control (Extended Data Fig. 6d–g), indicating that the negative impact of STM9005 on cancer cells could be partially connected to negative regulation of MYC and its pathways.

Finally, we confirmed that, despite the transcript and protein level dysregulation of several cancer-associated pathways after treatment with STM9005, transcript and protein levels of METTL1 remained unaffected (Extended Data Fig. 6h and Extended Data Fig. 1j), highlighting again that the effects observed were due to the catalytic inhibition of METTL1.

Taken together, our mechanistic analysis further confirms the specificity and selectivity of our small-molecule approach and that treatment with STM9005 affects METTL1-mediated m7G modification levels, which in turn causes defects in the translation and gene regulation of cancer-essential biomarkers.

Given our strong evidence for potency, specificity and anti-cancer efficacy of STM9005 in vitro, we performed a series of in vivo experiments using both solid cancers and leukaemia models.

Initially, we tested the in vivo activity of STM9005 using three solid tumour models from different tissues (melanoma, pancreatic ductal carcinoma (PDAC) and lung adenocarcinoma). For the first in vivo solid-tumour experiment, we transplanted immunocompetent mice subcutaneously with B16F10 mouse melanoma cells and treated them twice daily with 30 mg per kg STM9005 for 5 days (Extended Data Fig. 7a). This treatment plan led to a significant decrease in tumour size of the STM9005-treated cohort in comparison to the vehicle-treated mice (Fig. 4a,b and Extended Data Fig. 7b). To confirm on-target activity of STM9005 in vivo, we quantified m7G levels on tRNA extracted from melanoma tumours and kidney tissues of control and treated mice. Notably, we detected significantly lower levels of m7G tRNA modification in the tumours (Fig. 4c) and kidneys (Fig. 4d) of animals treated with STM9005 compared with the vehicle-treated cohort, demonstrating catalytic inhibition of METTL1 in vivo. We also confirmed a significant decrease in MYC and, simultaneously, a significant increase in p53 after in vivo treatment of melanoma tumours with STM9005 (Fig. 4e–g), providing strong proof of a mechanism consistent with reduction of cancer proliferation in vivo and complementing our previous in vitro findings (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b).
