#1454. Buoyant Bairns are a different beast this year after summer rebuild... and that spells bad news for Celtic

Published: 15:07 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 15:14 EDT, 31 October 2026

Was there ever any doubt that Falkirk would eventually get over their sticky start to the season and begin making their way up the Premiership table?

Well yes, actually. Quite a lot of it, in fact.

A mass exodus over the summer saw 17 depart, including a host of key players who helped the side upset the odds last season by making the top six.

Barney Stewart and Calvin Miller left for West Bromwich Albion and Hearts respectively – both bringing in a tidy profit for the club in the process – with Dylan Tait making the move to Premiership rivals Dundee United and Ben Broggio going back to Aston Villa after an impressive loan spell north of the border.

The excellent defensive pair of Filip Lissah and Kyrell Wilson also returned to parent club Swansea, with the former now an automatic starter for the promotion-chasers while the latter is plying his trade in the Belgian top flight with Gent.

Replacing that lot was rightly viewed by most as a near-impossible task. Top six? Forget it.

And results over the first couple of months suggested that survival might have to be the main priority for this year.

Falkirk striker Jacob Murrell has scored four goals in his last five Premiership games

But as we enter November, it appears as though those fears were unfounded. We should have known better than to doubt Falkirk at all.

It’s taken a while – certainly longer than manager John McGlynn would have liked – but his new-look squad are finally starting to find their feet.

Winning three on the bounce in the Premiership is no small feat. Indeed, for all the plaudits Falkirk rightly earned on their march to the top half last season, that was something they failed to achieve.

And the most encouraging aspect of this mini-run is that they’ve managed to do it in a very un-Falkirk way.

Motherwell aside, Falkirk were the most entertaining side to watch in the top flight last term, just as they were as they swept away the opposition in League One and the Championship on their incredible journey up the divisions.

It’s not necessarily for a lack of trying, but the free-flowing style which has been the blueprint for so much of their success in recent times has been all but abandoned over the past fortnight.

Aside from two moments of real quality from striker Jacob Murrell at Easter Road, the three points were largely earned thanks to a gritty, dig-your-heels-in kind of performance.

Murrell and fellow American CJ Fodrey have been taken into the hearts of Bairns fans

The 3-0 victory against Kilmarnock the following week was fairly comfortable in terms of the scoreline. But the hoolie provided by Storm Boelo rendered that affair a war of attrition rather than a game of football.

And then up at Pittodrie midweek, McGlynn himself admitted that the display was one to be endured rather than enjoyed.

That his side have collected nine points from nine in their last three outings despite being miles off their top level bodes well going forward. Not chucking in late goals has certainly helped spark this upturn in fortunes too.

Dundee United, St Johnstone and Dundee have all taken points off the Bairns this season with virtually the last kick of the ball. They could be five points better off at this stage had they managed to hold out. All ifs and buts, of course.

Yet, at the moment, they don’t even look like conceding. From back to front, the team is gelling together nicely.

Winning with a swagger is all good and well, and that will always be the aim for as long as McGlynn is at the helm. But we’re now seeing a side demonstrating they are every bit as capable of doing it the ugly way if required.

In some ways, the manager might take greater satisfaction in that, at least in the short term.

McGlynn, of course, deserves the bulk of the credit for turning things around. He has completely rebuilt this squad without complaint. The nature of the job and all that.

John McGlynn has once again proven himself a master in the art of squad rebuilding

And, in that regard, he has put several others with significantly bigger budgets to shame. Not that he has ever needed a particularly big budget to succeed anyway.

His eye for a player remains razor sharp. Nineteen-year-old Owen Eames isn’t realistically going to produce anything like the numbers supplied by his predecessor Miller – few could. But the Derby County loanee has taken no time at all to settle into this team. He’s getting better with each passing week.

The same can be said of the chap playing in front of him. Murrell has come a long way from missing two absolute sitters against Rangers on his home debut back in September, scoring five in his seven appearances since.

The American was never remotely prolific throughout his time with DC United in the MLS. In truth, there was little on his CV that would suggest he would be able to cut it. But fair play to him – and the Falkirk scouting team for that matter – for proving the rest of us wrong.

Murrell will no doubt be rubbing his hands at the prospect of going up against a Celtic defence which has been a doddle to get at all season long.

He is playing with the confidence of a guy who only needs one chance to find the back of the net. Against this opposition – top of the table or not – he may well get a few opportunities.

Falkirk have lost their last ten against Sunday’s visitors. However, considering the way they’re playing, this should be viewed as a genuine opportunity to halt that horrid sequence.

#1452. Lethal Trent Alexander-Arnold sends Tuchel a statement in England victory

Thomas Tuchel has never been inclined to place much faith in the most famous right-back at his disposal, Trent Alexander-Arnold, once of Liverpool, now of Real Madrid, and – back in an England shirt – still capable of changing games in the blink of an eye.

England always looked likely to defeat a beleaguered Czech Republic team down to 10 men with just 25 minutes played, but it still required one man to conjure the moment of inspiration in this Nations League tie. This was the first cap in 15 months for the right-back now known simply as “Trent” in an England shirt – as well as his Real Madrid jersey – rather than the six syllables of his surname. With the game level at half-time, two minutes into the new half, he twice won the ball before landing a cross on the head of Anthony Gordon for the first goal.

TRENT ➡️ GORDON ⚽️🔥Anthony Gordon can't stop scoring for England, 3 goals in his last 3 games for England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/xmqPIULJ24

Will the Alexander-Arnold with England experiment survive? One feels that Tuchel will need a little more to convince him to abandon whatever reservations he has about the Liverpudlian. A week short of his 28th birthday, Alexander-Arnold was winning just his 35th cap. His Real Madrid team-mate Jude Bellingham, a second-half substitute, was earning his 58th cap less than two months after his 23rd birthday. Bellingham was on as captain in place of the man he replaced, Harry Kane, scorer of England’s second. Bellingham’s international career has taken a much less rocky path than that of his Real team-mate.

Having missed the World Cup finals this summer, and had little good fortune around previous tournaments, one wonders if Euro 2028 might be the watershed moment for Alexander-Arnold. Either way, against opponents who sit back, he is lethal when it is time for the big delivery. Alexander-Arnold may not have the breadth of England experience that some of his peers have accumulated, but he does have plenty of experience of big games.

“I make that run time and time again,” Gordon said of his anticipation of the Alexander-Arnold cross, “but only a set number of players have that ability, that technique and the bravery to risk a mistake to play that pass. And that’s why I have been dying to play with him [Alexander-Arnold]. He’s been on his own journey but has trained really well this week. He should have played more. Sorry – he would have loved to have played more.”

A Freudian slip from the Barcelona winger, another Liverpudlian in Spain, who himself has barely put a foot wrong for England of late. He has three goals in three games for England, including the World Cup semi-final against Argentina. This was an England team that Tuchel fine-tuned, first to give a rest to Bellingham and in other quarters, too. Lewis Hall started at left-back. Trevoh Chalobah won his third England cap at centre-back. Alex Scott, of Bournemouth, was given his debut off the bench in the second half and Rio Ngumoha won the second cap of his England career, just one month after his 18th birthday.

As for Kane, his 87th goal for England now puts him within two goals of Robert Lewandowski, among four greats in the seven ahead of Kane on the all-time international goalscorers’ list. By the end of this international break the England captain should have equalled Peter Shilton’s record 125 caps. It has been an astonishing career even if it ends tomorrow. Following the missed penalty against Spain, Kane was again the man in the right place at the right time when Morgan Rogers’s shot was blocked in the second half.

“Strange to get an early red card,” Tuchel said. “Not the best for the team and spectators. It’s an awkward one, but we kept going, got a win and that’s what counts.” Not quite a vintage Czech Republic team, either, and when their best player of the opening stages, the attacking midfielder Pavel Sulc, of Lyon in Ligue 1, was dismissed after 25 minutes, it certainly did not become any easier for the home team. Sulc, the Czech player of the year in 2025, had mistimed a tackle on Elliot Anderson, which on a VAR review, the Turkish referee Umut Meler decided was worthy of an upgrade from yellow to red. It was high on the right calf of the England midfielder.

Czech Republic DOWN TO 10 MEN! 🟥Pavel Šulc sees red for a dangerous challenge on Elliot Anderson#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/B2YOLuS0vL

England had looked once more a little open to the counter-attack in the early stages, with Sulc one notable runner. This was not an opponent of the quality of Spain and Tuchel’s players were able to recover the situation. When they lose the ball in the opposition’s half, England tend to look vulnerable.

Even before the red card Rogers had hit a post. Myles Lewis-Skelly, playing in midfield, was booked for a foul on Lukas Serv and was pursued thereafter by the Czech players hoping to get an upgrade on the yellow card. He was substituted at half-time, with Eberechi Eze on in his place.

“I spoke to Ant [Gordon] at half-time,” Alexander-Arnold said later to ITV, “and I said if I’m getting in those spaces make sure you get to the back post. You don’t expect to get it that fast, but it did and it worked.”

Two minutes after the break, Alexander-Arnold suddenly burst into life. He won the ball back in his own area and then drove forward in search of the return. When that did not come, he raced back to win the ball again and unleashed one of those right-footed outswingers to the back post, where Gordon guided in the header. “Really proud to score that,” Gordon said, “because I can’t tell you the number of hours I’ve spent practising headers.”

Kane scored the second just a minute before he was replaced and Bellingham took the captain’s armband and the role as a No 9. One day someone will have to step into those goalscorer’s boots on a permanent basis and try to replace Kane – although it may be a while yet.

Thomas Tuchel has backed Jude Bellingham as a future England captain after giving him the armband in the victory over the Czech Republic.

In the absence of Declan Rice, who was vice-captain at the World Cup, Bellingham assumed the role when he came on for Harry Kane, who is now in his 10th season as England captain and also scored in the 2-0 win in Prague.

Tuchel, who needs to check on Bellingham ahead of Saturday’s game against Croatia after a “niggle,” has praised the midfielder’s attitude during the extended international break one year after he was back from an injury but left out of the squad.

“If you are the captain at the end of these matches, you can be the permanent captain,” Tuchel said when asked whether Bellingham could eventually lead the team. “He was the captain against New Zealand before the World Cup. It is always a reward and always an honour.

“I think he loves to be with us at the moment. That’s what I feel, and we had this small talk today about his role. We felt in our hearts or our stomachs to say ‘let’s go again, let’s start again’ and also our heads told us maybe 30 minutes is enough for this match because he hasn’t played in this quick turnaround through this season. He has done it before, but not in the season, so we didn’t want to be the first ones to try that.

“But even in this little encounter, you can see that he’s confident and happy to help from the bench. So it’s a reward. It’s good. He had a little niggle at the end of the match, so hopefully it’s nothing serious, and he’s available for Croatia.”

Nico O’Reilly is a doubt for the Croatia match in Rijeka and there are also concerns over Ezri Konsa, who was on the bench but not fit enough to play.

Trent Alexander-Arnold provided an assist for Anthony Gordon in the Real Madrid full-back’s first cap in 15 months. Gordon, meanwhile, has now scored in the first two Nations League games of the campaign and is staking his case to be an indispensable player for Tuchel.

“He’s getting there. He’s defending his shirt, he’s defending his position, an excellent performance again after his performance against Spain,” Tuchel said.

“He was very decisive today and had an excellent goal. It was very, very difficult, but the technique and finishing was excellent. He scored against Spain, so he has decisive actions and he’s defending his shirt and his position. He does it on the highest level and he’s a very important player.”

England returned to winning ways with a 2-0 win over Czech Republic in Prague.

Pavel Sulc’s first-half red card after a VAR review of his clumsy challenge on Elliot Anderson took the sting out of the initially lively hosts and Anthony Gordon gave Thomas Tuchel’s men a deserved lead early in the second half.

The forward headed home a fantastic cross by Trent Alexander-Arnold, who was making his first start under the German coach, before skipper Harry Kane scored to settle any nerves.

So who played well for England and who failed to impress? Rate each player with our voting tool, and have your say in the comments.

I thought we were very professional second half. We stepped up and needed to be more dynamic, bring more urgency into our play, which we did. We kept that intensity going and and the effort was till there. Deserved victory.

Strange to get an early red card. Not the best for the spectators, not the best for the team. It’s an awkward one. But we got the win.

To guide it into the goal, there was an awful lot [for Anthony Gordon] to do. Good pass, good goal. Both full-backs were good. The position in the second half suited Trent more than the position in the first half. Lewis was excellent on the other side.

We have used all the outfield players after two matches so credit to all of them. Now it’s important to relax and enjoy the evening, do a good recovery and prepare for Saturday.

I think it was good. They go down to 10 men and it should be easier for us to win the game, But in fact it makes it more difficult. They get very compact and defend with a lot of players around the box and it’s hard to break them down.

We got that [goal] at the start of the second half which is what we needed. The longer it’s 0-0, it gets harder and harder and harder.

[Where do you place your assist?]  It’s up there for sure. I spoke to Ant at half-time and said if I get into those half-spaces I’m looking to put it in so make sure you get to the back post. I didn’t expect it to work so quickly.

He’s a willing runner, great to play with him. I saw the run and was able to execute the pass,

It’s always a pleasure and an honour to represent my country. It’s been a long time. I’ve always believed that I can play for England and I want to. The manager’s given me the opportunity and I tried to do what he wanted me to do to the best of my ability and I hope he’s happy with how I played.

🦁 #1301Alex Scott reflects on a special night, earning his first senior England cap 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @gabrielclarke05 | @England pic.twitter.com/lC34bAPbbd

It was good, quite dominant. We created a lot of chances but without the quality. When they went a man down, we were too passive at times. We need to be dominant, as I said earlier, go for the throat and put teams away.

I said that to him [Trent, on the quality of the ‘assist’]. I make that run time and time again but only a set number of players have that ability, that technique and the bravery to risk a mistake to play that pass. And that’s why I have been dying to play with him. He’s been on his own journey but has trained really well this week. He should have played more. Sorry, he would have loved to have played more.

I’ve missed playing with Hally. He’s a good lad. We had great chemistry at Newcastle and it’s great to share this stage with him.

It’s my only header. I’d be the worst header of the ball you’ll ever see. Really happy, resally proud to score that because I can’t tell you the number of hours I’ve spent practising headers.

Perfectly competent and signs of promise in the left-back/left-wing axis. England looked too open against 11 men and better teams – hola España – may have capitalised on the sloppiness. But once Sulc was sent off, England gradually turned the screw and created a hatful of chances, running out easy winners.

Another tidy save from Kovar when Bellingham receives a pass from the left, strides towards the D, then drives a daisy-cutter towards the left of goal. The keeper swoops down early to turn it behind with a stiff wrist.

Two minutes of stoppage time are signalled as England try to pen the home side in their own half.

Tuchel has kept the back four on the pitch for the 90 minutes. He was not entirely happy with them in the first half – or his body language suggested that, anyway. But it is a welcomed clean sheet for England after the chaotic defeats to Spain and France.

Ngumoha is enjoying himself and showing off some excellent close control.

Scott and Eze smash shots over the bar from 22 yards within a minute of each other.

Rogers’ diagonal cross is chested down by Eze as he sets up an opportunity to shoot in the area but a defender hacks it away. Ngumoha pounces on the loose ball and plays a neat reverse pass with the outside of his boot to Rogers on the underlap. Rogers goes for power rather than lift to find Eze or Bellingham and the keeper makes another smart save.

Gibbs-White’s pace and direct running have the beating of Chaloupek and he tees up Eze to hammer a left-foot shot that seemed to be arrowing into the net until Kovar stuck up his right hand to paw it over.

Gordon stops, then from a standing start drives past bursts past Chaloupek to the byline and stands up a near-post cross that Rogers flashes wide.

Czech Republic break after England’s attack down the right hits the skids. Hlozek gallops down the middle and lets fly before Scott can catch him. Trafford sees it all the way, dives to his right to save and gathers the loopy effort from the rebound.

Slama hounds Ngumoha into conceding a corner as the Liverpool winger slips under pressure.

Jude Bellingham is wearing the England captain’s armband again. He was also wearing it during the pre-World Cup camp against New Zealand. Thomas Tuchel explained afterwards that the player with the most caps is skipper when Harry Kane is subbed off. Bellingham is also playing centrally, as a False Nine.

Bellingham → KaneNgumoha → SakaScott → Anderson.

England have switched to the Revie Plan with Bellingham as the deep-lying centre-forward.

Czech Republic 0 England 2 (Kane) Eze plays Rogers in down the left of the box. He gets there but falls under the tackle of Krejci, knocking the ball to Kane who thumps it through Hranac’s legs with his left foot from about seven yards.

KANE DOUBLES ENGLAND'S LEAD 🔥Harry Kane in the right place at the right time for the Three Lions 🦁#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/Od9x5kXOsH

Kane stuck around five finishes into that corner in the warm-up. Same finish - accurate and powerful. Finally a first cap for Alex Scott.

As Sam Matterface points out. England having a left-footed left-back has added an extra dimension to their attacking play. I never thought I’d be quoting Sam Matterface but it’s been one of those days. Ambros had taken up a good position in space on the left but the crossfield pass wasn’t good enough and sailed beyond him.

Alexander-Arnold shoots from the right after some slow-slow-slow-quick passing between him and Saka opens up a gap. But he drills it across goal and wide of the left post.

Now Hall does find the target at his third attempt this half but only because Krejci is there to deflect his cross on to the post with the keeper beaten.

Corner on the right for England who procrastinate so long over their positions the referee warns them but does not take it off them. Krejci and Kane have their arms around each other as the ball comes in and the Czech captain pulls Kane to the ground but the referee waves play on.

Saka takes it short and plays a one-two with Alexander-Arnold. Saka cuts it back to Eze to shoot in a pre-cooked move but he is closed down too quickly so he rolls it to Hall 20 yards out and the left-black leans back and launches his shot 20 rows back behind the goal.

England have a corner on the left after a last gasp tackle by Chaloupek on Gordon.

Czech Republic have switched to 3-3-3 in possession and are trying to play. Sadilek is struggling after being kicked by person or persons unknown. Apologies.

Although the goal was built from the right, England have been so dominant down the left. Hall and Gordon, who combined so well for Newcastle, do so again here with the left-back creeping up the inside while the winger goes down the outside and plays it into the box for his former colleague who wafts his shot wide with a lazy air from 15 yards. Should have scored.

Czech Republic 0 England 1 (Gordon) Alexander-Arnold clears Lingr’s cross and runs upfield to join the counter that seems to break down. But a crossfield pass from the home side is picked off by the right-back facing his own goal 30 yards from the Czechs’. He turns and arrows a fine cross to the left of the penalty spot. Gordon lets it bounce and cushions a header back across the keeper and in at the right post. Great finish. High IQ finish as he might say.

TRENT ➡️ GORDON ⚽️🔥Anthony Gordon can't stop scoring for England, 3️⃣ goals in his last 4️⃣ games for England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/iej0PCW8Ar

That goal was all about Trent. He intercepted in his own penalty area before making a 70-run up the pitch to get on the end of a throughball. That doesn’t work but he wins the ball back and crosses for Gordon to score. The full house from Trent there – showing Tuchel what he brings to the team in just a few seconds of action.

England are attcking from right to left in the second half. England’s trumpeter is in the house and reprises the national anthem.

Eze → Lewis-Skelly who was on a yellow card.

Just before half-time, Krejci, the Wolves centre-half wiped out Saka, watching the man, not the ball, and bodychecking him.

Thomas Tuchel was furious with the fourth official Cihan Aydin, wagging his finger in anger after Bukayo Saka was taken out by Ladislav Krejci. Before that he was quite passive on the touchline, hands in pockets as he watched England trying to break down the Czechs.

Could be another tactical half-time substitution for Myles Lewis-Skelly. Czech players definitely see him as the best chance of a red for England.

The Czech Republic were causing England problems with 11 men but having been reduced to 10 have concentrated on trying to persuade the referee to even up the numbers and also on defending in a low block. Gordon and Hall have the key to unlock the defence but too often when they have sent crosses in, Kane has been in wild rover mode.

Kane takes the ball by the left of the D, spins to wrap his right instep around the ball and try to bend it into the top right corner. Kovar, the PSV goalkeeper, soars to his left to claw it away with his top hand.

Kovář DENIS Harry Kane! 🛑England pushing for a goal before half time 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/l4lAeAl6IE

Karabec is not going to be able to continue. Good cross from Hall from the left wins the applause of Kane. So near.

Karabec is hurt in a collision with Alexander-Arnold that the referee does not deem a foul.

Every tackle, every collision inspires a Czech demand for a red card. Karabec hits the deck like a bag of hammers when brushed by Rogers’ arm but the referee isn’t buying the implication that he had been elbowed.

Lewis-Skelly ignores Hall’s underlapping run down the inside left and pops it short to Guehi instead. The City defender slips a pass down the outside for Gordon who dribbles into the box and clips an inviting, low cross through the six-yard box. Rogers may have got a touch at the near post and the ball runs across goal. Karabec juts about gets it away,  avoiding the risk of shanking it into his own goal.

Krejci wants a tot-for-tat red card for Lewis-Skelly who slid in and caught Cerv on the foot. He never raised his studs and yellow suffices. The manager Santi is also booked for protesting the colour.

The system seems to be working again. Apologies for the break in updates.

Good work by Kane down the left to get away from Chaloupek and run into the box. He clips a short pass to the near post that Saka tries to finish, improvising a flick, that balloons wide off a defender. The angle made that all but impossible.

That is a big moment in the game, with Pavel Sulc dismissed for a stamp on Elliot Anderson. There was little protest about the foul when it occurred. In fact, even a yellow was a bit surprising. But Umut Meler was sent to the pitchside monitor. Czech Republic looked lively but you would now expect them to sit back and defend.

Czechs are now in a 5-4-0 formation. This will be a test of England to break through the two lines of defence. It will be like the Ghana match at the World Cup.

Pavel Sulc, who was playing so well, has been sent off after the referee was sent to the monitor by VAR. It was a high tackle, catching Anderson’scalf with his studs.

Czech Republic DOWN TO 10 MEN! 🟥Pavel Šulc sees red for a dangerous challenge on Elliot Anderson#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/B2YOLuS0vL

That red card has deprived the Czech Republic of their best player so far. He took it well rather than going off in a Sulc.

Big test for Czech manager Santi Denia, once of Atlético Madrid, who was manager of Spain U17s when they lost the 2017 final to an England team featuring – among other luminaries – Marc Guéhi and Morgan Gibbs-White.

Gordon cuts in from the left on to his right and flashes a shot across goal that flies past the right post.

SO CLOSE FROM GORDON!🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/MUiKO8TqvC

Apologies we have been having some technical issues.

England had their best chance in the 16th minute when Rogers spun by the penalty spot. He was facing Anthony Gordon to collect his pass in from the left. Pirouetting, he steadies himself to thump a left-foot shot into the foot of the right post. The ball rebounds to Anderson who flays a shot from 18 yards that Chaloupek throws himself in front of to block only to divert it to Saka and Hranac is there to block that one.

How have England not scored!? 🤯Somehow Czech Republic keep the score at 0-0 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 🇨🇿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/51tmBwgRRf

England are dicing with danger in not picking up Sulc.

What was Thomas Tuchel saying about his England players being a danger to themselves around the box? It was an error there from Elliot Anderson that let Czech Republic through on goal and a better touch from Pavel Sulc would have seen them take the lead. Harry Kane dropped deep to start England’s attack down the right. The flanks will be their route to goal in this game.

Alexander-Arnold loses the ball in the middle of the park. Radosta is sent down the right by a cute pass and he gulls Hall by crossing early after shaping to go down the line. Alexander-Arnold is back to head it away but only as far as Cerv who torpedoes a volley from 25 yards barely a foot wide of the right post.

Kane is given a talking to for tangling with the Czech captain Krejci, giving him a deserved shove hopefully for the heinous crime of wearing the No 7 shirt while playing at centre-half.

Lewis-Skelly mops up at the back after a third rapid Czech Republic break, this one down the right with Chaloupek to the fore. Shielding the ball in the penalty area, he buys a foul and England build again from a free-kick.

Lovely pass by Rogers sends Saka down the right and the Arsenal winger tries to whip over a cross to pick up Kane’s near-post dart but it goes behind the England captain.

Mistake by Anderson lets Lyon’s Sulc pounce on to possession and dribble down the inside-left, cutting into the centre of the field as he approaches the box with Chalobah in pursuit. The ball skids off the greasy turf as he gets closer to the 18-yard line and Trafford sprints and slides to get there first.

Chaloupek is stalking Gordon all over the pitch and Slama is sticking close to Saka. First decent move down the Czech right catches Guehi a little off guard but out comes Trafford to gather.

No clean sheets for England in six games since the victory over Panama in the last group game in the United States and they have made three changes in the back four.

You can read an obituary of the former West Ham goalkeeper here.

Every fan, player, coach and journalist on their feet for the tribute to Luděk Mikloško, who passed away earlier this month.

We had a chat this morning. Both our hearts said 60 minutes, but both our heads said 30 minutes make more sense.

Time for the national anthems. God Save the King followed by Kde domov muj. England are in all white, the home side in red shirts, navy shorts and socks (or, as the old Rothmans’ annuals used to put it, ‘hose’).

Thomas Tuchel’s name was read out by the stadium announcer here at Fortuna Arena – unlike at Wembley last weekend. There was no way to gauge the fans’ view of Tuchel before the win over Spain as he was not mentioned and his image was not on the big screens. England have 1,000 away tickets for this game so no cheers or jeers could be heard tonight.

James Trafford went into the dressing for the final part of the warm-up, which appears to be a planned part of the preparations. Jordan Pickford did the same at the Azteca before England’s win against Mexico in the summer. England players were split for the final part of the warm-up, with defenders doing drills as a unit, while midfielders and attackers did shooting.

Yes, for sure [this is as good as I’ve felt in an England shirt. My football IQ, I’m getting better and better, smarter and smarter. I need time to really feel at home, to feel comfortable and once I have that I don’t look back.

I knew exactly where I wanted to go, where I needed to go but I needed some guidance. I think the same way as him [Jude]. We don’t think there’s any limit on what we can achieve, wanting to win, wanting to win in a good way by going for the throat. Fearlessness.

It ate me up for a good couple of weeks after [losing the semi-final]. I’d scored… on the same pitch as Messi, the man I idolised as a kid. It was the highest possible moment of my entire life. And within 20 minutes it had come completely crashing down. There’s been a lot of controversy, a lot of talk about that. Going forward, if we are going to lose a game, it’s going to be like how we lost to Spain. We went for their throats, we missed a penalty and lost the game. But the way we went for them, no regrets. I want to stay as far away from that [regret] as possible.

[Did you ever think you would sign for Barcelona?] Yes. No one ever achieves anything in life by playing it safe. My personality is based on being bold, taking risks and going for whatever you want.

At this level we’re all as talented as each other but only the most mentally competitive and driven people can maintain success for a long time.

I always thought in England that people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never respected my quality and people are starting to take notice that I’m not just quick. In Barcelona if you’re not technical, if you’re not smart, you’d stand out like a sore thumb.

[Where do you see this squad in two years?] European champions.

The intensity we played with and the way we took it to the best team in the world [is what we’ve taken out of the Spain game]. We can be really proud of that. It was really good. Obviously tight margins decide games but overall we’re happy with the way we dusted the World Cup off and all that emotion.

Massively [relishing a run in the No 10 position in place of Bellingham]. I want to try and show what I can do in that role and make a positive impact.

The atmosphere here [is always intense] and they have a new coach. We’ve done our research. We have to respect them. It’s going to be difficult and it’s up to us to hold our nerve.

The Professional Footballers’ Association has leapt to Cole Palmer’s defence following his withdrawal from the England squad.

The union’s CEO,  Maheta Molango, said the Chelsea forward is a victim of a “sick” system that is demanding too much from players physically.

“When England see five players who need to withdraw when the single most proud moment a player has is to be called up for the national team, you just ask yourself, what’s wrong about the industry?” Molango said at the Fifpro performance summit in London.

“You see people like Cole Palmer, someone who would have played four consecutive summers in a row had he gone to the World Cup, and you wonder why is he missing?”He’s missing because he’s a victim of the calendar and that’s something that needs to absolutely trigger the alarm bells.”

Proti Anglii vybral Santi Denia tuto základní jedenáctku! 🇨🇿 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 #VamosCesko pic.twitter.com/dgoXhkP2Pt

Santi makes two changes, Wolves’ Ladislav Krejci, the captain, replaces Vladimir Coufal, once of West Ham now of Hoffenheim. On the left wing Anderlecht’s Lukas Ambros makes way for Matej Radosta of Teplice.

Trafford; Trent, Chalobah, Guéhi, Hall; Anderson, Lewis-Skelly; Saka, Rogers, Gordon; Kane

Alexander-Arnold is being called “Trent” on the England team-sheet.

Ready for Czechia 👊 pic.twitter.com/8aMMdnH99I

Trevoh Chalobah will earn his third England cap in tonight’s Nations League match against Czech Republic. The Como centre-back, 27, played in the 6-4 defeat of France in the Bronze final at the World Cup and his other appearance for the Three Lions was in the defeat by Senegal last year.

Trent Alexander-Arnold will make his first England appearance in 15 months after being given a start. The Real Madrid full-back, who was not selected for the World Cup in the summer, earned his last cap against Andorra in 2025.

He replaces Jarell Quansah in Thomas Tuchel’s line-up that lost to Spain at the weekend.

“Trent had a very good training week and the excellent training in Wembley after the match, where he showed that he absolutely wants to play and wants to be with us,” said Tuchel on the eve of the game at Fortuna Arena.

“We’re good. Everything is fine. He’s ready to go. He has qualities that you all know, like he’s strong on the ball, excellent crossing, good finishing. And very, very good on the ball. That’s basically what he brings.”

Ezri Konsa, who missed team training on the day before this game, is out. Morgan Rogers, meanwhile, steps in for Jude Bellingham in the No10 role as Tuchel looks to juggle four matches in 11 days during this extended international break.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is in line to make his first England start under head coach Thomas Tuchel for tonight’s Nations League game against Czech Republic.

Injuries to Nico O’Reilly and Ezri Konsa have forced Tuchel into changes at the back, with Alexander-Arnold expected to come in at right-back, Trevoh Chalobah to replace Konsa and Lewis Hall to step in for O’Reilly.

Alexander-Arnold has made only one appearance under Tuchel, as a substitute in a World Cup qualifying win against Andorra in June 2025. His last start for England came under interim head coach Lee Carsley, when he scored in a victory over Finland.

Jude Belllingham could be given a rest after playing the full 90 minutes in the defeat by Spain, which would give Morgan Rogers an opportunity in the No 10 position.

Man City used ‘sham’ sponsorships in £830m cheating scheme

Manchester City arranged “sham” sponsorships in a near-£1bn plot to flout Premier League rules, an independent commission has found.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that City had been found guilty of all charges related to “serious breaches” of the league’s financial rules, with the commission also upholding all but one in relation to their failure to co-operate with an investigation spanning over three years.

The commission found that, of £949.94m City claimed in commercial income over a nine-year period, only £119.25m was legitimate, with the remaining £830.69m illicitly paid by their Abu Dhabi owners.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Uefa Nations League match between Czech Republic and England from Slavia Prague’s Eden Stadium. The home side, 49th in the Fifa rankings, scrambled their way to World Cup qualification with victories in the play-offs in penalty shoot-outs over Ireland and Denmark, promptly stank Group A out in Mexico/Canada/United States, drawing with South Africa but losing to South Korea and Mexico to finish last.

Miroslav Koubek, their 74-year-old manager, the oldest in the competition’s history, promptly stood down and has been replaced by their first foreign head coach, Santi, the former Atlético Madrid centre-half, who spent 15 years moving from managing Spain’s U17s, to the U19s and then the U21s. Little wonder, given his CV, that he is looking to refresh his squad with a transfusion of young players, a requirement made all the more urgent by the international retirement of stalwart centre-forward Patrick Schick and the absence of West Ham’s Tomas Soucek who damaged his ankle in that 3-0 defeat by Mexico on June 25 and has not kicked a ball since.

Santi started his stint in charge and this campaign in Group A3 with a 2-1 defeat by Croatia but there were some very positive signs – they set up as a 4-3-3 in classic Spanish/Cruyff style and pressed like dervishes. England, who conceded three goals when players made mistakes when subjected to aggressive pressing in their opening 3-2 defeat by world champions Spain, will have to find better solutions tonight, either by holding their nerve or counterpressing with fewer mistakes.

Given England are ranked 45 places higher, their results, if not all performances, at the World Cup were commendable and the way in which they rattled Spain and should really have given themselves a bulwark against the comeback by converting their penalty at 2-1 up,  an away win should be relatively straightforward. But they did lose on their last visit to Prague in a Euro 2020 qualifier having won 5-0 in the home leg.

#1450. Presynaptic homeostasis mediated by exocytosis of a SNARE protein

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The neural plasticity that underlies adaptation and learning requires countervailing homeostatic mechanisms to maintain the stability and responsiveness of neural circuits. Previous work has described several forms of synaptic homeostasis1, but the mechanisms that detect changes in activity and transduce these into altered neurotransmission have remained poorly understood. Here we show that high-frequency stimulation alters the subsequent properties of neurotransmitter release to confer a presynaptic form of homeostasis, independent of postsynaptic receptors. The mechanism involves vesicular SNARE protein (v-SNARE) VAMP7 (vesicle-associated membrane protein 7), which reduces neurotransmitter release by inhibiting the entry of Ca2+ specifically through P/Q-type presynaptic Ca2+ channels. Previous work has implicated target SNARE proteins (t-SNAREs) in the inhibition of Ca2+ channels2, but without clear physiological rationale. We show that the activity-dependent regulation of release mediated by VAMP7 requires the t-SNARE syntaxin. Although VAMP7 acts at the plasma membrane to inhibit P/Q-type channels, it localizes predominantly to a subset of synaptic vesicles made by adaptor protein-3 (AP-3) that respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation3,4. The localization of VAMP7 to AP-3-derived synaptic vesicles thus provides a mechanism for the activity-dependent delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane, where it associates with syntaxin to inhibit P/Q-type Ca2+ channels and transmitter release. This homeostatic form of metaplasticity operates at multiple excitatory synapses, and in its absence, the fraction of FOS+ neurons increases several fold, revealing a general property of excitatory neurotransmission that might also maintain the sparsity of neural connections.

Homeostatic synaptic plasticity can involve pre- or postsynaptic mechanisms. In response to a global change in activity, mammalian central neurons alter the expression of glutamate receptors1,5,6,7. By contrast, a presynaptic form of homeostasis occurs at the neuromuscular junction. First established in Drosophila melanogaster, this involves increased release of glutamate in response to reduced postsynaptic receptor function8,9. An effect of activity on neurotransmitter release has also been reported at central synapses10,11,12,13,14,15,16,17,18. Although previous work has identified several elements that are required for the different forms of homeostatic plasticity, the mechanisms involved remain poorly understood.

To determine the time course over which presynaptic homeostatic plasticity develops, we suppressed network activity by treating primary mouse hippocampal cultures, which contain almost entirely glutamatergic neurons (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b), with the glutamate receptor antagonists 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX) and 3-(2-carboxypiperazin-4-yl)propyl-1-phosphonic acid (commonly known as APV). We monitored the consequent changes in transmitter release using a fusion of the strongly pH-sensitive GFP variant ecliptic pHluorin to a luminal loop of the vesicular glutamate transporter VGLUT1 (VGLUT1–pH). Quenched at the low pH of synaptic vesicles (SVs), the pHluorin-based reporter brightens on exposure to the higher external pH at exocytosis; the reacidification that accompanies endocytosis results in requenching. Figure 1a,b shows that silencing with CNQX and APV increases both the rate and the extent of VGLUT1+ SV exocytosis. The reacidification that accompanies endocytosis also slows (Fig. 1a,b), but stimulation in the presence of the v-type H+-ATPase inhibitor bafilomycin to block SV reacidification results in an increase in the proportion of VGLUT1+ SVs available for release, independent of any change in endocytosis16 (Fig. 1c). We detect no change in the punctate distribution of SVs or the active zone (Extended Data Fig. 1c). To assess the initial release probability, we monitored glutamate release at individual presynaptic boutons using the glutamate sensor iGluSnFR (ref. 19). Stimulating at a low frequency (0.2 Hz), we find that silencing the cultures increases the proportion of synapses that release glutamate (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 1d). Because a change in release probability can reflect a change in the presynaptic Ca2+ entry that triggers release, we monitored presynaptic Ca2+ with the low-affinity Ca2+ dye Fluo5F. Figure 1e,f shows that silencing the cultures greatly increases the presynaptic Ca2+ response to both 5-Hz and 25-Hz stimulus trains. This large increase in Ca2+ entry might be expected to increase the release probability more than the doubling that was observed, but we used iGluSnFR only to indicate whether release occurred, and this binary measure underestimates the actual increase in release probability. In addition, stimulation at 1 Hz and 5 Hz triggers Ca2+ entry with near 100% reliability in all presynaptic boutons (Extended Data Fig. 2). Thus, silencing cannot increase the proportion of responsive boutons, excluding effects on action potential invasion of the nerve terminal. Ongoing neural activity thus seems to reduce glutamate release by suppressing presynaptic Ca2+ entry.

a, Wild-type (WT) hippocampal neurons expressing VGLUT1–pH were treated with CNQX (10 μM) and APV (50 μM) for the times indicated and stimulated at 25 Hz for 20 s. The fluorescence response normalized to total fluorescence was revealed in 50 mM NH4Cl. b, Left, peak response and initial rate (first 4 s) of fluorescence increase. Right, time constant (τ) of endocytosis (0 h and 24 h, n = 20/3 (see end of legend for explanation of n numbers); 3 h, n = 14/3; 6 h and 48 h, n = 16/3). c, WT hippocampal neurons expressing VGLUT1–pH were silenced for 24 h, stimulated at 25 Hz for 120 s in the presence of 100 nM bafilomycin A1 (Baf) and the response was normalized as above. Scatter plots show exocytosis rate and recycling pool size (control, n = 14/3; CNQX + APV, n = 16/3). d, WT hippocampal neurons expressing iGluSnFR–stargazin were silenced for 24 h and stimulated 30 times at 0.2 Hz to measure the release probability (Pr). Pr is shown as a cumulative frequency distribution and as a box-and-whisker plot, with centre line indicating the median, box bounds 25th−75th percentiles and whiskers minimum and maximum values (n = 12/3). e,f,h, WT hippocampal neurons silenced with CNQX + APV (e,f) or 1 μM TTX (h) for 24 h and loaded with Fluo5F were stimulated at 5 Hz for 5 s (e) (control, n = 16/3; CNQX + APV, n = 18/3) or stimulated repeatedly at 25 Hz for 5 s each, with 15 s between bursts and fluorescence normalized to baseline (f,h) (f, control, n = 14/3; CNQX + APV, n = 20/3; h, n = 10/2, both conditions). AUC, area under the curve. g,i, WT hippocampal neurons expressing VGLUT1–pH and silenced with CNQX + APV (g) or TTX (i) for 24 h were stimulated twice at 25 Hz for 20 s and the response was normalized as above. Scatter plots show the slope of fluorescence increase and the fluorescence at the end of the stimulus (g, control, n = 11/3; CNQX + APV, n = 10/3; i, n = 14/3, both conditions). Data are mean ± s.e.m.; n = x/y, where x indicates the fields examined and y the number of independent experiments. Significance by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (c–e), one-way (b) or two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (f–i).

To determine whether activity can reverse the effects of silencing, we stimulated the neurons with repeated 25-Hz bursts. We find that two to three bursts reduces the Ca2+ entry in silenced neurons back to baseline, with no effect on presynaptic Ca2+ entry in unsilenced cultures (Fig. 1f). To assess the effects on release, we imaged VGLUT1–pH. Stimulation at 25 Hz also reverses the increased rate and extent of release due to silencing, with no effect on the unsilenced neurons (Fig. 1g). Thus, activity can acutely reverse the homeostatic increase in transmitter release. Stimulation reverses the effects of silencing despite the continued presence of glutamate receptor antagonists, indicating that the mechanism does not require the activation of postsynaptic receptors and is thus induced presynaptically. Silencing with tetrodotoxin (TTX) for 24 h similarly enhances presynaptic Ca2+ entry and transmitter release that reverses rapidly with repeated 25-Hz stimulation (in the absence of TTX) (Fig. 1h,i), supporting the role of neural activity, rather than being a phenomenon restricted to the inactivation of glutamate receptors.

To determine whether activity suppresses release in a more physiological preparation, we extended the analysis to Schaffer-collateral synapses in the stratum radiatum of CA1 hippocampus. We compared the effect of 100 action potentials (APs) delivered at either 5 Hz or 50 Hz (followed by a 20-s gap to allow some recovery) on the response to test stimulation at 5 Hz. With intervening stimulation at 5 Hz, the final stimulus train shows incomplete recovery of the first response but synaptic depression similar to that observed with the first train (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3a), indicating that the properties of release have not changed. Despite delivering the same number of APs, intervening stimulation at 50 Hz increases facilitation and reduces subsequent synaptic depression (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3a). This suggests a reduction in the initial release probability that enables the accumulation of Ca2+ without depleting SVs20—a fundamental change in the properties of release.

a–e, Left, sample traces from CA1 stratum radiatum showing the effects of 100 stimuli (blue), delivered at either 5 Hz or 50 Hz, on test stimulation (also 100 AP) delivered before (black) and after (red) at 5 Hz in hippocampal slices from WT (a,b), mocha (c), Atp8a1-KO (d) and Vamp7-KO (e) mice. Hatched lines indicate a gap of 20 s. Middle, response to each stimulus normalized to the first response. Right, response of different cells to action potential 2 (AP2) (b–e) and AP95 (a–e), normalized by the response to AP1 (a, n = 17/3; b,c, n = 21/3; d,e, n = 22/3). EPSC, excitatory postsynaptic current. f, After incubation for 10 min in the presence of MK-801, CA1 pyramidal neurons were held at −70 mV and Schaffer-collateral inputs were stimulated at 0 Hz, 5 Hz or 50 Hz (100 AP). Twenty seconds after this stimulation (the hatched lines), cells were held at +40 mV and NMDAR-EPSCs were elicited at 0.2 Hz. Graphs show progressive MK-801 inhibition normalized to the first response and the corresponding decay time constants (τ) in WT and Vamp7-KO slices (n = 13/3). g, WT and Vamp7-KO hippocampal neurons expressing VGLUT1–pH were silenced with CNQX + APV for 24 h, stimulated at 5 Hz or 25 Hz for 20 s and the response normalized as above. Scatter plots (right) show fluorescence at the end of the stimulus (n = 16/3). Data are mean ± s.e.m.; n = x/y, where x indicates the cell or field number and y the number of independent experiments. Significance by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (a–f) or two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (g).

We wanted to understand how high-frequency stimulation suppresses subsequent transmitter release. Previous work has shown that the heterotetrameric adaptor protein AP-3 produces a subset of SVs from endosomes21,22, distinct from the production of canonical SVs at the plasma membrane (or immediately after endocytosis) by clathrin and the related adaptor AP-2 (refs. 23,24,25). We previously found that loss of AP-3 impairs release specifically to stimulation at a high frequency3,4. Thus, we investigated whether loss of AP-3 impairs the suppression of release that follows high-frequency stimulation. Slices from mocha mice, which lack AP-3, show increased rather than reduced synaptic depression after 50-Hz stimulation (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3b). Consistent with the role of AP-3 in producing SVs that are responsive specifically to strong stimulation (that is, of low release probability), AP-3 is thus required for the suppression of release after high-frequency stimulation, and previous work has shown that loss of AP-3 has little effect on response to the 5-Hz test stimulation itself3.

The dependence on AP-3 predicted that a specific component of SVs made by this adaptor is responsible for the suppression of release after strong stimulation. Indeed, a small subset of SV proteins depend on AP-3 for targeting to SVs. These include the zinc transporter ZnT3 (ref. 26), the phospholipid flippase ATP8A1 (ref. 3) and the endolysosomal v-SNARE (vesicular soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor) VAMP7 (refs. 27,28). Because a zinc transporter seemed to be more likely to influence postsynaptic glutamate receptors29 than to affect release, we focused on the two other proteins. Although enriched in mossy-fibre terminals, ATP8A1 and VAMP7 are highly expressed throughout the hippocampus, including in CA1 and CA3, and localize to SVs30 (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis indicates that both genes are expressed in CA3 pyramidal neurons31 (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Western blot analysis confirms the enrichment of both proteins in SVs from the stratum radiatum and stratum lacunosum-moleculare (Extended Data Fig. 4d). In hippocampal slices from Atp8a1-knockout (KO) mice, 50-Hz stimulation still reduces subsequent synaptic depression in the CA1 stratum radiatum (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3c). However, loss of VAMP7 (Vamp7 KO) increases synaptic depression, and 50-Hz stimulation does not alter the increased depression (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3d). Loss of VAMP7 thus seems to account for the role of AP-3 in the effect of high-frequency activity on subsequent release.

Differences in synaptic depression might result from differential recruitment of Schaffer-collateral input, but varying the stimulus intensity threefold does not affect the kinetics or the extent of short-term depression with 5-Hz stimulation (Extended Data Fig. 3e). The effect also persists under more physiological recording conditions (1.5 mM Ca2+, 1 mM Mg2+), which reduce the initial release probability but still allow 50-Hz stimulation to reduce the subsequent release probability in wild-type (WT) but not in Vamp7-KO slices (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f).

To assess the release probability directly, we took advantage of the use-dependent N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antagonist MK-801. Slices pre-incubated in MK-801 were subjected to a conditioning train at either 5 Hz or 50 Hz while the postsynaptic cell was held at −70 mV. Stimulating at 0.2 Hz to assess the ‘initial’ response, NMDAR-EPSCs were then recorded at +40 mV in the continued presence of MK-801. As shown in Fig. 2f, previous 50-Hz stimulation of WT slices slows MK-801 blockade to a greater extent than does previous stimulation at 5 Hz, whereas blockade by MK-801 in Vamp7-KO slices does not change with previous stimulation. Thus, high-frequency stimulation reduces the release probability, and loss of VAMP7 blocks this effect.

VAMP7 is widely expressed throughout the nervous system (Extended Data Fig. 5a). We thus examined three other facilitating synapses: perforant-path synapses formed by layer 2 and 3 neurons of the entorhinal cortex onto dentate granule cells; corticothalamic synapses made by cortical layer 6 pyramidal cells onto ventrobasal thalamic relay neurons; and cerebellar parallel-fibre synapses onto Purkinje cells. Similar to CA1 stratum radiatum, 50-Hz stimulation at each of these synapses reduces synaptic depression (Extended Data Fig. 5b–d). In addition, loss of VAMP7 increases synaptic depression and eliminates the effect of 50-Hz stimulation, supporting a general role for VAMP7 in neurotransmission. Loss of VAMP7 does not affect the presynaptic expression of canonical SNARE proteins in SVs, the punctate distribution of SVs or the active-zone protein Piccolo (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b), suggesting that VAMP7 has a specific effect on release.

If VAMP7 is required for suppression of release after high-frequency stimulation, it should also have a key role in the increase in release due to silencing. We thus used VGLUT1–pH to monitor SV exocytosis. In unsilenced cultures, loss of VAMP7 increases SV exocytosis relative to WT across a range of stimulation frequencies (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). Although silencing with glutamate receptor antagonists increases release from WT neurons, silencing does not further increase release in Vamp7-KO neurons (Fig. 2g). Thus, the increased release observed in the absence of VAMP7 occludes the effect of silencing, suggesting that silencing inactivates VAMP7. Consistent with the hypothesis that VAMP7 has a role in the inhibition of release, overexpression of VAMP7 inhibits the exocytosis of VGLUT1–pH and VGLUT2–pH, particularly at a high frequency (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d).

We next investigated how VAMP7 suppresses release. In hippocampal slices, loss of VAMP7 impairs synaptic facilitation and increases depression with low-frequency stimulation (Fig. 3a,b and Extended Data Fig. 7a), consistent with the results in culture and suggesting an increased initial release probability. Mossy fibres in the hippocampus express high levels of VAMP7 (refs. 28,32), and a recent study33 has investigated the properties of mossy-fibre synapses in the absence of VAMP7. In contrast to our findings in CA1 stratum radiatum, this study found no change in the properties of transmitter release at mossy-fibre synapses33. This might reflect a difference between the two synapses, but the experiments were also performed at room temperature rather than at the 35 °C used here. We thus repeated the analysis of Schaffer-collateral synapses in CA1 stratum radiatum at room temperature, and found that the effect of Vamp7 KO on 5-Hz and 25-Hz stimulus trains disappears (Extended Data Fig. 7b). Vamp7 KO has no effect on the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) at room temperature, but at 34–35 °C it results in a clear reduction in the PPR, consistent with an increased release probability at this more physiological temperature34 (Extended Data Fig. 7c). At 34–35 °C, mossy-fibre synapses show modestly reduced facilitation in the absence of VAMP7 (Extended Data Fig. 7d), consistent with an increase in the release probability at this synapse as well as at Schaffer collaterals. Temperature thus accounts for the discrepant results, and VAMP7 has qualitatively similar effects at both Schaffer-collateral and mossy-fibre synapses.

The analysis of initial release probability after stimulation suggested that loss of VAMP7 increases the release probability (Fig. 2f). A direct comparison of WT and Vamp7-KO slices confirms this observation (Fig. 3c). Because the initial release probability mostly reflects Ca2+ entry, we varied the external Ca2+ concentration and found that 4 mM Ca2+ occludes the effect of Vamp7 KO on release by Schaffer collaterals (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 7e), consistent with an increase in Ca2+ entry owing to the loss of VAMP7. To determine whether loss of VAMP7 affects Ca2+ at individual presynaptic boutons, we used the low-affinity Ca2+ indicator Fluo5F to monitor Ca2+ entry at the boutons of cultured hippocampal neurons labelled with the red-shifted styryl dye FM4-64 (Extended Data Fig. 8a). Figure 3e shows that at all frequencies tested (1–50 Hz), cultured Vamp7-KO neurons exhibit higher evoked Ca2+ transients than do WT cells, and that the low-affinity Fluo5F does not saturate under these conditions (Extended Data Fig. 8b). At a high frequency, Vamp7-KO but not WT neurons progressively accumulate Ca2+, perhaps because an increased Ca2+ load overwhelms the mechanisms for Ca2+ clearance.

To determine whether the effect of VAMP7 on Ca2+ entry extends to other v-SNAREs, we used lentiviral transduction of the light chain of tetanus toxin (TeNT) to cleave the canonical SV SNARE VAMP2 (ref. 35). Despite complete cleavage of VAMP2 (Fig. 3f) and the resulting inhibition of release (Extended Data Fig. 8c), TeNT has no effect on the punctate localization of SV and active-zone proteins (Fig. 3g), and does not alter the presynaptic entry of Ca2+ at a wide range of stimulation frequencies in WT or Vamp7-KO neurons (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 8d,e). Because TeNT also cleaves the related v-SNAREs VAMP1 and VAMP3 but not VAMP7 (ref. 36), the regulation of presynaptic Ca2+ entry by v-SNAREs seems to be unique to the non-canonical v-SNARE VAMP7.

VAMP7 localizes mainly to intracellular membranes, so we wondered how it could suppress presynaptic Ca2+ entry evoked by stimulation. Depolarization of the nerve terminal activates voltage-gated channels to allow Ca2+ entry, but release from intracellular stores might contribute37,38,39. To determine whether VAMP7 inhibits presynaptic Ca2+ entry across the plasma membrane, we took advantage of a mutation that blocks the endocytosis of VAMP2, trapping it at the cell surface40 (Extended Data Fig. 9a–c). Introducing the equivalent mutation (M140A) into VAMP7–pH disrupts its punctate localization at presynaptic boutons in hippocampal cultures (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 9c), greatly increases the surface fraction, as determined by quenching with cell-impermeant, low-pH buffer (Fig. 3j and Extended Data Fig. 9d), and eliminates the response of VAMP7–pH to stimulation at multiple frequencies (Fig. 3k and Extended Data Fig. 9e). VAMP7(M140A) thus localizes almost exclusively to the plasma membrane. In Vamp7-KO neurons, VAMP7(M140A) reduces presynaptic Ca2+ entry back to the level observed in WT neurons (Fig. 3l) and inhibits SV exocytosis to the same extent that WT VAMP7 does (Extended Data Fig. 9f). Thus, VAMP7 inhibits presynaptic Ca2+ entry at the plasma membrane.

The presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels that trigger transmitter release generally belong to the N and P/Q types41. To determine which type is inhibited by VAMP7, we took advantage of neurotoxins that block specific channel types. Figure 3m shows that ω-agatoxin IVA, which targets Cav2.1 (the P/Q/-type voltage-gated calcium channel), greatly reduces the increased presynaptic Ca2+ entry that is triggered at a wide range of stimulation frequencies in cultured Vamp7-KO neurons, including the progressive increase in Ca2+ that is observed with high-frequency stimulation. ω-Agatoxin also inhibits Ca2+ entry in WT neurons, but the extent of inhibition is greater in Vamp7-KO neurons. Consistent with this, previous work has shown that Ca2+ entry specifically through P/Q-type channels changes as a function of neural activity17. By contrast, the N-type Ca2+ channel inhibitor ω-conotoxin GVIA has a more modest effect that is similar in Vamp7-KO and in WT neurons (Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 10a). The L-type Ca2+ channel inhibitor nimodipine and R-type inhibitor SNX-482 have little effect on presynaptic Ca2+ entry in WT neurons, and little effect in Vamp7-KO neurons stimulated at a low frequency (Extended Data Fig. 10b). However, nimodipine substantially reduces Ca2+ entry in Vamp7-KO neurons stimulated at 25 Hz (Extended Data Fig. 10b). Thus, VAMP7 inhibits P/Q-type Ca2+ channels at all frequencies and L-type channels at a high frequency. Because previous work has implicated intracellular Ca2+ stores in transmitter release42,43, we also depleted intracellular Ca2+ using the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA) inhibitor thapsigargin. Thapsigargin reduces Ca2+ entry at low and high frequencies, but loss of VAMP7 has no effect on the extent of inhibition (Extended Data Fig. 10c).

To determine whether the observed effect of VAMP7 on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels accounts for the changes in transmitter release in the Vamp7 KO, we used slice recording. ω-Agatoxin IVA inhibits release (1 AP) to a greater extent in Vamp7-KO slices than it does in WT slices (Extended Data Fig. 10d,e), consistent with the disinhibition of P/Q-type channels. By contrast, ω-conotoxin has the same, small effect in both WT and Vamp7-KO slices, and nimodipine has essentially no effect on the response to single stimuli in either genotype (Extended Data Fig. 10d,e). A change in Ca2+ entry should also influence short-term plasticity. Extended Data Fig. 10e,f shows that ω-agatoxin reduces synaptic depression to a much greater extent in the Vamp7 KO than in the WT, reflecting a greater reduction in release probability. By contrast, ω-conotoxin has little effect in either WT or Vamp7 KO. Thus, loss of VAMP7 increases the reliance on P/Q-type channels specifically for release.

Next, we examined how VAMP7 contributes to the inhibition of P/Q-type Ca2+ channels. Previous work has shown that the t-SNAREs syntaxin and SNAP25 interact with N- and P/Q-type Ca2+ channels at a specific (‘synprint’) site between the second and third homology repeats44,45,46. In heterologous expression systems, the t-SNAREs inhibit voltage-gated Ca2+ channels47, but when assembled with synaptotagmin, their disinhibition has been suggested to promote the coupling of release to Ca2+ entry48,49,50. The role of v-SNAREs in this form of regulation has remained unclear. We find that loss of VAMP7 does not alter the punctate distribution of Cav2.1 or Cav2.2, or their colocalization with the SV protein synaptophysin or with the active-zone protein Piccolo (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 11a,b). However, loss of VAMP7 reduces the colocalization of syntaxin 1 with Cav2.1 (Fig. 4b), whereas colocalization with Cav2.2 does not change (Extended Data Fig. 11c). In terms of biochemical interaction, VAMP7 and syntaxin 1 co-immunoprecipitate with P/Q-type channels in synaptosomes from WT mice (Fig. 4c). In membranes from Vamp7-KO mice, however, less syntaxin co-immunoprecipitates with the channel, suggesting that VAMP7 stabilizes the interaction of syntaxin with Cav2.1. By contrast, the association of SNAP25 with the channel does not depend on VAMP7 (Fig. 4c).

To determine whether syntaxin and SNAP25 are required for the effect of VAMP7 on Ca2+ channels, we made use of the clostridial neurotoxins that cleave these t-SNAREs51. Botulinum neurotoxin C (BoNT/C) cleaves syntaxins52, and previous work has shown that it increases Ca2+ entry53,54. Complete loss of syntaxin 1 impairs the development of hippocampal cultures55, so we added the holotoxin one day before imaging, which results in the cleavage of syntaxin 1 without apparent toxicity (Extended Data Fig. 11d,e). BoNT/C increases presynaptic Ca2+ entry in primary neuronal culture stimulated at frequencies from 1 Hz to 50 Hz (Fig. 4d). With 1-AP stimulation, treatment of Vamp7-KO neurons with BoNT/C produces no further increase in Ca2+ entry, and loss of VAMP7 has no additional effect on the increase due to BoNT/C (Fig. 4d), indicating that VAMP7 and syntaxin are both required to inhibit Ca2+ entry triggered by single APs. Consistent with a common mechanism, the increased Ca2+ entry produced by BoNT/C in response to 1-AP stimulation is inhibited by ω-agatoxin IVA, but not by the N- and L-type channel inhibitors, supporting the disinhibition of mainly P/Q-type channels (Fig. 4e). Although BoNT/C also partially cleaves SNAP25 (Extended Data Fig. 11d), complete cleavage of SNAP25 by lentiviral transduction of the more selective BoNT/A light chain54 has minimal effect on Ca2+ entry in WT neurons (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 12a,b). In the Vamp7 KO, however, BoNT/A increases Ca2+ entry with low-frequency as well as with high-frequency stimulation (Extended Data Fig. 12c). Thus, in contrast to VAMP7 and syntaxin, which are both required to inhibit Ca2+ entry through P/Q-type channels, SNAP25 regulates Ca2+ entry only in the absence of VAMP7.

To understand how VAMP7 and syntaxin contribute to the inhibition of presynaptic Ca2+ channels, we first determined whether the proteins can form a complex. Expressed in HEK293 cells, Strep-tagged Cav2.1 immunoprecipitates VAMP7 when co-expressed with syntaxin 1 and the auxiliary Ca2+ channel subunits β3 and α2δ1 (Fig. 4g). SNAP25 can by itself associate with the channel, but—consistent with the selective effect of BoNT/C but not BoNT/A on Ca2+ entry in WT neurons—syntaxin 1, but not SNAP25, is required for co-immunoprecipitation of VAMP7 by Cav2.1 (Fig. 4g). Deletion of the synprint domain in Cav2.1 eliminates the interaction (Extended Data Fig. 13a). Extending the analysis to cortical neurons, immunoprecipitation of GFP–VAMP7 introduced into the Vamp7 KO pulls down Cav2.1, particularly when syntaxin 1 is also introduced (Extended Data Fig. 13b).

In addition to a SNARE domain, VAMP7 contains several domains not present in VAMP2 that might account for the inhibition of P/Q-type Ca2+ channels. In particular, VAMP7 contains a longin domain, which binds to AP-3 and influences SNARE-complex formation27,56. To test the role of this and other domains, we introduced luminally GFP-tagged WT and mutant VAMP2 and VAMP7 into cortical cultures from the Vamp7 KO. Figure 4h shows that VAMP2 interacts as anticipated with syntaxin and SNAP25 but does not immunoprecipitate endogenous Cav2.1. By contrast, VAMP7 immunoprecipitates Cav2.1 as well as the t-SNAREs, but the longin domain is not required (Fig. 4h). Chimerae of VAMP2 and VAMP7 in the SNARE domain are all sufficient to immunoprecipitate Cav2.1, but removing the linker between the longin and SNARE domains eliminates the interaction with Cav2.1. Consistent with this, replacing the linker in VAMP7 with the VAMP2 linker disrupts the interaction, and replacing the linker in VAMP2 with the VAMP7 linker promotes it, but none of these mutations interferes with the formation of SNARE complexes (Fig. 4h).

If the linker is required for interaction of VAMP7 with Cav2.1, it should also be required for VAMP7 to inhibit Ca2+ entry. Introducing WT and mutant VAMP7 into cultured hippocampal neurons from the Vamp7 KO, we find that deletion of the longin domain does not affect the inhibition of Ca2+ entry by VAMP7 for either 1 AP or 25-Hz stimulation (Fig. 4i and Extended Data Fig. 13c). However, a larger deletion that includes the linker eliminates the inhibition of Ca2+ entry. As shown above for the interaction with Cav2.1, replacing the linker in VAMP7 with the VAMP2 linker also eliminates the inhibition of Ca2+ entry, and replacing the linker in VAMP2 with the VAMP7 linker enables the inhibition (Fig. 4i). Interaction with Cav2.1 might retain VAMP7 at the plasma membrane, but the linker mutant defective in Cav2.1 binding exhibits exo- and endocytosis kinetics indistinguishable from those of the WT (Extended Data Fig. 13d). Thus, the VAMP7 linker is required specifically to bind to and inhibit P/Q-type Ca2+ channels.

Plasma membrane VAMP7 inhibits P/Q-type Ca2+ channels, but VAMP7 localizes predominantly to the subset of SVs made by AP-3. Because AP-3-derived SVs respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation3, we hypothesized that localization of VAMP7 to these SVs provides a mechanism for the activity-dependent delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane, where it inhibits presynaptic Ca2+ entry. This hypothesis makes several predictions. First, strong stimulation should suppress release in a VAMP7-dependent manner. Indeed, repeated stimulation of WT hippocampal neurons at 50 Hz reduces the subsequent exocytic response monitored with VGLUT1–pH (Fig. 5a). Although there are many potential causes, loss of VAMP7 greatly reduces the decline (Fig. 5a), even though the initial response is greater in the absence of VAMP7. Extending the analysis to CA1 hippocampus, repeated 50-Hz bursts progressively reduce synaptic responses in WT slices, and loss of VAMP7 again attenuates the decline (Extended Data Fig. 14a). Loss of AP-3 has a similar but more modest effect because although delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane is impaired, the absence of AP-3-derived SVs limits the exocytic response3 (Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 14a). In the absence of VAMP7, loss of AP-3 limits release even at a low frequency (Extended Data Fig. 14b), presumably owing to the absence of low-release-probability SVs made by AP-3.
