Second, silencing neurons should reduce the inhibition of Ca2+ entry by allowing the clearance of VAMP7 from the plasma membrane. To test this prediction, we used VAMP7–pH, quenching at low external pH and normalizing to total protein in NH4Cl to estimate the cell-surface fraction. As shown in Fig. 5c (and Extended Data Fig. 14c), neurons silenced for one day in glutamate receptor antagonists or TTX exhibit less cell-surface VAMP7 than do controls. The slow endocytic recycling of VAMP7 might contribute to the time course (hours) over which an increased release probability develops after silencing3 (Fig. 1a,b). Consistent with the inactivation of VAMP7 by silencing, silenced WT neurons show less colocalization of syntaxin with Cav2.1 (Extended Data Fig. 14d), similar to the Vamp7 KO (Fig. 4b).

Third, blocking regulated exocytosis should prevent the inhibition of Ca2+ entry produced by high-frequency stimulation. To test this, we silenced neurons after the cleavage of SNARE proteins with clostridial toxins (Fig. 5d). In contrast to WT neurons silenced for 24 h, which show suppression of Ca2+ entry by repeated burst stimulation at 25 Hz, neurons treated with BoNT/C show high Ca2+ entry that is not suppressed by burst stimulation (Fig. 5e). However, syntaxin is also required to inhibit Ca2+ entry. We thus expressed TeNT light chain, which inhibits exocytosis but does not increase Ca2+ entry under these conditions (Extended Data Fig. 8c,d). In this case, burst stimulation progressively reduces Ca2+ entry after silencing, but this occurs more slowly than it does in controls without TeNT (Fig. 5e). Previous work has shown that the exocytosis of AP-3-derived SVs depends predominantly on VAMP2, but residual release persists at a high frequency owing to the TeNT-resistant VAMP7 (ref. 3), and this presumably accounts for the suppression of Ca2+ entry by stimulation even with expression of TeNT. Indeed, substantial cell-surface VAMP7 persists despite TeNT expression (Extended Data Fig. 14e), and this might account for the unchanged presynaptic Ca2+ entry noted above with TeNT expression (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 8d). BoNT/A has only a modest effect on Ca2+ entry (Extended Data Fig. 12b) but mostly prevents the suppression of Ca2+ entry produced by burst stimulation after silencing (Fig. 5e). At a high frequency, BoNT/A also blocks SV exocytosis more completely than TeNT does (Extended Data Fig. 14f). Thus, exocytosis is required for the suppression of Ca2+ entry by high-frequency stimulation.

The analysis of Ca2+ entry should also enable us to monitor the activity-dependent inhibition of Ca2+ entry by VAMP7 in real time. To determine the kinetics of inhibition, we stimulated neurons in culture at 10 Hz for 5 s, then delivered single test pulses at 1 Hz. Figure 5f shows that the increased Ca2+ entry observed in silenced neurons does not decline substantially during the burst. Rather, the inhibition develops several seconds after stimulation. We infer that this delay reflects the time from the arrival of VAMP7 at the plasma membrane to the inhibition of P/Q-type Ca2+ channels. Finally, the increased Ca2+ entry produced by silencing should enable the recruitment of low-release-probability AP-3-derived SVs by low-frequency stimulation, as observed with loss of VAMP7 (Extended Data Fig. 14b). To monitor the fusion of AP-3-derived SVs, we used VAMP7–pH, and find that silencing specifically increases their release at low frequency (Extended Data Fig. 14g). Thus, silencing enables the recruitment of SVs that would otherwise require stronger stimulation, changing the set point for release.

If VAMP7 acts homeostatically to restrain transmitter release, its loss should increase the activity in neural networks. To test this role in vivo, we quantified expression of the immediate early gene Fos, which increases in response to recent neural activity57. In WT mice, expression of FOS is restricted to a small proportion of hippocampal neurons. By contrast, Vamp7-KO mice show a two- to fivefold increase in the number of FOS+ neurons across multiple hippocampal fields (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 15). In addition, FOS immunoreactivity per cell shifts upward. VAMP7 thus limits the strength of synaptic activation in vivo. However, the increased proportion of FOS+ cells in the KO suggests that VAMP7 also limits the number of postsynaptic neurons activated.

Our results elucidate a presynaptic form of homeostatic plasticity. Silencing cultured neurons increases the initial release probability by increasing presynaptic Ca2+ entry. High levels of activity reduce release and Ca2+ entry, and this occurs despite the continued presence of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists, indicating that induction occurs presynaptically rather than postsynaptically. The reduced release probability due to strong stimulation requires SVs made by AP-3, which respond specifically to high frequency. Among the proteins that localize specifically to AP-3-derived SVs, VAMP7 mediates the activity-dependent suppression of Ca2+ entry and release. VAMP7 acts by inhibiting P/Q-type presynaptic Ca2+ channels specifically, indicating that this form of homeostatic plasticity is also expressed presynaptically, and canonical v-SNARE VAMP2 does not have this role. Although VAMP7 at the plasma membrane inhibits P/Q-type channels, the predominant localization of VAMP7 to SVs made by AP-3 confers the activity dependence required for its role in homeostatic plasticity.

Previous work suggested that SNARE-complex formation might alleviate the inhibition of Ca2+ channels by syntaxin and SNAP25, but the role of v-SNAREs remained unclear48,49. We now find that the role of VAMP7 in Ca2+ entry requires syntaxin, not the other presynaptic t-SNARE SNAP25. VAMP7 promotes the association of syntaxin 1 with Cav2.1 in neurons, and syntaxin—but not SNAP25—promotes the association of VAMP7 with Cav2.1 by heterologous expression. Rather than relieving the inhibition of Ca2+ channels by t-SNAREs, VAMP7 thus serves as an activity-dependent rheostat for the inhibition of Ca2+ entry by a complex involving syntaxin. Both the interaction with Cav2.1 and the inhibition of Ca2+ channels depend on a unique, highly conserved linker between the longin and SNARE domains of VAMP7 that diverges in VAMP2, suggesting that although it associates with syntaxin, VAMP7 interacts directly with Cav2.1. Consistent with the specificity conferred by direct interaction, VAMP7 inhibits mainly P/Q-type channels, with little effect on N-type ones, but it also suppresses Ca2+ entry through L-type channels activated at a high frequency. Thus, we describe a new function for VAMP7 independent of its role in membrane fusion3.

How this mechanism influences information transfer is unclear. The increase in release probability due to protracted inactivity makes the synapse more sensitive to information about timing than about frequency of firing. Strong stimulation converts this high release probability to a low one, increasing the sensitivity of the synapse to frequency. The role of VAMP7 in P/Q-type Ca2+ channel regulation is also asymmetrical. Disinhibition of the channels requires hours of silencing, whereas strong stimulation inhibits the channels acutely. This asymmetry reflects the mechanisms involved: clearance of cell-surface VAMP7 by endocytosis, and delivery of VAMP7 by exocytosis. However, the asymmetry also contributes to the properties of this homeostatic mechanism, increasing the memory for recent activity as well as the speed at which this plasticity operates.

Our results show that the role of AP-3-derived SVs extends beyond transmitter release at high frequency. The exocytosis of AP-3-derived SVs in response to strong stimulation also increases the cell-surface expression of proteins that influence subsequent release. Although AP-3-derived SVs do not contribute to the initial release probability directly3, they influence the properties of release from SVs that are not made by AP-3. Regulation of cell-surface VAMP7 could thus contribute to the synaptic metaplasticity observed with changes in ongoing activity58.

In summary, activity regulates the cell-surface expression of VAMP7 by driving the exocytosis of AP-3-derived SVs. At the plasma membrane, VAMP7 associates with syntaxin to inhibit P/Q-type Ca2+ channels specifically, thereby influencing the probability of release to mediate a presynaptic form of homeostatic plasticity. VAMP7 is widely expressed by neurons, and P/Q-type channels are the main presynaptic Ca2+ channel at central synapses, which suggests that this mechanism confers homeostasis throughout the nervous system. In line with this, we observe similar effects of high-frequency stimulation on release at four excitatory synapses, and loss of VAMP7 eliminates the effect of high-frequency stimulation at each. Consistent with a general role, loss of VAMP7 increases FOS immunoreactivity in vivo. The increase in the proportion of FOS+ neurons further suggests that VAMP7 limits the number of presynaptic neurons that innervate a postsynaptic cell as well as the strength of their synaptic input.

C57BL6/J (strain 000664), Atp8a1-KO (strain 006433) and Ap3d1 (mocha, strain 000279) mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory. AP-3-deficient mocha mice have been maintained in the lab. Vamp7-KO mice were obtained from the RIKEN Bioresource Center (strain RBRC01926). All mouse lines were maintained as heterozygous breeder pairs, and the gender of pups used for culture was not determined; mice of both sexes were included in all experiments. All mice were housed under standard laboratory conditions with unlimited access to food and water, 12-h light–dark cycles and an ambient temperature of approximately 25.5 °C with 40–60% humidity. All animal housing, breeding and experimental procedures complied with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Guide for the Care and Use of Experimental Animals and were approved by the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) (AN202379).

The VAMP7 (158.2) mouse monoclonal (1:500 dilution, 232011), VAMP2 rabbit monoclonal (1:1,000 dilution, 104008), syntaxin 1 mouse monoclonal (1:2,000 dilution, 110011), SNAP25 mouse monoclonal (1:2,000 dilution, 111011), synaptotagmin 1 mouse monoclonal (1:1,000 dilution, 105011), VGLUT1 mouse monoclonal (1:1,000 dilution, 135011), VGLUT2 mouse monoclonal (1:1,000 dilution, 135421), synaptophysin mouse monoclonal (1:2,000 dilution, 101011), synaptophysin rabbit monoclonal (1:1,000 dilution, 101008), P/Q-type α-1A rabbit polyclonal (1:500 dilution, 152103), N-type α-1B antibody rabbit polyclonal (1:500 dilution, 152313) and Piccolo chicken polyclonal (1:2,000 dilution, 142116) antibodies were obtained from Synaptic Systems. The GFP (D5.1) rabbit monoclonal antibody (1:500 dilution, 2956) and FOS (9F6) rabbit monoclonal antibody (Alexa Fluor 647 Conjugate, 1:500 dilution, 14188) were obtained from Cell Signaling. The β-actin mouse monoclonal antibody (1:2,000 dilution) was obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific (MA1-140). The anti-dihydropyridine receptor (α2 subunit, 1:1,000 dilution) monoclonal antibody was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (D219). The HA.11 mouse monoclonal (1:1,000 dilution) was obtained from BioLegend (901513). The following secondary antibodies were obtained from Invitrogen: Alexa Fluor 488 conjugated to goat anti-mouse (1:400 dilution, A-11001), Alexa Fluor 555 conjugated to goat anti-rabbit (1:400 dilution, A-21428) and Alexa Fluor 647 conjugated to goat anti-chicken (1:400 dilution, A-21449).

The plasmids encoding VGLUT1–pH, VGLUT2–pH, VAMP2–pH and VAMP7–pH were reported previously59,60,61. For synaptic expression, iGluSnFR (Addgene, 98929) was fused at its C terminus to the C-terminal domain of Stargazin and subcloned into a lentiviral vector under the control of the human synapsin promoter. The M140A mutation in VAMP7–pH and M46A mutation in VAMP2–pH were generated by overlap extension PCR mutagenesis. Deletion mutants of the longin domain (ΔLD, amino acids (aa) 1–101) and linker (aa 102–121) of VAMP7–pH were amplified using PCR to add 5′ XbaI and 3′ HapI sites, then inserted into the modified FUGW vector digested with the same enzymes by ligase-independent cloning (ClonExpress II One Step Cloning Kit, C112, Vazyme). The pHluorin-tagged chimerae of VAMP7(SNARE-1) and VAMP7(SNARE-2) were synthesized by Twist Bioscience and inserted into FUGW digested with 5′ XbaI and 3′ HapI by ligase-independent cloning. To fuse the longin domain of VAMP7 to VAMP2–pH, the longin domain was amplified by PCR to add 5′ XbaI and VAMP2–pH was amplified by PCR to add 3′ HapI, then inserted into FUGW digested with the same enzymes by ligase-independent cloning (ClonExpress MultiS One Step Cloning Kit, C113, Vazyme). To replace the VAMP2 linker with the VAMP7 linker (aa 102–121), the VAMP7 linker and VAMP2–pH were amplified by PCR to add a 5′ XbaI site to the linker and a 3′ HapI site to VAMP2–pH, then inserted into FUGW digested with the same enzymes by ligase-independent cloning. To replace the VAMP7 linker with the VAMP2 linker, the longin domain and VAMP2 linker were amplified by PCR from VAMP2(LD) to add a 5′ XbaI site, and the VAMP7–pH lacking both the longin domain and the linker were amplified by PCR from full-length VAMP7-pH to add a 3′ HapI site, and then inserted into FUGW digested with the same enzymes by ligase-independent cloning. The untagged WT VAMP7, VAMP7(M140A), VAMP7(ΔLD), VAMP7(SNARE), VAMP7(VAMP2-linker) and VAMP2(VAMP7-linker) were amplified by PCR to add 5′ AgeI and 3′ NheI sites, then subcloned into the FU-IRES2-mCherry lentiviral vector digested with the same enzymes. Mouse SNAP25 and codon-optimized light chain of BoNT/A were synthesized by Twist Bioscience. SNAP25 was amplified by PCR to add 5′ XbaI and 3′ HapI sites, then subcloned into FUGW digested with the same enzymes. BoNT/A was amplified by PCR to add 5′ AgeI and 3′ NheI sites, then subcloned into a FU-IRES2-mCherry vector digested with the same enzymes. The TeNT light chain construct pFsynW-TeTx-LC (197284), Ca2+ channel subunit construct pCAGGS-Cav2.1-HA (206076), pCAGGS-CACNα2δ1 (206104), pcDNA3.1-Cavβ3 (26574) and syntaxin construct Stx1a-12aa-mCer (53236) were obtained from Addgene. HA-tagged syntaxin 1A was amplified by PCR to add a 5′ AgeI site with HA tag and 3′ NheI site, then subcloned into FU-IRES2-mCherry digested with the same enzymes. For the Cav2.1 construct, the HA tag was removed and 5 bp was added to the C terminus to restore the stop codon missing from the Addgene construct. A Twin-Strep tag was added to the N terminus of Cav2.1 by PCR. All constructs were sequenced to confirm the desired changes and exclude off-target mutations. Supplementary Table 1 contains the sequences of the primers and synthesized DNA sequences.

As previously described3, HEK293T cells were obtained from ATCC (CRL-3216) and were not independently authenticated. Cultures were tested and confirmed negative for contamination with mycoplasma. Low-passage HEK293T cells were seeded onto six-well plates coated with poly-l-lysine. The third-generation lentiviral vector pFUGW encoding the gene of interest (1.5 μg), as well as accessory plasmids pMDLG/pRRE, pIVS-VSVG and pRSV-Rev (0.5 μg each), were mixed with 12 μl FuGene HD transfection reagent (Promega) in 200 μl opti-MEM and incubated at room temperature for 15 min. The cells were incubated with transfection mixture overnight. The next morning, the medium was replaced with 2 ml fresh culture medium and collected after 48 h. Cell debris was removed by sedimentation at 1,000g. The viral supernatant was either used immediately or aliquoted and frozen at −80 °C; 35 μl virus supernatant was used per coverslip to infect primary hippocampal neuron cultures. To infect primary cortical neurons, the viral supernatant was incubated with Lenti-X concentrator (1:3, volume/volume ratio, TaKaRa, 631231) overnight and centrifuged at 1,500g for 45 min at 4 °C, and the white pellet was resuspended in PBS and frozen at −80 °C.

As previously described3, the hippocampus and cortex were dissected from postnatal day (P) 0–P1 mouse pups and dissociated in Hank’s balanced salt solution (HBSS) containing 10 mM HEPES and 20 mM glucose. Tissues were digested in 0.25% trypsin at 37 °C for 15 min (hippocampal cultures) and 20 min (cortical cultures), followed by three washes in HBSS. The cells were gently triturated and plated on poly-l-lysine-coated coverslips at 400 cells per mm2 in minimal essential medium (MEM) containing B27 (Gibco, 17504-044), 2 mM GlutaMAX (Gibco, 35050-061), 5% fetal bovine serum (Defined, HyClone) and 21 mM glucose (Sigma, G8769). After one day in vitro (DIV1), three-quarters of the medium was replaced with neurobasal medium (Gibco, 21103-049) containing B27 and 2.6 mM GlutaMAX. Lentiviral infection was performed at DIV7 and cells were used for imaging or biochemical analysis on DIV14–DIV15.

As previously described3, hippocampal cultures at DIV14–DIV15 were mounted in a laminar flow perfusion and stimulation chamber (Warner Instruments) on an inverted Nikon TE300 fluorescence microscope equipped with a 60× water-immersion objective. Neurons were illuminated using a Xenon lamp (Sutter Instruments) with 470/40-nm excitation and 525/50-nm emission filters. Field stimulation was applied using platinum–iridium electrodes delivering 1-ms bipolar current pulses that generated electric fields of 10 V cm−1. Cells were continuously perfused with Tyrode’s solution (in mM, 119 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 2 CaCl2, 2 MgCl2, 30 glucose and 25 HEPES; pH 7.4) supplemented with 10 μM CNQX and 50 μM APV to block AMPA and NMDA receptors, respectively. To quench surface pHluorin fluorescence, cells were exposed to MES solution (in mM, 119 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 2 MgCl2, 2 CaCl2, 30 glucose and 25 MES; pH 5.5). The total cellular pHluorin content was revealed using Tyrode’s solution with 50 mM NH4Cl, in which NaCl was reduced to 69 mM. To silence neuronal activity, neurons were incubated in complete culture medium containing either the glutamate receptor antagonists 10 μM CNQX and 50 μM APV, or 1 μM TTX (Cayman Chemical, 14964). To block reacidification after endocytosis, the neurons were incubated in Tyrode’s solution with 100 nM bafilomycin A1 (Cayman Chemical, 11038) for 30 s before stimulation. To image calcium entry, neurons were incubated in Tyrode’s solution containing 2.5 μM Fluo5F-AM (0.05% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO); Thermo Fisher Scientific, F14222) at 37 °C for 15 min in 5% CO2. For experiments with calcium channel blockers, neurons were incubated with 300 nM ω-agatoxin IVA (Tocris, 2799), 1 μM ω-conotoxin GVIA (Tocris, 2085), 100 nM SNX-482 (Abcam, ab120259) or 10 μM nimodipine (Abcam, ab120135) for 30 min at 37 °C in 5% CO2. The vehicles were as follows: water for agatoxin and conotoxin, 0.01% DMSO for nimodipine and 0.02% DMSO for SNX-482. To test the role of VAMP2, SNAP25 and syntaxin 1 in calcium entry, lentivirus encoding the catalytic light chain of either TeNT and BoNT/A was added at DIV7 and imaged at DIV14. BoNT/C toxin complex was obtained from Metabiologics (300). Neurons were incubated overnight with different concentrations of BoNT/C before imaging. To image the release of glutamate from cultured neurons, hippocampal neurons expressing iGluSnFR were stimulated at 0.2 Hz. To identify synapses, hippocampal neurons were either loaded with styryl dye FM4-64 by stimulation at 10 Hz for 60 s (washing for 10 min after) or transduced by lentivirus to express BFP-tagged synaptophysin. Images were acquired at 1 Hz for pHluorin imaging and at 20 Hz for Fluo5F and iGluSnFR using a QuantEM CCD camera (Photometrics). Imaging was done at 35 °C and was controlled by a dual automatic temperature controller (TC-344B, Warner Instruments). Image acquisition and data collection were managed using MetaMorph v.7.8.10.0 (Molecular Devices).

One entire brain from a 6–8-week-old mouse was disrupted in 10 ml ice-cold homogenization buffer (in mM, 300 sucrose, 1 MgEGTA and 10 HEPES-Tris; pH 7.4) supplemented with cOmplete protease inhibitors (Roche) by nine strokes at 900 rpm using a Teflon homogenizer, as previously described3. The homogenate was centrifuged at 871g for 10 min at 4 °C in an SS34 rotor (Sorvall). The supernatant (S1) was collected and centrifuged at 12,000g for 15 min at 4 °C in the same rotor. The synaptosome-enriched pellet (P2) was resuspended in 10 ml homogenization buffer and washed once by centrifugation at 14,500g for 15 min at 4 °C. To obtain SVs, the pellet (P2′) was resuspended in 1.2 ml homogenization buffer and then osmotic lysis in 13.5 ml cold water containing 8 mM HEPES-Tris (pH 7.4) for 45 min. The lysed P2′ was then disrupted by five strokes at 3,000 rpm and centrifuged at 32,500g for 20 min. The supernatant (LS1) was then centrifuged at 280,000g for 2 h in a Beckman Type 70 Ti rotor. The final pellet (LP2) was gently resuspended by repeated pipetting. To perform the immunoprecipitation, the pellet P2’ was resuspended in 1 ml lysis buffer (in mM, 100 NaCl, 5 EDTA and 50 HEPES; pH 7.4) containing 1% Triton X-100 and protease inhibitors. Cells were rotated at 4 °C for 2 h before being transferred to room temperature for a further 15 min. The lysate was sedimented at 16,000g for 10 min and the supernatant was incubated for 2 h at 4 °C with 5 μg Cav2.1 antibodies and then with 30 μl Dynabeads Protein A (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10001D) for another hour. After immunoprecipitation, the beads were washed four times with lysis buffer and the bound proteins were released in 1× SDS sample buffer (NEB, B7703S).

HEK293 cells or primary cortical neurons grown in a 10-cm dish were washed with 1× PBS and lysed for 2 h at 4 °C in 1 ml lysis buffer (1% DDM, 0.1% CHS, 100 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA and 50 mM HEPES; pH 7.4) supplemented with protease inhibitors. The cell lysate was sedimented at 16,000g for 10 min, and the supernatant was incubated for 2 h at 4 °C with 40 μl Strep-Tactin XT magnetic beads (IBA Lifesciences, 21613002) or 20 μL GFP-Trap Magnetic Particles M-270 (Proteintech, gtd). After immunoprecipitation, the beads were washed four times with lysis buffer, and bound proteins were released in 1× SDS sample buffer before separation by SDS–PAGE.

Proteins and all blue pre-stained protein standards (Bio-Rad, 1610373) were separated by electrophoresis through 4–20% precast SDS polyacrylamide gels (Bio-Rad, 5671095) and electrotransferred to nitrocellulose membrane. Membranes were blocked for 30 min at room temperature in TBS-T (Tris-buffered saline, pH 7.4, with 0.1% Tween-20) containing 5% non-fat dry milk. Primary antibodies were incubated in TBS-T containing 1% non-fat dry milk for 1.5 h at room temperature. After washing three times in TBS-T, the membranes were incubated with secondary antibodies, IRDye 800CW goat anti-mouse IgG (1:10,000 dilution, 926-32210) and IRDye 680RD goat anti-rabbit IgG (1:20,000 dilution, 926-68071) (LI-COR Biosciences) for 1 h. After three washes, the blots were visualized by quantitative fluorescence imaging with a LI-COR system (Odyssey v.2.0.3, LI-COR Biosciences).

As previously described3, P21–P25 mice were anaesthetized by intraperitoneal administration of ketamine and xylazine and perfused transcardially with ice-cold cutting artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF) composed of (in mM) 2.5 KCl, 0.5 CaCl2, 7 MgSO4, 1.25 NaH2PO4, 25 NaHCO3, 7 d-glucose, 210 sucrose and 1.3 ascorbic acid (305–310 mOsm; pH 7.4) saturated with 95% O2/5% CO2. Brains were rapidly removed and sectioned using a vibratome (Leica) in continuously aerated cutting aCSF into near-horizontal slices (300 μm) to record from Schaffer-collateral, mossy-fibre and perforant-path synapses, and into sagittal slices for corticothalamic and parallel-fibre synapses. The slices were then transferred to recording aCSF (in mM, 119 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 2.5 CaCl2, 1.3 MgSO4, 1 NaH2PO4, 26.2 NaHCO3 and 11 d-glucose; 305–310 mOsm; pH 7.4) or aCSF containing 1.5 CaCl2 and 1 MgSO4 (shown in Extended Data Figs. 7 and 11a) saturated with 95% O2/5% CO2. Slices were incubated at 32 °C for 30 min and maintained at room temperature for a further 30 min before use. A cut was made between CA1 and CA3 to prevent recurrent network activity.

All electrophysiological recordings were performed on an upright Olympus BX51WI microscope. Brain slices were continuously perfused (3 ml per min) with recording aCSF saturated with 95% O2/5% CO2. Patch electrodes were fabricated from borosilicate glass capillaries using a Flaming/Brown puller (P-87, Sutter Instruments) and exhibited resistances of 3–5 MΩ when filled with the internal solution (in mM, 135 CsMeSO3, 10 HEPES, 8 NaCl, 0.3 EGTA, 4 Mg-ATP, 0.3 Na-GTP, 5 QX-314 and 0.1 spermine; 290–295 mOsm; pH 7.4). All recordings were done at 34–35 °C (except for those at 21–22 °C shown in Extended Data Fig. 11b,c). AMPAR-mediated responses were recorded in the presence of 10 µM APV to block NMDAR currents and 100 µM picrotoxin to block inhibition. To measure the initial release probability, NMDAR-mediated responses were collected in the presence of 100 µM picrotoxin, 10 µM 6,7-dinitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (DNQX) and 50 μM MK-801 after 10-min incubation in the bath. To test the role of presynaptic Ca2+ channels, slices were first recorded without Ca2+ channel blockers, then incubated for 30 min in blockers or vehicle (water or 0.01% DMSO) and recorded again. A Tungsten bipolar stimulating electrode (WE3ST30.1A3 SS, MicroProbes) was positioned in the stratum radiatum (to stimulate Schaffer-collateral synapses), the hilus adjacent to the dentate granule cell layer (mossy-fibre synapses), the outer molecular layer of the hippocampus (perforant-path synapses), the internal capsule (corticothalamic synapses) and parallel-fibre synapses of the cerebellum. AMPA EPSCs were recorded in whole-cell voltage-clamp mode held at −70 mV, and NMDA EPSCs were recorded at 40 mV. Amplitude was measured from the peak response. For the recordings in CA3, l-2-amino-4-phosphonobutyric acid (L-AP4, 10 μM) was added to the bath for 10 min at the end of the recording to confirm that the responses were mediated by mossy fibres. To ensure stable recording, membrane holding current, input resistance and pipette series resistance were monitored throughout. The series resistance typically ranged from 10 to 20 MΩ, and recordings were discarded if it exceeded 30 MΩ. Only recordings with a seal resistance larger than 1 GΩ were included in the analysis. Data were collected with a MultiClamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices), stored using Igor Pro v.6.3.4.1 (Wavemetrics), digitized at 10 kHz and filtered at 2 kHz.

Primary hippocampal neurons were fixed for 15 min with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in 1× PBS, followed by permeabilization and blocking in PBS for 30 min with 0.1% Triton X-100 and 4% normal goat serum (NGS). Cells were incubated with primary antibodies in PBS containing 1% NGS and 0.025% Triton X-100 for 1.5 h at room temperature. After three 10-min washes in PBS, cells were incubated with the appropriate secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature and washed again as above. Coverslips were mounted in ProLong Diamond Antifade Mountant (P36961, Invitrogen).

To immunostain brain slices, mice were perfused sequentially with cold PBS followed by 4% PFA in PBS. The brains were dissected, post-fixed overnight in 4% PFA in PBS and cryoprotected in PBS containing, sequentially, 15% and 30% sucrose. Sagittal sections (35 μm) were cut using a Leica CM3050S cryostat, blocked and permeabilized in PBS containing 4% NGS and 0.2% Triton X-100 and incubated in primary antibodies diluted in PBS containing 1% NGS and 0.2% Triton X-100 overnight at 4 °C, followed by three 10-min washes in PBS. The sections were incubated with appropriate secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature in the dark, and washed as above and then in PBS containing 1.5 μM Hoechst 33342 for 5 min before mounting as above.

The stained cells were imaged using a Nikon Ti Microscope equipped with a CSU-W1 spinning disk confocal module, a Plan Apo 40× or 60× oil-immersion objective and an Andor Zyla scientific CMOS camera. Super-resolution structured illumination microscopy (SIM) images were captured on a DeltaVision OMX SR microscope (GE Healthcare) with a Plan ApoN 60× 1.42 objective (Olympus), 1.516 index immersion oil and three PCO 15-bit CMOS cameras. Images were acquired using a 50-ms exposure, a pre-amplifier gain of 1 and variable EM gain. Alexa Fluor 488 fluorescence was excited with a 488-nm laser and detected with a 528/488-nm emission filter. Alexa Fluor 555 fluorescence was excited with a 568-nm laser and detected with a 609/37-nm filter. Alexa Fluor 647 fluorescence was excited with a 642-nm laser and emission collected with a 683/40-nm filter. Confocal images were collected using Micro-Manager (v.2.0-gamma). SIM imaging was controlled with OMX AquireSR software (GE Healthcare) and aligned using SoftWoRx (GE Healthcare). All images were processed and analysed with ImageJ v.1.54g (NIH).

Acquired fluorescence images were analysed using ImageJ, as previously described3. For pHluorin imaging, the ImageJ Time Series Analyzer (v.3.0) plug-in was used and individual boutons were identified manually on the basis of their fluorescence in NH4Cl and hence independent of the response to stimulation. Circular regions of interest (ROIs; 10 × 10 areas of pixel intensities) were positioned manually at the centre of fluorescent punctae. Background signal was estimated from three cell-free regions and subtracted from each trace. The integrated fluorescence in each bouton was then normalized to the baseline fluorescence before stimulation and to the maximal unquenched signal obtained in NH4Cl. For Fluo5F and iGluSnFR imaging experiments, circular ROIs (5 × 5 areas of pixel intensities) were used and the data were normalized to baseline before stimulation. All acquired data were included in the analysis; no randomization or group allocation was applied. Sample sizes were chosen to detect 1–2 s.d. with 80% probability. ROIs were selected blind to the results. Analysis of the whole-cell recording was not performed blind to genotype or experimental condition but no recordings were excluded. Curve fitting and quantitative analysis were performed in GraphPad Prism (v.11.0.2).

No formal statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size, but the number of replicates in this study is comparable with those in previous reports3,4. Quantification was performed using data collected from multiple coverslips derived from at least three independent experimental preparations, as detailed in the Source Data. Statistical analyses were performed with GraphPad Prism. Data generally followed a normal distribution and were evaluated by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests or one-way or two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc comparisons. All summary values are presented as mean ± s.e.m., and n denotes either the number of coverslips or the number of recorded cells.

All animal procedures were performed in accordance with the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the IACUC at UCSF.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

The publicly available single-nucleus RNA-sequencing dataset analysed in this study is available through the Broad Institute Single Cell Portal under accession code SCP2162 (ref. 31). All other data supporting the findings of this study are available in the paper and its Supplementary Information. Source data are provided with this paper.

The code used for analysis of the pHluorin imaging was reported previously3. Further information is available from the corresponding author upon request.

a, Representative images of hippocampal cultures immunostained for synaptophysin (Syp, green), VGLUT1 (magenta) and VGLUT2 (cyan), with the regions indicated (1,2) shown below at higher magnification. Arrowheads indicate Syp+ puncta that colocalize with VGLUT1 or VGLUT2. Scale bars, 20 and 2 μm. b, Scatter plots show the correlation between synaptophysin and either VGLUT1 (left) or VGLUT2 (middle) fluorescence. Dashed lines indicate the threshold (2 x s.d.) used to define VGLUT+ synapses. Quantification (right) shows that 97.25% and 93.28% of VGLUT1- and VGLUT2-positive puncta respectively were positive for synaptophysin (n = 3529 boutons from 13 images). c, Silencing does not affect the punctate morphology of presynaptic boutons. WT hippocampal neurons (DIV14) were treated with 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX, 10 μM) and 3-(2-carboxypiperazin-4-yl)propyl-1-phosphonic acid (APV, 50 μM) for 24 h and immunostained for synaptophysin (Syp, green), VAMP2 (magenta) and Piccolo (cyan). Line scans show the distribution of Syp, VAMP2 and Piccolo. The scatter plots indicate Pearson’s correlation coefficient for Syp or VAMP2 with Piccolo (n = 6/3). Scale bars, 100 μm; inset, 20 μm. d, WT hippocampal neurons expressing iGluSnFR–stargazin were silenced for 24 h (in CNQX and APV) and stimulated 30 times at 0.2 Hz to calculate release probability. Four representative presynaptic boutons (ROIs) are shown. Data indicate mean ± s.e.m. n = x/y, where x is the number of fields examined and y the number of independent experiments. Significance was determined by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (c).

a, WT hippocampal neurons loaded with Fluo5F for 15 min were stimulated at 1 Hz for 10 action potentials (APs). Representative Fluo5F fluorescence traces recorded from individual presynaptic boutons in three independent imaging fields. Vertical dotted lines indicate stimuli. Horizontal dashed red line indicates the threshold (2 x s.d.) used to define the Ca2+ response. b, Quantification of response success rate for each stimulus in the train. Success was defined as a fluorescence response exceeding the threshold indicated in a. c, Peak Ca2+ responses (ΔF/F0) evoked by each stimulus during the train. Left, distribution of peak fluorescence responses for each stimulus. Right, cumulative frequency distributions of response amplitudes for each stimulus. Comparable response amplitudes across the stimulus train indicate reliable action potential-evoked Ca2+ entry with minimal response failures (n = 63 boutons from 3 fields). d, WT hippocampal neurons loaded with Fluo5F for 15 min were stimulated at 5 Hz for 25 APs. Representative Fluo5F fluorescence traces recorded from individual presynaptic boutons in three independent imaging fields. e, Success was defined as a fluorescence response exceeding the baseline. Data indicate mean ± s.e.m. (n = 3 independent coverslips).

a–d, Averaged traces (left) from CA1 stratum radiatum show the response to 5 Hz test stimulus trains (100 AP) delivered before (black) and after (red) 100 stimuli (blue) delivered at either 5 or 50 Hz in hippocampal slices from WT (a), mocha (b), Atp8a1-KO (c) and Vamp7-KO (d) mice. The response to each stimulus is normalized to the first EPSC of the first test stimulus train. Scatter plots (right) show the magnitude of the first EPSC of the second test stimulus train relative to the magnitude of the first EPSC in the first stimulus train (a, n = 17/3; b, n = 21/3; c, n = 22/3; d, n = 11/3). e, Schematic of the experimental design. Schaffer-collateral fibres in stratum radiatum were stimulated at either standard (1x) or elevated (3x) stimulus intensity while recording EPSCs from CA1 pyramidal neurons. Representative traces show responses evoked by 100 stimuli delivered at 5 Hz. Bottom, normalized EPSC amplitudes plotted as a function of stimulus number for 1x and 3x stimulation intensities. Right, quantification of EPSC amplitudes at AP2, AP10, AP50, and AP95, normalized to the first response (AP1). Increasing stimulus intensity did not alter short-term depression during the stimulus train (n = 7/2). Data indicate mean ± s.e.m. n = x/y, where x is the number of cells and y the number of mice. Significance was determined by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test.

a, Representative hippocampal sections from WT, mocha and Atp8a1-KO mice immunostained for ATP8A1, synaptophysin and Hoechst. Scale bar, 500 μm. b, Representative hippocampal sections from WT, mocha, and Vamp7-KO mice immunostained for VAMP7, synaptophysin, and Hoechst. Scale bar, 500 μm. Representative images were obtained from three mice per genotype. c, RNA expression of SV proteins across major brain regions and cell types. Dot size indicates the percentage of cells expressing each gene, and colour indicates the normalized expression level (https://singlecell.broadinstitute.org/single_cell). d, Immunoblot of synaptosomal (P2) and SV-enriched (LP2) fractions isolated from hippocampal stratum radiatum (rad) and lacunosum-moleculare (l-m) (left) with quantification of protein abundance in rad relative to l-m (right). Dots represent independent biological replicates (n = 3 independent experiments). e–g, Sample traces (left) from CA1 stratum radiatum show the effect of 100 stimuli (blue) delivered at either 5 or 50 Hz on test stimulation at 5 Hz (also 100 AP) in hippocampal slices from WT (e,f) and Vamp7-KO (g) mice in aCSF containing 1.5 mM Ca2+/1 mM Mg2+; hatched lines indicate a gap of 20 s. The graph (middle) shows the mean response to each stimulus normalized to the first. Scatter plots (right) show the response of different cells to AP2 (f,g) and AP95 (e–g) normalized by the response to AP1 (e, n = 15/3; f,g, 16/3). Data indicate mean ± s.e.m. n = x/y, where x is the number of cells and y the number of mice. Significance was determined by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test.

a, Sagittal brain slices from WT or Vamp7-KO mice were immunolabelled for VAMP7 (green) and synaptophysin (magenta) with the regions indicated (1,2) shown on the right at higher magnification. Scale bars, 500 µm (lower magnification) and 200 µm (higher magnification). Representative images were obtained from two mice per genotype. b–d, Sample traces (left) show the effect of 50 Hz stimulation (100 AP, blue) on 5 Hz test stimulation (also 100 AP) delivered before (black) and after (red) in WT or Vamp7-KO mice, recording from lateral perforant-path synapses in the dentate gyrus (b), corticothalamic synapses (c) and parallel-fibre synapses in the cerebellum (d). The hatched lines indicate a gap of 20 s. The plots (middle) show the response to each stimulus normalized to the first response. Scatter plots (right) show the response of different cells to AP2 and AP95 relative to AP1 (b, n = 18/3 for WT, n = 19/3 for Vamp7 KO; c, n = 13/3 for WT, n = 12/3 for Vamp7 KO; d, n = 21/3 for WT, n = 18/3 for Vamp7 KO). Data indicate mean ± s.e.m. n = x/y, where x is the number of cells and y the number of mice. Significance was determined by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test.

a, Quantitative immunoblots showing SV proteins from the LP2 fraction of WT and Vamp7-KO mice. Scatter plots show the amounts in Vamp7 KO relative to WT (n = 3). b, Loss of VAMP7 does not affect the punctate morphology of presynaptic boutons. Hippocampal neurons from WT and Vamp7-KO mice were immunostained for synaptophysin (Syp, magenta), Piccolo (cyan) and VGLUT1 (green) or VGLUT2 (green). Scatter plots indicate the mean size of a presynaptic bouton fitted by a Gaussian (n = 120 boutons/6/3). Scale bars, 20 μm. c,d, WT (with and without VAMP7 overexpression) and Vamp7-KO hippocampal neurons expressing VGLUT1–pH (c) or VGLUT2–pH (d) were stimulated at 5, 10, 25 or 50 Hz for 20 s, and the response normalized to total pHluorin fluorescence revealed in NH4Cl. Graphs below show the initial rate of fluorescence increase per AP (left) and end-stimulus fluorescence (right) (WT with VAMP7 overexpression, n = 16/3; all other conditions, 18/3). Data indicate mean ± s.e.m. n = x/y, where x is the number of coverslips examined and y the number of independent experiments. Significance was determined by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (a,b) and two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (c,d).

a, EPSC amplitude in CA1 stratum radiatum at 34–35 °C in response to 100 AP delivered at 5 and 25 Hz in aCSF containing 1.5 mM Ca2+/1 mM Mg2+, normalized to the first response. Graphs (below) show the normalized EPSC magnitude at AP2 and AP95 as a function of stimulation frequency (n = 12/3). b, EPSC amplitude in CA1 stratum radiatum at room temperature (21–22 °C) in response to stimulus trains (100 AP) delivered at 5 and 25 Hz in aCSF containing 2.5 mM Ca2+, normalized to the first response. Scatter plots (right) show the normalized EPSC magnitude at AP2 and AP90 as a function of stimulation frequency (5 Hz: n = 25/4 for WT; 29/4 for Vamp7 KO. 25 Hz: n = 21/4 for WT; 25/4 for Vamp7 KO). c, Paired-pulse ratio (PPR) for the interstimulus intervals (ISI) indicated at room temperature or 34–35 °C (n = 3 mice). d, Amplitude of the mossy-fibre EPSCs recorded in CA3 pyramidal cells in response to 100 AP delivered at 5 and 25 Hz at 34–35 °C in aCSF containing 2.5 mM Ca2+, normalized to the first response. Scatter plots (right) show the normalized EPSCs at AP2 and AP90 as a function of stimulation frequency (5 Hz: n = 21/4 for WT; 25/4 for Vamp7 KO; 25 Hz: n = 20/4 for WT; 17/4 for Vamp7 KO). e, EPSC amplitude in CA1 stratum radiatum at 34–35 °C in response to 5 Hz stimulation (100 AP) in aCSF containing 1.5, 2.5 or 4 mM Ca2+, normalized to the first response. Increased extracellular Ca2+ (4 mM) occludes the increased synaptic depression observed in the Vamp7 KO. Graph shows the amplitude of the EPSC evoked by AP90 in a 5 Hz stimulus train, normalized to the first response (n = 12/3 for 1.5 mM, 18/3 for 2.5 mM and 17/3 for 4 mM Ca2+). The data indicate mean ± s.e.m. n = x/y, where x is the number of cells recorded and y the number of mice. Significance was determined by two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test.

a, WT hippocampal neurons loaded with Fluo5F for 15 min were stimulated at 10 Hz for 30 s in Tyrode’s buffer containing FM4-64 to label presynaptic boutons. Scatter plot indicates Pearson’s correlation coefficient for Fluo5F with FM4-64 (n = 10/2). Scale bar, 20 μm. b, Hippocampal neurons were loaded with Fluo5F, stimulated at 10 Hz in Tyrode’s solution containing 2 mM Ca2+ followed by 8 mM Ca2+ and the response normalized to baseline fluorescence. Scatter plot indicates the area under the curve (AUC) for the corresponding calcium responses (n = 10/2). c, WT hippocampal neurons were transduced with lentiviruses encoding TeNT light chain and VGLUT1–pH at DIV7. At DIV14, the cells were stimulated at 25 Hz for 20 s and the response normalized to total pHluorin fluorescence revealed in NH4Cl. Scatter plot shows the fluorescence at the end of the stimulus (n = 6/3). d,e, WT (d) or Vamp7-KO (e) hippocampal neurons expressing TeNT light chain were loaded with Fluo5F and stimulated with a single action potential (1 AP) or at 5 or 25 Hz and the response normalized to baseline fluorescence. Scatter plots show the peak response for 1-AP stimulation and the AUC for the stimulus trains (d, n = 14/3; e, n = 16/3). The data indicate mean ± s.e.m. n = x/y, where x is the number of fields examined and y the number of independent experiments. Significance was assessed by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test.

a, Sequence alignment of VAMP SNARE motifs, with the 16 stacked SNARE layers indicated. The methionine (yellow) located at layer −3 is highly conserved. b, WT hippocampal neurons expressing WT or M46A VAMP2–pH were immunostained for endogenous synaptophysin (magenta) and Piccolo (cyan). Scale bar, 20 μm. Representative images were obtained from two independent cultures. c, Scatter plots indicate the Pearson’s correlation coefficient for VAMP2 (left) or VAMP7 (right) with synaptophysin (n = 12/3). d,e, Hippocampal neurons expressing WT or M140A VAMP7–pH were perfused with MES (pH 5.5) to quench cell-surface pHluorin (d) or stimulated at 10 and 25 Hz for 20 s (e) and the response normalized to total pHluorin fluorescence revealed in NH4Cl (d, n = 12/3; e, n = 14/3). f, Vamp7-KO hippocampal neurons expressing untagged WT or M140A VAMP7 and VGLUT1–pH were stimulated at 5, 10, 25 and 50 Hz for 20 s, and the response normalized as above. Scatter plot shows fluorescence at the end of the stimulus (n = 12/3). Data indicate mean ± s.e.m. n = x/y, where x is the number of fields examined and y the number of independent experiments. Significance was determined by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (c) or one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (f).

a, WT and Vamp7-KO hippocampal neurons were incubated with ω-agatoxin IVA (300 nM), conotoxin GVIA (1 µM) or both for 30 min and loaded with 2.5 μM Fluo5F for 15 min before delivering 5 s stimulus trains at 5 or 25 Hz; the response was normalized to baseline fluorescence. Scatter plots show the area under the curve (AUC) for the stimulus trains (5 Hz: control, agatoxin and conotoxin, n = 18/3 for WT and Vamp7 KO; agatoxin + conotoxin, n = 17/3 for WT and n = 14/3 for Vamp7 KO. 25 Hz: control, agatoxin and conotoxin, n = 18/3 for WT and Vamp7 KO; agatoxin + conotoxin, n = 16/3 for WT and n = 15/3 for Vamp7 KO). b, WT and Vamp7-KO hippocampal neurons were incubated with nimodipine (10 µM) or SNX-482 (100 nM) for 30 min and then with Fluo5F (2.5 μM) for 15 min before delivering a single stimulus (1 AP) or 5 s stimulus trains at 5 or 25 Hz; the response was normalized to baseline fluorescence. Scatter plots show the peak response to 1 AP and the area under the curve for the trains (1 AP: n = 22/3 for Vamp7 KO under control conditions; n = 14/3 for all other conditions. 5 Hz and 25 Hz: n = 18/3 for WT and Vamp7-KO neurons treated with nimodipine; n = 14/3 for all other conditions). c, WT and Vamp7-KO hippocampal neurons were incubated with thapsigargin (TG, 1 μM) and Fluo5F for 15 min before delivering 1 AP or 5 s stimulus trains at 25 Hz; the response was normalized to baseline fluorescence. Scatter plots show the percent inhibition by TG (1 AP: n = 20/3 for Vamp7 KO treated with TG; n = 18/3 for all other conditions. 25 Hz: n = 18/3). d, WT and Vamp7-KO hippocampal slices were stimulated with a single AP before and after incubation with ω-agatoxin IVA, conotoxin GVIA and nimodipine for 30 min. Scatter plot shows the inhibition by neurotoxin (agatoxin: n = 19/3 for WT; 16/3 for Vamp7 KO. Conotoxin: n = 17/3 for WT; 15/3 for Vamp7 KO. Nimodipine: n = 9/3). e, Scatter plots show the percent inhibition by ω-agatoxin IVA (n = 19/3 for WT, 16/3 for KO), conotoxin GVIA (n = 17/3 for WT and 15/3 for KO) or nimodipine (n = 9/3). f,g, Hippocampal slices from WT and Vamp7-KO mice were stimulated at 5 Hz (100 AP) without toxin before (pre) and 30 min after incubation (post) with agatoxin (f) or conotoxin (g). The responses were normalized to the first EPSC (left) and the scatter plots show the normalized response at AP2 and AP90 (n = 13/3 for WT, 14/3 for KO). Data indicate mean ± s.e.m. n = x/y, where x indicates the fields or cells examined and y the independent experiments. Significance was determined by one-way ANOVA (a,b), two-way ANOVA (d,f,g) with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test or two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (c,e).

a, Hippocampal neurons from WT and Vamp7-KO mice were immunostained for endogenous Cav2.1 (magenta), syntaxin 1 (green) and Piccolo (cyan) and the images reconstructed from 125 nm sections by structured illumination. The representative 3D SIM volume rendering shows colocalization of Cav2.1 with syntaxin 1 and Piccolo. Scale bar, 1 μm. b,c, Hippocampal neurons from WT or Vamp7-KO mice were immunostained for endogenous Cav2.2 (magenta), Piccolo (cyan) and synaptophysin (green, b) or syntaxin 1 (green, c). Scatter plots indicate the Pearson’s coefficient of Cav2.2 with synaptophysin (Syp, b) and with syntaxin 1 (c) (n = 12/3). Scale bars, 20 μm (left) and 2 μm (right). d,e, Hippocampal neurons from WT mice were treated with 0.5, 1 and 3 nM BoNT/C toxin at DIV14 for 18 h, collected for western blot (d) or immunostained for synaptophysin (e). Scatter plots (d, right) indicate the percentage of uncleaved syntaxin 1, SNAP25 and VAMP2 in neurons treated with different concentrations of BoNT/C toxin (n = 3). BoNT/C (0.5 nM) efficiently cleaves syntaxin 1 without obvious cellular toxicity (e). Scale bar, 20 μm. The data indicate mean ± s.e.m. n = x/y, where x is the number of images examined and y the number of independent experiments. Significance was determined by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (b,c) or one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (d).

a, Hippocampal neurons were transduced with lentivirus encoding TeNT or BoNT/A light chains at DIV7 and collected at DIV14 for western blot. #1449. James Trafford's old ghost returns to haunt him as Marco Rose's Bournemouth side claim another heavyweight scalp to make it six wins on the spin

Published: 13:23 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 16:56 EDT, 31 October 2026

How fitting it was, amid this season of werewolves and vampires, that it was one of James Trafford’s old ghosts that came back to haunt him.

No witches or zombies will give the Leeds goalkeeper a sleepless night quite like this familiar howler that cost his side the game.

The visitors dominated Bournemouth for most of the first half with confident, flowing football and thought they had a deserved lead when Dominic Calvert-Lewin bundled the ball into the net early on after a stunning passing move only for the goal to be ruled out for a handball.

Leeds were firmly on top…and then they had a goal-kick. Trafford didn’t take it but received it short and tried to pass it out to Ao Tanaka only to play it straight to the lurking Justin Kluivert, who squared it to Evanlison for a tap-in.

It was almost identical to the goal Trafford conceded at the Etihad Stadium against Tottenham at the start of last season, on his second league start for Manchester City, when he - again - received a short goal-kick and tried to pass it to a team-mate who was already surrounded. City signed Gianluigi Donnarumma 10 days later and Trafford’s City career was all-but over.

The England keeper has been able to resurrect it at Leeds, and came into the game with the best save percentage of any stopper in the Premier League, and marshaller of the second-best defence in the division behind only champions Arsenal.

Trafford made a fine save from a Marcus Tavernier free-kick, and another effort late on from Junior Kroupi but the damage had been done. He could do little about Amine Adli’s finish that doubled Bournemouth’s lead in second-half stoppage time. The Bournemouth supporters, who jeered him every time he touched the ball, made sure he didn’t forget it.

‘James is a terrific young goalkeeper,’ said Leeds boss Daniel Farke. ‘I’m pretty sure he will save us way more points than he perhaps has cost us today. We win together, we lose together. We’re all happy to have him. He’s still top class and has all my trust and all my love. My recommendation is that he shouldn’t watch the scene back!’

It was almost identical to the goal Trafford conceded against Tottenham at the start of last season when he - again - received a short goal-kick and passed it straight to the opposition

The English goalkeeper could do little about Amine Adli’s finish that doubled Bournemouth’s lead in second-half stoppage time

Bournemouth have made such a habit of punching above their weight in recent years, that victories over traditional Premier League big boys no longer seem as remarkable as they once did. Running your club brilliantly, signing excellent players and developing them with superb coaches season after season will tend to normalise such success for a club of this size.

The Cherries are no longer content to constrain their heroics to slaying mere domestic giants. In the space of 10 days, they have dispatched former European Cup winners AC Milan, Manchester United and Aston Villa — all 3-0 — and now former runners-up Leeds.

Yes, they needed a bit of luck and a glaring mistake to get them ahead but, once they got in front, they rarely looked like letting it slip. Brazilian sensation Rayan went close before substitute Adli wrapped it up late on after a stunning through ball from Kroupi.

Bournemouth needed a bit of luck and a glaring mistake to get them ahead but, once they got in front, they rarely looked like letting it slip

Bournemouth (4-2-3-1): Petrovic 7; Smith 7 (Diakite 88), Hill 8, Silva 7, Truffert 6; Adams 7, Christie 7 (Cook 6); Rayan 6 (Adli 88), Kluivert 7 (Kroupi 68, 8), Tavernier 7; EVANILSON 8 (Rodriguez 76).

Leeds (3-4-2-1): Trafford 5; Justin 6 (Bahoya 84), Elvedi 6, Muharemovic 7; Bogle 6, Ampadu 6, Tanaka 5 (Stach 65, 6); Gudmudsson 6 (Longstaff 65, 5); Wilson 6 (Aaronson 84), James 7 (Nmecha 65, 6); Calvert-Lewin 6.

What is even more impressive is that Bournemouth are doing it without Andoni Iraola at the helm, and under a manager in Marco Rose who was even feeling early grumblings of discontent from sections of the fanbase after failing to win any of their first six league games.

Now, it’s six wins in a row in all competitions. Sixteen goals scored, none conceded. Even for Bournemouth, who make the remarkable look normal, that’s quite something.

Not only that, they are doing it without influential midfielder Alex Scott, out with a hamstring injury, pulling the strings. When you have Ryan Christie and Tyler Adams keeping things ticking in the middle, with Justin Kluivert and Kroupi ahead of them, you barely even noticed.

Marco Rose was feeling early grumblings of discontent from sections of the fanbase after failing to win any of their first six league games

We’re approaching that time of year, with Halloween already upon us and Christmas coming into view, when the constant churn of January transfer rumours will soon become inescapable.

An early one doing the rounds is how Manchester United are ‘exploring a move’ for Calvert-Lewin.

Don’t fall for it, Dominic. He lost here but how different the afternoon could have gone had the ball not bounced on to his arm before going into the net. Even in defeat, this is still a club under Daniel Farke that’s stable, competent and moving in the right direction.

If United are really in the market for someone who knows where the net is, few are doing it with more ruthless efficiency than Bournemouth striker Evanlison, who made it four goals in as many games for the Cherries.

‘I just saw him said: “You are a real number 9”,’ said Bournemouth boss Marco Rose.

#1448. Kevin Nisbet's lack of cool proved so costly for Aberdeen at Hampden... and underlines why he's not a man for the big occasion

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 18:27 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 18:32 EDT, 31 October 2026

In the build-up to this Premier Sports Cup semi-final, Aberdeen captain Kevin Nisbet spoke about the players needing to step up and deliver.

On a woeful run of form as they arrived at Hampden, and with huge pressure mounting on Stephen Robinson, Nisbet insisted the players owed the manager a performance and a result.

Just to take the heat off as much as anything else. With 76 minutes on the clock in this tense and cagey affair with Rangers, Nisbet had a golden opportunity.

With the score locked at 0-0, Stuart Armstrong fed a pass into Nisbet’s path and the ball was crying out to be struck first time.

Nisbet could probably see the whites of Ivor Pandur’s eyes. In the context of the game, it was as good a chance as Aberdeen could have hoped for.

But his finish was absolutely awful. Nisbet hesitated when he should have pulled the trigger straight away, allowing Olwethu Makhanya to make a block.

Aberdeen striker Kevin Nisbet reflects on a golden chance to fire Aberdeen ahead at Hampden

On such moments are cup semi-finals won and lost. Just seven minutes later, at the other end of the pitch, Ryan Naderi prodded home from close range to send Rangers through to the final.

Nisbet will surely be haunted by his miss. He has scored 13 goals this season. For all Aberdeen’s struggles, some have even touted him for a Scotland recall.

But he is not up to scratch at the top level. In some respects, he finds himself in the same boat as Lawrence Shankland.

Any time Shankland has been given an opportunity with Scotland, he hasn’t really taken it. Particularly in the World Cup in the summer.

Nisbet is a decent enough striker at Scottish Professional Football League level. But in the big moments in big games, he’s not good enough.

It was a chance he had to take. In the end, Aberdeen were left to rue what might have been as Rangers, who were poor for much of the game, edged through to the final.

All in all, this is a defeat which just piles more pressure on Stephen Robinson. His team did not play poorly but they did not win.

Nisbet took too long with the ball and allowed Olwethu Makhanya the chance to block his shot

There is no sense in trotting out excuses about being competitive and unlucky. Aberdeen were not unlucky.

They had a glorious chance to go in front late in the game and their captain wasted it. That is not misfortune. It is profligacy.

Robinson and his players now face a huge game against Hibs at Pittodrie next Saturday.

With the international break just around the corner, a time when clubs invariably change manager once the rot has set in, it could well be last-chance saloon for Robinson.

#1446. RANGERS 1 ABERDEEN 0: Ryan Naderi the Hampden hero as Light Blues squeeze past dogged Dons to reach final

Published: 16:41 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 18:41 EDT, 31 October 2026

Ryan Naderi is developing the happy knack of turning up in the right place at the right time for Rangers. And, by Jove, how they needed him to deliver something to break the deadlock in this one and book a spot in the Premier Sports Cup final back at Hampden next month.

Derek McInnes’ side weren’t as bad at the national stadium as they were midweek in scraping a 2-2 draw away to Hearts, but they certainly weren’t all that good. Aberdeen turned up to frustrate them last night and succeeded for the large part, making a number of notable chances themselves.

There’s an obligation to drop in some kind of pun about Hallowe’en in this account of what went down between these two sides, so let's discuss how Dons’ captain Kevin Nisbet must have spent last night suffering nightmares following his own personal horror show just 14 minutes from time.

With the game back hanging in the balance in the wake of a strong period of Rangers pressure, Stephen Robinson’s side broke forward in numbers and, even after Nisbet had failed to find substitute Mitchy Ntelo with a pass, the ball was picked up by Stuart Armstrong and fed back into the skipper’s path on the right-hand side of the box.

He had to smash it first-time. Hard and low across the keeper. Inexplicably, for a guy who does know how to find the net and has done it plenty of times throughout his career, he took a touch and allowed Olwethu Makhanya the opportunity to get across and put in a crucial block.

In that instant, you wondered if the Dons’ big chance had come and gone. Naderi provided the answer just seven minutes later.

Rangers striker Ryan Naderi celebrates his late semi-final winner at Hampden Park

Rangers boss Derek McInnes enjoys the moment at full-time as his side are through to the final

The Czech internationalist endured a grim start to the season as a lone frontman, but has come into his own since being deployed beside Kevin Kelsy and shown that precious ability to score goals that really change things, really matter.

He scored the winner at Celtic Park in September, of course, as well as a home winner against Motherwell. Last time out against St Johnstone, his second-half effort to notch the second goal of what ended up a 4-0 romp was expertly timed as his team-mates had failed to wake up at the start of the second 45 and looked like they might fall flat on their faces.

Once again, he rode to the rescue here, reading the play, making a run, getting into space and finishing from close-in for his eighth of the campaign. The kind of bread-and-butter goal you want your strikers to score.

A cross in from the left from Rangers’ best player Badredine Bouanani, turning up on the wrong wing for some reason, was cleared by Connor Ronan to substitute Dan Neil 25 yards out.

His short pass to James Penrice resulted in a low shot into the area and Naderi timed his run perfectly to ghost in and convert from close range.

It was a sickening blow to under-pressure Robinson and his players. They had dug in really well, pulled off the game plan nicely and kept themselves in it throughout. Their display belied the league form that has put the manager’s job on the line ahead of next Saturday’s teatime visit of Hibernian.

It all counts for nothing in the end, though. As they reflect on events in Mount Florida, they will know that they came up against a Rangers side that most definitely dominated possession — and probably deserved the win in the end — but was vulnerable at times and failed to function as McInnes would have wanted.

The Ibrox boss pulled something of a surprise in his starting line-up by dropping vice-captain Neil and putting left-back Penrice in beside skipper-for-the-night Nico Raskin. It didn’t really work, though.

Listen, those guys weren’t exactly the core of the problem. A lot of the time, the ball wasn’t even being played through midfield, but the switch-up just didn’t feel like it worked. The balance wasn’t right.

For most of the first half, in particular, not very much was right about Rangers. They had plenty of the ball but Aberdeen set up in a 5-3-2 formation and kept them quiet while managing to create good chances of their own on the counter-attack.

Rangers were too slow. Not creative enough. Everything truly positive and dangerous they did went through Badredine Bouanani on the right, but there has to be infinitely more variation in their play rather than just getting it to the on-loan Algerian and hoping those quick feet of his can work some magic.

It was heartbreak for Aberdeen's Nicky Devlin as they fell just short in the semi-final

When he was brought in from German side VfB Stuttgart, the chat was that the management team saw him as an ideal weapon to break down teams playing a low block. He has the ability to beat a man, play in tight spots, have a shot.

However, there’s got to be more about Rangers than that. In this game, as with the 2-2 midweek draw with Hearts at Tynecastle, there just wasn’t enough in the way of fluent, purposeful play. They’ve looked nothing like the side that blew St Johnstone away last weekend with some exhilarating football and that must be a worry for McInnes.

By this stage of the season, they should be starting to find their stride, develop more in the way of consistency.

It took Rangers 44 minutes, for example, to fashion a shot on target. Naturally, it came from Bouanani, a low effort from a central position being saved low to his right by Aberdeen goalkeeper Marius Muller.

Up until that point, the better of the opportunities had fallen to the Dons. Midway through the opening period, Raskin played a pass wide to Dujon Sterling that carried just too much jeopardy.

Nesta Guinness-Walker nipped in to steal possession and then took the ball for a run all the way into the final third before releasing a decent low effort which Ibrox No1 Ivor Pandur had to save to his left.

With ten minutes of the half to play, Nisbet then sent a header wide from a great position after moving onto a cross from Brad Lyons.

At that stage, all Rangers had to shout about was an appeal for a penalty turned down on the 16-minute mark when Dons striker Ayoub Mouloua clearly handled the ball in his own area under pressure from Manny Fernandez.

Referee Ryan Lee didn’t give the award with VAR John Beaton backing up that call. It was controversial and no mistake.

Towards the end of the first half, however, it looked like things might be starting to click for McInnes’ men. Naderi put a header just over from a Raskin cross after getting in behind Jack Milne and Min-su Kim, massively disappointing again and eventually replaced by Djeidi Gassama, sliced an effort wide directly in front of goal.

Yet, it remained stodgy for Rangers after the restart. In the wake of Naderi just failing to get on the end of a low shot from Bouanani at the back post, a deflected Nisbet shot at the other end had to be saved low and smartly by Pandur.

Kelsy missed a sitter just after the hour when putting a header miles wide from a brilliant Bouanani cross and Muller had to block a shot from the Algerian wide man with his right boot as Rangers enjoyed their most dangerous and insistent period of the match.

It didn’t last, but Nisbet dallied when it mattered while Naderi just let his instinct take control for a sharp little conversion from that Penrice effort.

McInnes now has his first shot at silverware as Rangers manager pending and that’s what he wanted going into this game.

However, he needs to find a way to get this team slicker, tighter, more joined-up. More relentless. More focused. More composed in key areas.

As if a reminder of that was needed, it came in time added-on when Armstrong picked up the ball at the edge of their box and bent a fine effort just wide of Pandur’s left-hand post.

So near and yet so far. The story of Aberdeen’s night, really. A night where a big chance definitely existed, but just couldn’t be taken.
