#1426. Guimaraes looks a £75m bargain as ‘super sub’ makes difference

Arsenal have played six Premier League games this season and Bruno Guimarães has been a match-winning force in two of them. At this rate, he might justify his enormous £75m transfer fee by Christmas.

The Brazilian was not signed to be Arsenal’s super sub but that is the role he appears to be playing in these early days in north London. Against Leeds United here, as it was against Sunderland last month, he came off the bench when the champions were struggling. And as it was at Sunderland, he produced a thumping finish to put Arsenal on their way to three points.

Liquid football from Arsenal 😮‍💨 Bruno Guimarães finishes off a well-worked team move! 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/fbLJiaZbX5

This is the value of signing a 28-year-old with significant Premier League experience. As Arsenal laboured against an impressively organised and courageous Leeds side, Mikel Arteta knew that Guimarães was capable of coming into the game and adjusting to its demands. There has been no adaptation period required for Guimarães, who is fast becoming one of the most popular players in north London.

The finish, which put Arsenal 2-1 ahead at the Emirates Stadium, marked an emphatic conclusion to a fabulous passing sequence. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard and Declan Rice all combined at speed before Guimarães charged on to Rice’s flick. “It was a beauty,” said Arteta of the goal. The move had actually begun at the feet of Guimarães a few moments earlier, when he nutmegged an opponent in style.

The winning goal came just eight minutes after Riccardo Calafiori, Arsenal’s thrilling left-back/centre-forward hybrid, had pulled them level in the game. James Justin had struck for Leeds shortly after half-time, creating a horrible anxiety among the home fans here, and for much of the afternoon Daniel Farke’s side were the better team.

Leeds finally have their opener! 🤩 James Justin arrives at the back post to fire them ahead. 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/ITjUMSlrG1

Leeds, though, could not compete with Arsenal for depth. The arrival of Guimarães as a 63rd-minute substitute represented a flexing of Arteta’s managerial muscle, in his first match since signing a new long-term contract, and the Brazilian offered a moment of attacking quality that his opponents were unable to replicate.

It was actually the first competitive home game that Guimarães had played for Arsenal since his transfer from Newcastle United, as a result of a few niggles and the club’s unusual run of four consecutive away matches before the international break. The most recent of those was the 3-0 thrashing by Brighton, which was one of their worst defeats of the last few seasons.

This gritty victory represented a necessary response to that defeat, even if the performance was far from dominant. “We had a point to prove,” said Arteta. “Something was touched in our identity against Brighton.”

Guimarães, too, clearly felt that some wrongs needed to be made right. For all his brilliance in this game and against Sunderland, he had produced a horrible showing at the Amex Stadium a few weeks ago. “He was not at that level against Brighton,” said Arteta. “This is the level for Arsenal. Every week, every game, every minute, every action you have to be at that level. At Brighton, he wasn’t. Today, he was much better.”

Leeds had not lost in their opening five Premier League matches of this season and it was easy to see why. They were willing to press Arsenal high up the pitch, taking risks and engaging in physical duels, and the strategy proved hugely effective for an hour.

If they had been more precise in the final third, they could have been a few goals ahead by the time Justin converted Gabriel Gudmundsson’s left-wing cross after 55 minutes. Anton Stach, who was accidentally blocked by team-mate Jayden Bogle, and Gudmundsson both went close in the first half.

Right, where were we? Three weeks on from the fifth round of Premier League fixtures in which the champions Arsenal were beaten 3-0 by Brighton and todays’ visitors, Leeds United, who remain unbeaten, drew in a tepid goalless fixture with Crystal Palace, we finally get to the sixth. As worrying as the result was at the Amex, Arsenal still created a shedload of chances and last season they were the one club that battered Leeds in both games – first early in the season when they were playing four at the back and before Dominic Calvert-Lewin, a late signing, was fully fit, and then later after they had successfully switched to a “base formation” of three centre-backs and the tactical flexibility that allowed.

It was a 5-0 tanking in August and 4-0 in January, so to say Leeds travel to a ground at which they have never won more in hope than expectation would be as true as much as it is hackneyed. Adding to a sense of foreboding and thanks to Opta’s excellent Jonny Cooper, we also have to take into account the fact that Leeds, floodlight kings, have not won a Premier League match kicking off before 3pm since August 2022 and have not won a match in London since beating Brentford in May that year to save themselves from relegation. However, they do boast the division’s best defensive record – three goals conceded – and the No1 ranked goalkeeper in James Trafford who has a save percentage of 87. For all the sense of doom, though, Leeds have become a very good side and their spine – Trafford–Muharemovic–Ampadu–Calvert-Lewin marries steel and class.

Arsenall need no fanfare. Until the set-back in dear old Sussex by the sea, they had looked formidable most of the time and will have been champing at the bit to get back out there and prove it was an aberration. Mikel Arteta mentioned he has doubts about Declan Rice, Kai Havertz and Ezri Konsa but Ben White, Max Dowman and Chrsthian Mosquera are all available. For Leeds Joe Rodon is still out and Dan James was injured on international duty but Harry Wilson and Jean-Matteo Bahoya returned to training after knocks this week and Daniel Farke was relatively optimistic about their prospects.

#1425. Blues Earn Solid Point Against United

Everton played out a goalless draw with Manchester United at Goodison Park on Saturday evening.

The Blues threatened throughout, with Yuka Momiki and Ornella Vignola both seeing strikes palmed away. At the other end, heroics from Courtney Brosnan kept the Toffees in it as they earned a solid point against the Red Devils on Halloween.

Brosnan and Clare Wheeler were presented with commemorative framed shirts prior to kick-off to mark the duo surpassing a century of appearances in royal blue.

Brosnan donned the captain’s armband in between the sticks, with a backline of Hikaru Kitagawa, Rion Ishikawa, Naomi Layzell and Hannah Blundell in front of her.

Ruby Mace and Wheeler sat deep in midfield, allowing Rosa van Gool – who scored in midweek against Sheffield United – to roam further forward.

Maz Pacheco started on the unfamiliar left-wing, with Momiki lining the opposite flank. Vignola shifted over to a central position to lead the line.

It was the hosts who threatened first as Momiki drifted inside and let fly from the edge of the box. Her effort had sufficient power, but whistled wide of the near-post.

The resilient Blues continued to show real spirit and battled hard throughout the opening 45, with neither side able to make the breakthrough.

Scott Phelan’s side emerged from the tunnel with an urgency about them – Vignola firing an effort in to the chest of Le Tissier from the edge of the box immediately after play resumed.

United reacted, with Brosnan called in to action to deny Dominique Janssen on 75 minutes. The Netherlands-international latched on to former-Blue Jess Park’s threaded through ball. With her first-touch, Janssen looked to catch the keeper off-guard, but Ireland’s number one was well-prepared.

Noemie Mouchon, who also netted against the Blades on Wednesday, replaced Momiki with nine minutes remaining as Phelan looked to his bench for a late goal.

After three minutes of injury time, the referee concluded the goalless affair to mark a solid point for the Toffees on home soil.

The Blues travel to face Chelsea in the capital next up, making the journey on Saturday 7 November (12pm KO).

#1424. Stephen Robinson proud of his battling Dons but injury crisis deepens

Published: 17:30 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 14:43 EDT, 2 November 2026

Aberdeen boss Stephen Robinson has revealed his injury crisis has become even more catastrophic ahead of the weekend league visit of Hibernian that has the potential to make or break his reign.

The Dons manager saw his side put in a fine, disciplined display in going down 1-0 to Rangers in the Premier Sports Cup final, but lost Emmanuel Gyamfi within 15 minutes after he collided with Kim Min-su and also has Brad Lyons battling a knock.

Robinson admitted afterwards that there is no chance of longer-term absentees Chris Cadden, Mats Knoester and Lewis Mayo being available, with Dan Happe the only player likely to return for the Saturday night showdown with Premiership bottom dogs Hibs after being suspended last night.

‘Gyamfi will be out for a long period of time,’ reported Robinson. ‘It looked like it was maybe the other thigh that he’s had a problem with. It’s a heartbreaker for the boy.

‘Brad Lyons took a really bad knock. I’m not sure how serious that is. Hopefully, he’s got away with it.

‘Chris Cadden will be out for six weeks. Mats Knoester is four to six weeks.

Emmanuel Gyamfi limped off early with an injury in Aberdeen's semi-final defeat

‘The only plus point is Dan Happe. It’s very difficult because half the squad are not available. Any team that does well, there’s consistency and patience.

‘Over time, the last person that had prolonged success in Aberdeen was Derek (McInnes). He was given a lot of time and a lot of support, but we’ve not been able to put a consistent team, never mind a consistent shape, on the pitch.

‘It’s four changes every week at the moment.’

Robinson, however, stated his pride in the way his players performed and backed centre-back Jack Milne while taking a pop at the criticism he has come in for of late.

‘They rose against adversity this time. They put in a real performance,’ he said.

‘Rangers scored during our best spell in the game, which is unfortunate, but it’s been a tough week for us with injuries, really tough.

‘They showed great character and courage.

‘Jack’s a young man. Surprisingly, he’s from Aberdeen and he still gets an incredible amount of stick.

‘He’s had one full season and he’s a lovely boy that wants to learn. He’s just learning the game. I thought he showed real character.’

Dons boss Stephen Robinson on the touchline in the 1-0 defeat to Rangers

Robinson also refused to criticise captain Kevin Nisbet after seeing him pass up a couple of golden chances.

‘If you want chances to fall to anyone, it’s Kevin and he had the opportunity to play Mitchy Ntelo in with one of them when clean through,’ he reflected.

‘We had grown into the game. We were organised defensively despite not knowing what our team would be until Saturday morning.

‘I’m proud of the players because they gave me absolutely everything.

‘You’d need to ask the fans if they saw positive performances. I can only answer for myself. I saw a group of boys give everything in adversity.

‘Everyone expected us to roll over and get battered but that wasn’t the case. They’ve shown they have the character to play for Aberdeen in big games, no doubt.’

#1422. Stats not good enough! Derek McInnes issues warning to his Rangers players over their profligacy in front of goal

Published: 18:38 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 18:47 EDT, 31 October 2026

Rangers manager Derek McInnes last night warned his side they have to ramp up the killer instinct in front of goal after branding their attacking stats in the one-goal Premier Sports Cup semi-final win over Aberdeen ‘embarrassing’.

The Ibrox outfit had 25 shots on goal with only five on target at the end of a Hampden tussle settled by a close-range finish from striker Ryan Naderi with just seven minutes left to play.

McInnes feels his players are making too many bad decisions in the final third of the field and has told wide men such as Badredine Bouanani and Kim Min-su, who has yet to record an assist or goal this term, that they need to start pitching in with better figures.

He accepts there is a lack of top-level experience among a group of attackers notable for their youth, but knows there must be improvements in the quest for silverware.

‘We came with the intention of making sure we got the club into a cup final by hook or by crook, and we’ve done the job, so I am really pleased and delighted with the players, in the main, for their perseverance, for keeping going,’ said McInnes.

‘Semi-finals aren’t easy to get through, particularly when you play the way we did in the first half.

Derek McInnes labelled his team's attacking statistics 'embarrassing' after their Hampden win

‘We were ponderous when we needed to be quicker. When we needed to be calm in the final bit, we snatched and made poor decisions.

‘In terms of the stats, it is actually embarrassing we have had 25 shots and only five on target. It says a lot about the inexperience at the top end of the pitch.

‘That’s for another day. Today was just all about getting through. It’s so important for the club and the supporters to look forward to a cup final.

‘We need to keep arriving in cup finals and get the job done to win trophies.

‘I always feel there’s goals in us,’ said the Ibrox boss. ‘Equally, I was still a bit concerned on counter-attacks. Aberdeen had a couple of moments that gave them oxygen and belief that maybe they could get in the final, but the better team won.

‘Naderi, like all good strikers, is going that way when the defenders are on their heels and he gets these scruffy goals that you want your striker to score.

‘He’s always in the middle of the goal when the ball gets into good areas, but a lot of the time we don’t feed him enough. We make too many bad decisions.

Kevin Kelsy watches a header fly wide on a rare off night for the Venezuelan front man

‘Some of the stats that we’re seeing more or less every week at the minute, it’s like making poor decisions, snatching at things, rushing crosses, not making the right pass, not putting the extra pass in. I’m going to keep saying that we’re a young team up there and it’s hard sometimes.

‘You need an old man up there, an old head, nous, who knows just how to bring a bit of savvy and calmness to it.

‘Thankfully, we had that with the goal today, but there were so many other times where we could, if we just take more care, be less rushed and stay calm in those moments, create better opportunities rather than just 25 shots and 20 of them flying over the bar.

‘Those shots on target become double, triple more of what we get, and it’s those wee bits that we need to sharpen up if we’re going to be successful this season.’

Asked if he felt there would be more goals in man-of-the-match Bouanani, McInnes replied: ‘There had better! The wide players need to start scoring goals.

‘Min-su needs to get that demand on himself, Gassama. Bouanani’s got so much quality.

‘The thing with Bouanani is, as soon as he steps on the pitch on that left side, 25 yards out, you think it’s in the net because he does it time and time again in training. If he keeps chapping at the door, I’m sure the goals will come.

‘I’d like to have enjoyed this a wee bit more. Enjoyment comes now, a wee bit of satisfaction when I see the lads in the dressing room celebrating together, but the job now is to go and win the thing.

Badredine Bouanani goes close with a curling effort but McInnes wants to see more from him

‘We’ll get six weeks now between now and then where we need to get better at things I just spoke about.

‘We’re on a really strong run just now in terms of wins and being unbeaten over a period of time, but we know we’re not perfect. It’s important that we keep searching for those improvements.’

Naderi lapped up his eighth goal of the season and insisted the right team won.

‘It was wonderful. I am so happy. It was a wonderful second half and we deserved it. It was just a question of time until we scored,’ said Naderi.

‘We had so many corners back-to-back, so much pressure, so many shots on target.’

Captain-for-the-night Nico Raskin, meanwhile, agreed with McInnes’ view that the team has to become more ruthless in front of goal.

‘Their goalkeeper made loads of saves and we could maybe have been a bit more calm in front of goal, but I am just so happy for Ryan and the team we got the goal,’ he said.

‘It is about trying to be more clinical now and enjoying the game more as it is always tense at 0-0 or 1-0. We want to come back to Hampden and win the cup now.’

#1420. Hearts keeper Reus hopes to use inside knowledge of his old boss Reedijk to prolong Hibs manager's false start as they clash in derby

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 18:43 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 18:49 EDT, 31 October 2026

When Hibs appointed Marink Reedijk just over a month ago, there weren’t many people within Scottish football who could claim to know much about the Dutchman.

Especially among the Hibs support, the response was one largely of bemusement as to why the club had taken a gamble on a 34-year-old rookie whose only previous experience was in the Belgian second tier.

At Beveren, Reedijk carved a reputation for himself as a coach who played high-octane attacking football as his side finished last season unbeaten as champions, duly winning promotion to the top flight.

It was an achievement and a style of play which was sufficiently impressive enough to alert the data boffins at Jamestown Analytics.

Back in the summer, Reedijk’s name had actually been on Hearts’ radar before they eventually chose to appoint Wouter Vrancken instead.

There was never any formal approach, but Hearts and Jamestown were aware of his name and his reputation as a young coach of considerable promise.

Whether or not Reedijk’s style of play could translate to the SPFL Premiership was a topic of much intrigue when he arrived to replace the sacked David Gray.

Reus denies Martin Boyle back in September's Edinburgh derby meeting

It is fair to say he has made something of an inauspicious start. In beginning his reign with defeats to Dundee United, Falkirk and Celtic, he became the first Hibs boss since Pat Fenlon to lose his opening three games.

He finally arrested that sequence courtesy of a 1-1 draw against St Mirren in midweek, but Hibs remain mired in relegation trouble.

Now comes the small matter of an Edinburgh derby against Hearts, with the rivals set to clash at Hampden this afternoon in the semi-finals of the Premier Sports Cup.

Reedijk desperately needs a victory to finally ignite his reign, with many Hibs fans already questioning whether this is a gamble that may backfire.

In the 2-1 defeat to Celtic last weekend, Hibs finished the match with Grant Hanley playing up front for the final ten minutes. It was an act of desperation and one which would see Reedijk take a lot of criticism.

Yet, although Reedijk is struggling to convince so far, there’s a man behind enemy lines who will happily sing his praises.

Reedijk picked up his first point as Hibs boss in the midweek draw at St Mirren

Hearts goalkeeper Beau Reus played under Reedijk for two years at Beveren. Reus insists he would be happy to go out on a limb and vouch that his old boss is a top-class operator.

As is always the way in football, friends can be found in unlikely places. Prior to a Hampden derby showdown, Reus opened up on his relationship with his fellow Dutchman during their time in Belgium.

‘We were together in Belgium the last two years,’ said the Hearts keeper, who has been excellent since making the switch to Tynecastle. ‘For me, he’s a good manager. His gameplan is really clear.

‘Hopefully that helps us a bit to crack the code. I will have a meeting with our coach to tell him how he will play, probably!

‘But Marink is very adaptable. He’s a young coach. I know he will have some tricks up his sleeve.

‘We are both Dutch and, as always, if you are a guy from an outside country that plays in Belgium, it’s normal you have a certain connection. He helped me grow a lot.

‘He’s really straight, so if he has a plan, he will go to implement his plan as well as he can. Off the pitch he’s a really, really nice guy, really warm. But, yeah, as soon as you’re on the pitch with him, you know exactly what you have to do for him. He makes very clear.

‘We are very kind to each other, but I think on Sunday we will forget about it for 90 minutes. After that, we can shake hands again.

‘I knew there were rumours that he was coming to Hibs, so the day I left for the last international break, I flew back to Amsterdam and his plane was just landing.

‘I said to my girlfriend it’s unbelievable that I come across him again in this way. But in football it is always like this, you will see each other many times.’

Reus is impressing for Hearts, with his shootout heroics securing a Conference League spot

Hearts come into the semi-final on the back of a 2-2 draw against Rangers at Tynecastle on Wednesday night, a match in which they were the better side for large spells.

Vrancken’s men are battling through an injury crisis which currently sees eight first-team regulars out of action.

‘It is devastating when you see so many injuries,’ noted Reus. ‘But we will play with the players we have and give 100 per cent for sure.’

It promises to be a thriller in Mount Florida as Reedijk’s Hibs go up against Vrancken’s Hearts. Two coaches renowned for front-foot attacking football, it’ll be anything but dull.

Reus insists it would be a major sign of the continued progress being made at Hearts if they can reach the final.

‘I don’t know the numbers off the top of my head, but the last time the club won this competition was quite some time ago,’ he said. ‘So it’s massive.

‘And of course, it’s always great to play for cups, playing in tournaments, because you don’t win that many trophies in your career, so every chance is one.

‘The fact it is a derby is great. We have already played Hibs before this season and beaten them at Easter Road.

‘You see how much tension and how much build-up there was to the game. Also in the stadium, how much they hated us! So, if you win, it’s extra nice.

‘It is another massive game and we really want to bounce back from the disappointment of losing the late goal against Rangers in midweek.’

#1419. Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs

Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.

By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.

Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.

This time around they could not hold on to a lead against a Tottenham Hotspur side also navigating a numerical disadvantage following Rodrigo Bentancur’s sending off.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc

The sum total of it all is that United have now made their worst start to a season for 40 years, which is saying something given the traumas of the post-Ferguson era, and perhaps more disconcertingly, look to all intents and purposes like a team going backwards.

The bounce they enjoyed under Michael Carrick last season en route to Champions League qualification is over and, after just six points from as many games, it is hard to shake the feeling that it is going to be anything but a serious battle to finish in the top four or five.

The supporters did not hide their disgruntlement. There were boos around the half hour mark after an insipid opening when Spurs did everything but score and a slow, sluggish, dishevelled United almost looked impervious to their troubles.

Carrick had called for his players to show some “fire” coming into this match, but instead watched them ambling around like it was all a terrible inconvenience. The ease with which Spurs ran around them was alarming. There were more jeers at the interval and again at full time.

Carrick admitted that “hurt” although not as much you suspect as the sight of players feigning interest and then throwing away three points when they had finally summoned some fight to lead courtesy of Bryan Mbeumo’s goal.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe

It was a lovely finish after good work by the largely anonymous Matheus Cunha, and when Bentancur was sent off five minutes later after butting Luke Shaw, it should have been the cue to see out the game. To fail to do so against a side as toothless as Tottenham made it all the worse. Leading late on against Everton last month, they also failed to get over the line. It cannot keep happening.

Equally, United cannot play like they did in the first half here when they face Atlético Madrid in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night or at Elland Road against bitter rivals Leeds five days later and expect to get anything from either game. They are not the sort of matches Carrick would want with his team in this shape, but they need to find some inspiration from somewhere.

Carlos Baleba coming on around the hour mark and making a difference on his debut will at least offer Carrick some grounds for encouragement. The £65m midfield signing from Brighton offers some energy and urgency and looks a more natural bedfellow for Kobbie Mainoo than Youri Tielemans, who was woeful against Spurs and should have come off earlier.

In truth, Tielemans was not alone. Throughout the team there was a disconnect and unease and Carrick admitted it became contagious.

“We just couldn’t find a way to get ourselves into the game, whether that was with the ball or without the ball,” the United manager said. “We were a little bit slow with the decision-making, didn’t quite see the passing areas, the space. You don’t want it to happen, but sometimes it can and it probably spread through the team a little bit too much.”

It does not help that Bruno Fernandes is being hampered by an injury he has been carrying for weeks or that Carrick has no natural centre-forward to call upon with Benjamin Sesko again sidelined by the recurrence of a worrying shin problem. Amad Diallo did return here after a lengthy lay-off of his own, but did not look match fit.

In defence, Lisandro Martínez did enough to put off Dominic Solanke, who fired over from Sávio’s cross in the second half, but this was otherwise another poor showing from the Argentine centre-back, one of several positions where United need upgrades.

United needed shaking badly, but when Carrick turned to his bench he called upon Joshua Zirkzee, a fitful forward the club wanted to sell this summer, and right-back Diogo Dalot in addition to Baleba.

Marcus Rashford cannot have been fit given he was only introduced in the 95th minute and perhaps the same was true of the unused Mason Mount. As for £50m summer signing Andrey Santos, this was another league game when the Brazilian midfielder did not get a look in.

United fans had taunted Spurs when a goal and a man up. “You’re going down with the City,” they crowed, a nod to the possibility of City being expelled or relegated from the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching more than 100 financial rules.

United fans had also revived their Stretford End “ticker” after reaching the conclusion that none of City’s titles under Abu Dhabi ownership had been won fairly so, in their eyes, it is now 50 years since their rivals last won anything legitimately. City, of course, continue to maintain their innocence and have lodged an appeal.

But United fans were unable to crow for too long once Solanke levelled.

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw

It had been similar early in the game when the home fans had trained their sights on City. “You cheating b--------, you know what you are”, they sang lustily.

But as the match wore on, those chants began to quieten as the crowd, taking their lead from the team, fell decidedly flat.

Carrick is going to have to find a spark from somewhere and quickly.

Speaking to BBC Match of the Day, Carrick said: “It was a mixed game. We found it tough to start with. For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time.

“But the lads grew into the game, in the second half I thought we were better in everything. To get the game as we wanted it, in such a good position - we should see it through. We have to manage those situations. That’s two late goals which have hurt us, and things look very different. That’s the reality.”

When asked about the boos at half-time and full-time, he replied: “It’s not nice, it hurts a lot because I care about this club. But I understand the disappointment, the reality is what it is, we need to get back to winning games.”

3 - Manchester United have failed to win any of their last three Premier League games against sides that have received a red card (D1 L2). Disadvantage? https://t.co/DuSpvymZfu

We have to react in all ways we can. It is a bad way, it is not the right way. I kiss Bentancur in the dressing room. Football is character.

“We win the game if we play as a team. We didn’t win this game playing as a team. Every game like today, we will win many games.”

“We have to believe in ourselves and this football way. If we believe, improve and play as a team, we will score many goals and win many games. If we don’t play as a team, it is impossible.”

Still, it’s Tottenham forcing the issue as Kudus dashes past Shaw with his blistering pace. Cunha tracks back but can’t stop the winger from digging out a cross. Yoro’s skewed clearance is headed back to Lammens by Tielemans. Man Utd need to careful, they cannot continue playing like this.

We are under way at Old Trafford. Can either of these sides pick up a victory to relieve the pressure on their head coach?

“You cheating b******s, you know what you are,” is heard from the stands at Old Trafford. It’s pretty safe to say they are referring to Manchester City’s guilty verdict which was announced during the international break.

Man Utd, skippered by Fernandes, receive a feverish reception as they’re welcomed onto the pitch by the Old Trafford faithful. Tottenham are led out by Solanke, who captains the visitors today.

With kick-off fast approaching, here’s a recap of both line-ups.

Man Utd: Lammens, Yoro, Maguire, Martinez, Shaw, Tielemans, Mainoo, Diallo, Fernandes, Mbeumo, Cunha.

Subs: Darlow, Dalot, Mount, Rashford, Zirkzee, Santos, Baleba, Heaven, Lacey.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League game between Manchester United and Tottenham at Old Trafford.

If Manchester City had not entered a legal battle with the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching 114 charges relating to financial regulations by an independent panel, then surely there would be more pressure on the two head coaches in the dugout this evening?

Man Utd and Tottenham have undoubtedly both endured extremely disappointing starts to their respective top-flight campaigns. The hosts sit just inside the bottom half of the table after picking up just five points from their opening five matches. It’s going even worse for Tottenham, who languish in 20th with zero wins and just two points.

The perilous landscape leaves only one reasonable conclusion: this has all the ingredients for an early season six-pointer.

The strain is perhaps less intense on Michael Carrick, with the Englishman having built up a bundle of goodwill after cleaning up the mess left by Ruben Amorim last season as Man Utd eventually finished third, qualifying for the Champions League. Fans were left slightly underwhelmed by the club’s transfer window, with the players at Carrick’s disposal having not forged any momentum so far in this campaign.

The spotlight is definitely shining more intensely upon Roberto De Zerbi after big-spending Tottenham splashed over £300m in the summer on the likes of Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Jan Paul van Hecke and Savio. However, the Italian boss is yet to strike the correct rhythm with his newly-formed squad. An encouraging performance backed up by a positive result here at Old Trafford could be the perfect antidote to ease the worries of fans fearing that Tottenham could be embroiled in another relegation battle.

All eyes are on this one. Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1418. MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The heart possesses a dynamic capacity to oxidize a variety of fuels, including glucose and lactate, to meet its energetic demands under diverse dietary, exertion and injury stressors1. Oxidation of carbohydrate substrates is thought to converge on the cytosolic generation of pyruvate, which is transported by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) for entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle2. Here we find that glucose-derived carbon is oxidized in mouse myocardium even when the MPC is genetically ablated. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, we demonstrate that lactate monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by Slc16a1) is required for the oxidation of glucose carbon by MPC-deficient myocardium. We further observe that MCT1, traditionally localized to the plasma membrane, also resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mouse and human cardiomyocytes. Together with matrix-localized LDHB, MCT1 enables mitochondrial lactate conversion to pyruvate and NADH, directly fueling the electron transport chain. Loss of MCT1 impairs lactate oxidation, disrupts metabolic flexibility and accelerates the development of heart failure with increased mortality after hyperactivation of the neurohormonal axis or ischemia–reperfusion injury. Thus, the existence of a parallel lactate-based pathway for carbohydrate oxidation can sustain cardiac energetics and maintain myocardial structure and function under diverse stress conditions.

The oxidation of carbon fuels within the mitochondria is responsible for more than 95% of human ATP production1,3. Dietary carbohydrates supply energy beginning with glycolysis, producing pyruvate that is either reduced to lactate in the cytosol by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), which also regenerates NAD+, or is imported into the mitochondria for oxidation by the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle4. Circulating lactate turnover exceeds that of glucose in mammalian physiology5,6, establishing lactate production as the dominant mode of cytosolic NAD+ regeneration. Lactate has the same oxidation state as glucose, is a major circulating oxidative fuel source in both fasted and fed mammalian physiology, and is consumed primarily by the heart, skeletal muscle and kidney7,8,9.

Conventional models posit that lactate oxidation starts with the generation of cytosolic pyruvate by LDH, which is subsequently imported into the mitochondria by the obligate heterodimeric mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC, encoded by Mpc1 and Mpc2)2,10. This arrangement leads to competition between LDH and glycolytic enzymes for NAD+, restricting flux through these pathways when metabolic demand is high (Fig. 1a). However, the heart can oxidize both lactate and glucose simultaneously in response to energetic demand11,12,13, suggesting that there might be distinct routes for pyruvate and lactate oxidation14,15.

a, Schematic representation of the competition for cytosolic NAD+ between glycolysis and lactate oxidation, illustrating that redox-balanced metabolism produces lactate. MCT, lactate monocarboxylate transporter. b, Simplified schematic of carbon labelling of heart TCA cycle metabolites resulting from infusion of [U-13C]glucose or [U-13C]lactate. If the second turn (light grey) incorporates an unlabelled acetyl-CoA, M+1 labelling becomes dominant as is observed in vivo. Glc, glucose; Lac, lactate; Mal, malate; Pyr, pyruvate; Suc, succinate. d, Myocardial 13C metabolite labelling following [U-13C]lactate infusion in awake 4 wpi Mpc1iCKO (n = 10) and Mpc1fl/fl (n = 8) mice. e, 13C labelling of metabolites from primary cultured ACMs incubated with [U-13C]glucose with or without 1.6 mM lactate in DMEM, n = 3 wells. f, LVEF at 14 wpi with tamoxifen of Mpc1fl/fl (n = 3), and 14 wpi (n = 4), 17 wpi (n = 6) and 19 wpi (n = 8) Mpc1iCKO mice. g, Heart weight normalized to body weight from Mpc1fl/fl (n = 3) and Mpc1iCKO mice at 18–19 wpi (n = 6). h, Myocardial 13C metabolite labelling following [U-13C]glucose infusion in 18 wpi Mpc1iCKO (n = 6) and Mpc1fl/fl (n = 3) mice with heart failure. i, Myocardial 13C metabolite labelling following [U-13C]lactate infusion in anaesthetized 18 wpi Mpc1iCKO (n = 5) and Mpc1fl/fl (n = 5) mice. j, Immunoblots of the indicated proteins from cytosolic (C) and mitochondrial (M) lysates from Mpc1iCKO and Mpc1fl/fl hearts at 18 wpi. Data are mean ± s.e.m. P values from multiple comparisons-corrected (Holm–Sídák method) unpaired two-tailed t-tests (c–e,g–i) or one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple comparison test (f). NS, not significant (P ≥ 0.05).

Here we reconcile the conflict between lactate, glucose and pyruvate oxidation by demonstrating that MCT1, which is canonically on the plasma membrane, is also present on the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) of cardiomyocytes. MCT1 is necessary for the uptake and oxidation of lactate, providing metabolic redundancy that sustains cardiac energetics. Genetic ablation of MCT1 abolishes mitochondrial lactate oxidation, disrupts adaptation to neurohormonal, hemodynamic or ischemic stress and accelerates the development of heart failure with enhanced mortality.

To test the prevailing model of lactate oxidation in heart, we utilized our previously described tamoxifen-inducible cardiac-specific Mpc1-knockout mice (Mpc1fl/fl; αMHCMerCreMer+/−, hereafter Mpc1iCKO) to quantify the extent to which the oxidation of glucose and lactate in the myocardium requires the MPC16. We implanted jugular vein catheters into 4 week post-tamoxifen injection (wpi) Mpc1iCKO mice and Mpc1fl/fl littermate controls with normal cardiac function and subsequently infused awake mice with [U-13C]glucose or [U-13C]lactate to reach stable serum enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Hearts and serum were then collected for isotopic labelling analysis of metabolites by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS) (Fig. 1b). Similar to prior reports, we observed a rapid appearance of [1,2,3-13C]lactate in serum upon [U-13C]glucose infusion and labelled glucose with [U-13C]lactate infusion, reflecting high rates of interconversion between these metabolites6 (Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). There was no difference in total serum isotopic enrichment and endogenous rates of glucose and lactate appearance between Mpc1fl/fl and Mpc1iCKO mice (Extended Data Fig. 1b–e). We anticipated that the contribution of glucose to TCA cycle metabolites and thus cardiac ATP production would decrease in Mpc1iCKO mice. Unexpectedly, we observed that the glucose carbon contribution to lactate, pyruvate and TCA cycle metabolites increased in Mpc1iCKO mice compared with controls, a finding also reported by others17,18 (Fig. 1c). 13C labelling in the M+1 and M+2 isotopomers of representative TCA metabolites succinate and malate from Mpc1iCKO hearts was increased, but no changes in M+3 isotopomer labelling were seen, indicating enhanced glucose contribution through acetyl-CoA entry to the TCA cycle19 (Extended Data Fig. 1f,g). The contribution of lactate carbon to TCA cycle metabolites trended lower in Mpc1iCKO hearts but was not significantly different for any individual metabolite (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 1h,i). Using a linear algebra-based approach6, our combined glucose and lactate infusion data showed that Mpc1iCKO hearts used the same total amount of carbohydrate-sourced fuel to supply the TCA cycle, but that it was paradoxically shifted towards glucose in MPC1-deficient hearts (Extended Data Fig. 1j). We performed additional infusions of other major cardiac fuels (palmitate, oleate and 3-hydroxybutyrate) to determine whether Mpc1iCKO mice displayed systemic alterations in cardiac fuel choice that may have confounded our glucose and lactate tracing results (Extended Data Fig. 1k–m). However, the contributions of these fuels to the cardiac TCA cycle were not statistically different from controls, suggesting that heart glucose metabolism is resilient to loss of the MPC in the short term.

Our data from young Mpc1iCKO mice suggests the presence of an MPC-independent mitochondrial import pathway for glucose and lactate carbons. To better understand the cardiomyocyte-intrinsic metabolism of glucose and lactate, we used primary cultured adult cardiomyocytes (ACMs). Control ACMs were competent to oxidize glucose as assessed by 13C incorporation into TCA cycle metabolites (Fig. 1e). However, when unlabelled lactate was added to standard lactate-free ACM culture medium (DMEM) containing [U-13C]glucose, labelling from glucose was attenuated, suggesting a strong preference for lactate over glucose oxidation (Fig. 1e). Lactate consumption was not affected by loss of MPC1 as ACMs from Mpc1iCKO and Mpc1fl/fl mice metabolized lactate into TCA metabolites equivalently (Extended Data Fig. 2a).

Mpc1iCKO mice develop heart failure16,17,20,21 and we investigated whether changes in glucose and lactate oxidation were now present. Mpc1iCKO mice at 16–20 wpi exhibited reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and hypertrophy (Fig. 1f,g). To successfully introduce stable isotopes into these mice with heart failure, we adopted our protocol to employ a tail vein catheter infusion administered under anaesthesia. Oxidation of glucose and lactate carbon was significantly reduced in failing Mpc1iCKO hearts, despite similar pyruvate and lactate labelling indicating that carbohydrate uptake was not altered (Fig. 1h,i and Extended Data Fig. 2b–f). Total cardiac glycogen was unchanged (Extended Data Fig. 2g). The observed reduction in the oxidation of infused lactate in failing Mpc1iCKO hearts support the hypothesis that there is an MPC1-independent path for lactate oxidation that supports cardiac function.

To identity a potential alternative mitochondrial transporter of lactate, we conducted immunoblot analysis of purified mitochondria from myocardium and observed expression of the lactate transporter MCT1 (encoded by Slc16a1) in the mitochondrial fraction of healthy and failing Mpc1iCKO hearts (Fig. 1j and Extended Data Fig. 2h,i). MCT1 has previously been reported in mitochondria from cardiac tissue22,23. Analysis of published single-nuclei RNA-sequencing data from human hearts showed that SLC16A1 transcripts are predominantly expressed in cardiomyocytes24 (Extended Data Fig. 2j). Notably, MCT1 expression was increased in the mitochondria of young healthy Mpc1iCKO hearts but not failing hearts (Extended Data Fig. 2i,k,l). The existence of mitochondrial lactate import and metabolism has been proposed for decades, but its physiological relevance and mechanistic basis remain actively contested within the field25,26.

To test whether MCT1 can provide an alternative mechanism for carbohydrate carbon entry and oxidation in mitochondria, we repeated our [U-13C]glucose tracing in young, healthy Mpc1iCKO mice cotreated with AZD3965 (AZD), a potent MCT1 inhibitor with selectivity over MCT227. AZD treatment in control mice had no effect on the oxidation of glucose carbon as measured by TCA cycle metabolite labelling (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3a–e). However, when AZD was administered to Mpc1iCKO mice, glucose labelling of TCA cycle substrates was ablated. Although MCT1 may have a role in the transport of lactate across both the plasma membrane and IMM, our tracing data support an essential mitochondrial role, as glucose carbon uptake is not dependent on MCT1 activity. Overall, our data suggest functional redundancy between MCT1 and the MPC for the uptake of three-carbon equivalents into the mitochondria.

a, Myocardial 13C labelling of glycolytic and TCA cycle metabolites from Mpc1fl/fl and Mpc1iCKO mice treated with either AZD or vehicle and infused with [U-13C]glucose (Mpc1fl/fl vehicle n = 4, Mpc1iCKO vehicle n = 3, Mpc1fl/fl AZD n = 8, Mpc1iCKO n = 5). b, Expression of Slc16a1 transcripts in heart and liver tissue from Mct1fl/fl (n = 8) and Mct1iCKO (n = 7) mice quantified by real-time quantitative PCR. c, Representative immunoblots of the indicated proteins from mitochondrial and cytoplasmic fractions of Mct1fl/fl, Mct1iCKO and Mpc1iCKO hearts. Experiment repeated on three independent sets of mice. d, M+3 lactate ion counts from freshly isolated primary adult cardiomyocytes from Mct1fl/fl and Mct1iCKO hearts incubated with [U-13C]lactate for indicated times. e, M+3 pyruvate ion counts from the same experiment as d. f, 13C labelling of pyruvate and TCA cycle metabolites from Mct1fl/fl or Mct1iCKO ACMs incubated with [U-13C]lactate after 5 min saponin treatment. n = 4. g, Myocardial 13C metabolite labelling following [U-13C]glucose infusions in awake Mct1fl/fl (n = 4) or Mct1iCKO (n = 6) mice. h, Myocardial 13C metabolite labelling following [U-13C]lactate infusions in awake Mct1fl/fl (n = 10) or Mct1iCKO (n = 11) mice. i, Schematic representation of ex vivo heart perfusions. Created in BioRender; Carrington, J. https://BioRender.com/ps8ckjv (2026). j, Heart rates of Mct1fl/fl (n = 6), or Mct1iCKO (n = 6) mice 1 min prior to termination of ex vivo perfusions with 13C-labelled lactate. bpm, beats per minute. k, 13C labelling of metabolites from [U-13C]lactate perfusions in Mct1fl/fl (n = 4) or Mct1iCKO (n = 4) hearts. l, 13C labelling of metabolites from [U-13C]glucose perfusions in Mct1fl/fl (n = 7) or Mct1iCKO (n = 6) hearts. Data are mean ± s.e.m. P values from two-way ANOVA (a,b) or multiple comparisons-corrected (Holm–Sídák method) unpaired two-tailed t-tests (f–h,k,l).

To further explore the role of MCT1 as a mitochondrial lactate transporter, we developed a tamoxifen-inducible, cardiac-specific Mct1 knockout mouse: Mct1fl/fl; αMHCMerCreMer+/− (hereafter Mct1iCKO). We validated knockout by PCR and MCT1 immunoblots from whole-heart and mitochondrial preparations (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Across genotypes, a larger fraction of MCT1 signal was associated with mitochondria than MCT2 or MCT4 (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3f–h). When comparing Mpc1iCKO, Mct1iCKO and control hearts from young mice, we observed an increase in cytosolic and total MCT1, MCT4 and LHDB protein expression in Mpc1iCKO hearts, suggesting a compensatory lactate metabolism axis (Extended Data Fig. 3f,h,i). No significant changes in the expression of these proteins or MPC1 and MCT2 were observed in Mct1iCKO hearts (Extended Data Fig. 3f–j).

We incubated ACMs from Mct1fl/fl (control) and Mct1iCKO mice with [U-13C]lactate to test whether cytosolic uptake of lactate is lost without MCT1. The rate of cytosolic uptake of lactate and production of labelled pyruvate was unaffected by loss of MCT1, suggesting that the observed oxidative phenotypes were unlikely to be the result of changes in cytosolic import (Fig. 2d,e). At steady state, lactate contributed robustly to citrate (M+2) labelling in control ACMs, but this was sharply reduced in Mct1iCKO ACMs. The overall lactate labelling fraction was also reduced, but this was owing to a sharp increase in the total levels of lactate present (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). To further investigate whether changes in mitochondrial uptake and oxidation of lactate were dependent on MCT1 and independent of its known roles on the plasma membrane, we treated isolated ACMs with saponin to selectively permeabilize the plasma membrane28 (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d). Although plasma membrane integrity was disrupted, mitochondria membrane potential was maintained and cytochrome c was not released (Extended Data Fig. 4d–g). Upon incubation with [U-13C]lactate, we observed robust oxidation in Mct1fl/fl ACMs, as evidenced by TCA cycle labelling that was attenuated in Mct1iCKO cells and upon treatment with AZD3965 (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 4h,i).

We infused awake Mct1iCKO mice with [U-13C]glucose or [U-13C]lactate to determine whether MCT1 was necessary for the oxidation of lactate in vivo. Serum glucose and lactate metabolic parameters were not different by genotype (Extended Data Fig. 5a–d). In Mct1iCKO hearts, the entry of lactate carbon into TCA metabolites was significantly reduced, whereas labelling from glucose was unchanged (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 5a,b,e–h). Of note, loss of MCT1 did not alter tissue lactate or pyruvate enrichment, indicating that the observed TCA cycle defects were not due to a loss of plasma membrane lactate transport. Oxidation of 3-hydroxybutyrate was also not affected (Extended Data Fig. 5i). To isolate the effects of MCT1 on lactate oxidation alone, we used an ex vivo perfused heart model (Langendorff) with a non-recirculating solution to prevent isotopic exchange between substrates. We cannulated hearts and perfused them with a working buffer containing the major cardiac energy substrates (glucose, lactate, pyruvate and bovine serum albumin (BSA)-conjugated fatty acids)11 (Fig. 2i). Final heart rate was unchanged between Mct1iCKO and control mice (Fig. 2j and Extended Data Fig. 5j). We traced lactate utilization by replacing the unlabelled lactate with [U-13C]lactate (Fig. 2k). Loss of MCT1 prevented nearly all lactate oxidation, but had no effect on lactate enrichment within the tissue. In a second perfusion experiment, we observed that oxidation of [U-13C]glucose was increased in Mct1iCKO hearts, presumably compensating for the loss of lactate oxidation (Fig. 2l).

Paralleling our observations in mouse samples, we detected MCT1 in purified mitochondrial preparations obtained from myocardium of human donors and patients with heart failure (Fig. 3a). To confirm the identity of MCT1 within human mitochondria, we immunoprecipitated MCT1 from purified cardiac mitochondria followed by proteomic analysis. MCT1 peptides were identified together with a high representation of mitochondrial proteins, but not plasma membrane markers, supporting the existence of a mitochondrial MCT1 fraction (Extended Data Fig. 6a–d and Supplementary Table 3). To provide additional evidence of MCT1 and LDHB localization within the mitochondria, we performed proteinase K protection assays using purified mouse and human cardiac mitochondria. In isotonic buffer, intact membranes protect the IMM, intermembrane space and matrix proteins from proteinase K, whereas outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) proteins are digested. Hypotonic buffer disrupts the OMM, exposing OMM, intermembrane space and some IMM proteins. Detergent (Triton X-100) solubilizes all membranes and denatures protein, rendering all mitochondrial proteins sensitive to proteinase K. Mitochondria from mouse myocardium or isolated cardiomyocytes subjected to these conditions displayed an MCT1 protection pattern resembling that of an IMM protein (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 6e,f). Across preparations, MCT1 was relatively resistant to proteinase K in isotonic buffer, unlike OMM proteins such as TOM20. In these preparations, we also observed a protected LDHB band that showed similar digestion patterns to citrate synthase, a matrix protein. Similar protection patterns were observed in mitochondria from a human cell line, failing human hearts and non-failing human donor hearts (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 6g,h). Samples from human hearts showed higher variability and more overall degradation due to sample handling differences including freeze–thaw cycles.

a, Immunoblots of indicated protein markers from whole heart (H), cleared cytoplasmic fraction (C) and cleared mitochondrial fraction (M) of a representative non-failing donor heart and a heart failure (failing) explant. ER, endoplasmic reticulum. b, Immunoblots of indicated protein markers from a proteinase K (PK) protection assay conducted on freshly isolated mitochondria from mouse myocardium. Representative of n = 5 experiments. Hypo, hypotonic solution; IMS, intermembrane space; Iso, isotonic solution. TX100, Triton X-100. c, Immunoblots of indicated protein markers from a proteinase K protection assay conducted on mitochondria isolated from previously frozen myocardial tissue from two independent human heart failure explants. d, Schematic of [2-2H]lactate as a tracer for lactate metabolism. e, Immunoblots of indicated proteins from MITO-Tagfl/+ myocardium and mitochondrial lysates. Anti-HA IP, anti-haemagglutinin immunoprecipitation. f, Lactate M+1 labelling fractions from myocardial tissue and mitochondria from hearts of indicated genotypes subjected to ex vivo perfusion with [2-2H]lactate. g, LDH activity assays conducted on freshly isolated cardiac mitochondria pretreated with indicated reagents. ALA, alamethicin. h, Initial LDH reaction rates from mitochondria isolated from mouse organs with and without permeabilization (calculated from n = 3 per condition). Data are mean ± 95% confidence interval. i, Oxygen consumption rates (JO2) of isolated cardiac mitochondria respiring on pyruvate from the indicated genotypes (Mct1fl/fl n = 9, Mct1iCKO n = 10, Mpc1iCKO n = 9). j, Citrate M+2 labelling fraction from isolated mouse cardiac mitochondria incubated with [U-13C]pyruvate (Mct1fl/fl n = 3, Mct1iCKO n = 3, Mpc1iCKO n = 3). k, Oxygen consumption rates of isolated mouse cardiac mitochondria respiring on lactate (Mct1fl/fl n = 10, Mct1iCKO n = 10, Mpc1iCKO n = 10). l, Citrate M+2 labelling fraction from isolated mouse cardiac mitochondria incubated with [U-13C]lactate (Mct1fl/fl n = 3, Mct1iCKO n = 3, Mpc1iCKO n = 3). m, Oxygen consumption rates of isolated mouse cardiac mitochondria respiring on lactate treated with DMSO (n = 6), MCT1 inhibitor (MCTi; 7ACC2: n = 6) or pan-LDH inhibitor (LDHi; GSK 2837808A: n = 6). n, Normalized ion counts of lactate (M+3), pyruvate (M+3) and citrate (M+2) from non-failing human donor cardiac mitochondria incubated with [U-13C]lactate (n = 3 human hearts). Data are mean ± s.e.m. unless indicated. P values from multiple comparisons-corrected (Holm–Sídák method) unpaired two-tailed t-tests (f), one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple comparison test (i–m) or two-way ANOVA (n).

We next tested whether MCT1 was required for the mitochondrial uptake of lactate using [2-2H]lactate tracing. During LDH-mediated oxidation, the deuterium at C2 in [2-2H]lactate is transferred to NAD+, generating NAD2H (Fig. 3d). The presence of 2H-lactate in the mitochondria signifies that lactate entered the organelle before conversion to pyruvate29. However, because mitochondrial isolation from a mouse heart is slow compared with global LDH activity, this approach is unsuitable for in vivo studies. To overcome this limitation, we again employed our Langendorff ex vivo heart system in which we perfused [2-2H]lactate into Mct1iCKO hearts from mice also expressing a cardiomyocyte-specific mitochondria-localized affinity tag (MITO-Tag)30 (Extended Data Fig. 7a). We developed a protocol for the rapid isolation of cardiac mitochondria and quenching of lactate metabolism using inhibitor cocktails (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 7b). In perfused hearts, heart rate and whole-heart 2H-lactate labelling were similar across genotypes (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 7c). However, in the mitochondrial fraction, 2H-lactate was absent from Mct1iCKO samples (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 7d).

Proteinase K and immunoblot assays identified LDHB within the mitochondrial matrix (Fig. 3b,c). We quantified total matrix LDH activity by performing in vitro LDH assays on purified cardiac mitochondria with and without permeabilization and proteinase K treatment (Fig. 3g). Alamethicin treatment permeabilizes both mitochondrial membranes to small molecule transit (for example, NAD+ and ATP) while retaining normal matrix protein localization31. Cardiac LDH activity was both highly dependent on permeabilization and insensitive to proteinase K treatment, consistent with matrix localization (Fig. 3g,h and Extended Data Fig. 7e). Liver and kidney mitochondrial LDH activity showed different sensitivities to permeabilization and proteinase K treatment.

After identifying MCT1 in the IMM and LDH activity in mitochondrial preparations, we purified mitochondria from Mct1fl/fl (control), Mct1iCKO and Mpc1iCKO hearts and characterized their respiration and metabolism on different substrates. Mitochondria from control and Mct1iCKO hearts respired equivalently on pyruvate, but Mpc1iCKO mitochondria had reduced oxygen consumption rates (JO2), impaired 13C-citrate production and suppressed pyruvate uptake (Fig. 3i,j and Extended Data Fig. 7f). Conversely, respiration on lactate was similar in both control and Mpc1iCKO mitochondria but was reduced in mitochondria from Mct1iCKO hearts (Fig. 3k). [U-13C]lactate import and oxidation into TCA cycle metabolites was attenuated in Mct1iCKO mitochondria but unchanged in mitochondria isolated from the hearts of mice lacking the lactate exporter MCT4 (encoded by Slc16a3)16 (Fig. 3l and Extended Data Fig. 7g–k). Mitochondria from Mct1iCKO mice showed no gross defect in mitochondrial electron transport chain complex or supercomplex assembly (Extended Data Fig. 7l). Acute treatment of mitochondria isolated from control mice with an MCT1 inhibitor (7ACC2) or a pan-LDH inhibitor (GSK 2837808A) inhibited respiration on lactate (Fig. 3m). Finally, we treated purified mitochondria from non-failing donor hearts with [U-13C]lactate and observed impaired import and oxidation to pyruvate and citrate when treated with an MCT1 inhibitor but not with an MPC inhibitor (Fig. 3n).

The oxidation of one lactate molecule within the mitochondria by LDH to produce pyruvate generates one equivalent of NADH that can transfer electrons directly into the electron transport chain. To test whether this LDH activity could generate sufficient NADH for respiration, we inhibited the TCA cycle with the pyruvate- and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase inhibitor CPI-61332. As expected, mitochondrial respiration on pyruvate was sharply reduced by CPI-613 treatment, however lactate respiration was unaltered despite M+2 citrate production from 13C-lactate being suppressed (Extended Data Fig. 7m–o). NADH levels were unchanged (Extended Data Fig. 7p). Total oxygen consumption on lactate was consistently lower than on pyruvate under minimal assay conditions (buffer, mitochondria, substrate, malate and ADP). Because lactate is converted to pyruvate by LDH, equivalent respiration would be expected if oxidation proceeded identically, suggesting that lactate oxidation may be incomplete. We hypothesized that in the absence of exogenous pyruvate, lactate oxidation may be impaired through pyruvate efflux via the MPC. Pre-treatment of ACMs with UK5099, a potent MPC inhibitor, enhanced lactate-supported respiration (Extended Data Fig. 7q,r). Collectively, these data support a model in which mitochondrial LDH-dependent lactate metabolism supports respiratory flux.

Having established that MCT1 is required for lactate oxidation, we explored whether loss of this biochemical functionality affects cardiac physiology. Mct1iCKO mice did not show evidence of structural or functional cardiac abnormalities by 1 year of age as measured by echocardiography (Extended Data Fig. 8a–i). Consistent with this, Mct1iCKO mice exhibited unchanged maximal exercise capacity over time (Extended Data Fig. 8j,k). We hypothesized that the absence of a phenotype was a consequence of the functional redundancy between MCT1 and MPC in cardiomyocytes. Therefore, we turned to a neurohormonal agonist-induced model of cardiac hypertrophy that we previously reported to decrease Mpc1 activity16. We surgically implanted mice with osmotic minipumps delivering angiotensin II and phenylephrine (ATII/PE) to induce cardiac hypertrophy (Fig. 4a). After 6 weeks, all treated mice developed cardiac hypertrophy, which was more pronounced in Mct1iCKO mice (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 9a). Body weight, heart rate, left ventricular end systolic diameter and left ventricular end diastolic diameter were not significantly different between genotypes and were only modestly affected by treatment (Extended Data Fig. 9b–e). By contrast, systolic function as measured by stroke volume was reduced in Mct1iCKO mice, leading to lower cardiac output, fractional shortening and impaired LVEF (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 9f–i). Consequently, ATII/PE-treated Mct1iCKO mice exhibited increased mortality (Fig. 4d). Similarly, loss of MCT1 accelerated the development of heart failure in mice when cardiac hypertrophy was induced by pressure overload caused by transverse aortic constriction (TAC) (Fig. 4e and Extended Data Fig. 10a–k).
